steps.overview: This step builds the shared vocabulary for every exam on the path. It covers cloud service models, the shared responsibility model, global infrastructure (regions, zones, edge), service equivalents across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and the three main pricing models. Many exam questions test these basics indirectly, for example who patches the OS, how many zones give high availability, or which purchase option fits a workload.
objectives: Classify a given service as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or serverless and state who manages each layer.
Explain the shared responsibility model and identify the customer's duties for a given service type.
Describe regions, availability zones and edge locations on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and design for zone or region failure.
Map core compute, storage, database and networking services across the three providers without looking them up.
Choose between on-demand, reserved or committed use, and spot pricing for a described workload.

concepts.explanation: IaaS gives you virtual machines, disks and networks, and you manage the OS and everything above it (EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Compute Engine). PaaS gives you a managed runtime or database, and you manage only code, data and configuration (Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, App Engine, managed SQL). SaaS is a finished application such as Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, where you manage only users, data and settings.

Serverless means no servers to provision. The service scales automatically, including to zero for many services, and you pay per request or per unit of execution time. Examples are AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions), plus serverless containers such as Cloud Run and AWS Fargate. Watch for cold starts and execution time limits when choosing it.

The provider secures the cloud itself: physical data centres, hardware, the hypervisor and the global network. The customer secures what they put in the cloud. The customer's share shrinks as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS. In every model the customer still owns their data, identities and access management, and the configuration of their resources.

A region is a separate geographic area that contains one or more isolated data-centre zones. You choose a region based on data residency rules, latency to users, service availability and price, since prices differ by region. India has AWS Mumbai (ap-south-1) and Hyderabad (ap-south-2), Azure Central India, South India and West India, and Google Cloud Mumbai (asia-south1) and Delhi (asia-south2).

A zone is one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking inside a region. Zones are linked by low-latency connections. Spreading instances across two or more zones protects against a single data-centre failure. Naming differs by provider: AWS uses us-east-1a, Azure uses zones 1, 2 and 3, and Google Cloud uses us-central1-a.

Edge sites are smaller sites in many more cities than regions. They serve CDN caching, DNS and the entry point for global load balancing. AWS uses them for CloudFront and Route 53, and also offers Local Zones and Wavelength for low-latency compute. Azure uses edge points of presence for Front Door and Azure CDN. Google Cloud uses its edge PoPs for Cloud CDN and the global external Application Load Balancer.

Many Azure regions are paired with another region in the same geography, such as Central India with South India. Pairs give sequential platform updates, a priority order for recovery, and are the default replication target for geo-redundant storage (GRS). Some newer regions have no pair, so do not assume every region has one.

An AWS VPC is regional, and each subnet sits in exactly one AZ. An Azure VNet is regional, and its subnets can span all zones in that region. A Google Cloud VPC network is global, and its subnets are regional. As a result, one Google Cloud VPC can span many regions without peering, which is a frequent exam point.

On-demand means you pay per second or hour with no commitment; it suits unknown or short workloads. Reserved or committed use means a 1- or 3-year commitment for a large discount on steady workloads: AWS Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, Azure Reservations and Azure savings plan for compute, and Google Cloud committed use discounts. Spot uses spare capacity at a deep discount, but the provider can reclaim it at short notice, so it suits fault-tolerant, stateless or batch jobs.

keyFacts: AWS states every Region has a minimum of three physically separate Availability Zones. Most Azure zone-enabled regions and most Google Cloud regions also have three or more zones.
Customer always owns data, identities, access policies and resource configuration, whatever the service model. Under IaaS the customer also patches the guest OS.
Interruption notice for spot capacity: AWS Spot gives a 2-minute warning. Azure Spot VMs and Google Cloud Spot VMs give about 30 seconds.
Commitment terms are 1 year or 3 years on all three clouds. The 3-year term with more upfront payment gives the biggest discount.
Google Cloud also gives automatic sustained use discounts on some machine series when a VM runs for a large part of the month. No commitment is needed.
Object storage is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability: Amazon S3, Azure LRS (ZRS is designed for 12 nines) and Google Cloud Storage.
Core mapping: EC2 / Azure Virtual Machines / Compute Engine. S3 / Blob Storage / Cloud Storage. EBS / Managed Disks / Persistent Disk or Hyperdisk. RDS / Azure SQL Database / Cloud SQL.
For high availability within one region, spread instances across at least 2 zones behind a load balancer. For disaster recovery, replicate data to a second region.

Kubernetes    | Amazon EKS               | Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) | Google Kubernetes Engine

App platform  | Elastic Beanstalk        | Azure App Service              | App Engine / Cloud Run

Relational DB | Amazon RDS / Aurora      | Azure SQL Database             | Cloud SQL / AlloyDB
Global SQL    | Aurora DSQL              | Azure Cosmos DB (multi-region) | Cloud Spanner
NoSQL         | Amazon DynamoDB          | Azure Cosmos DB                | Firestore / Bigtable
Cache         | Amazon ElastiCache       | Azure Cache for Redis          | Memorystore
Data warehouse| Amazon Redshift          | Microsoft Fabric / Synapse     | BigQuery
Private net   | Amazon VPC (regional)    | Virtual Network (regional)     | VPC network (global)
Load balancer | Elastic Load Balancing   | Load Balancer / App Gateway    | Cloud Load Balancing
DNS           | Amazon Route 53          | Azure DNS                      | Cloud DNS
CDN           | Amazon CloudFront        | Azure Front Door               | Cloud CDN
Private link  | AWS Direct Connect       | ExpressRoute                   | Cloud Interconnect
VPN           | AWS Site-to-Site VPN     | VPN Gateway                    | Cloud VPN
Identity      | AWS IAM                  | Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC      | Cloud IAM
Keys          | AWS KMS                  | Azure Key Vault                | Cloud KMS
Monitoring    | Amazon CloudWatch        | Azure Monitor                  | Cloud Monitoring
IaC (native)  | AWS CloudFormation       | ARM / Bicep                    | Infrastructure Manager (Terraform)
Cost tool     | AWS Cost Explorer        | Cost Management + Billing      | Cloud Billing reports

pitfalls: Assuming the provider patches your VM's operating system. Under IaaS that is your job. With managed PaaS services such as RDS or Cloud SQL, the provider patches the OS and engine.
Treating a multi-AZ deployment as disaster recovery. Zones protect against a data-centre failure, not a full region outage. Disaster recovery needs a second region.
Running stateful or must-not-stop workloads on spot or preemptible capacity. Use spot only for interruptible, checkpointed or stateless jobs.
Mixing up network scope: a Google Cloud VPC is global, AWS and Azure networks are regional, and an AWS subnet cannot span AZs.
Buying 3-year reservations for a workload that is still changing in size. Use on-demand first, measure the steady baseline, then commit only to that baseline.
Confusing edge locations with regions. You cannot launch normal EC2 instances or most services at a CloudFront edge location.

steps.detail: Cover the steady baseline with a 1- or 3-year commitment, peaks with on-demand, and interruptible batch work with spot.
