files.code:
# log-archive-7y

Goal: store 200 TB of logs for 7 years (2557 days) at the lowest cost.
The design must still prove that nothing is deleted early.

## Design
| Age (days) | S3 class | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 0-30 | STANDARD | Engineers read fresh logs often |
| 30-180 | GLACIER_IR | Millisecond reads for audits. Minimum storage is 90 days, and 150 days here meets it |
| 180-2557 | DEEP_ARCHIVE | Cheapest class. Reads take hours, and the 180-day minimum is easily met |
| 2558+ | expired | Lifecycle rule deletes the object after the lock ends |

- Object Lock sets a default retention of 2557 days. This is WORM storage.
- GOVERNANCE mode is the lab default. Users with a special permission can bypass it.
- Set `lock_mode=COMPLIANCE` for real audits. In COMPLIANCE mode no one can delete the data, including the root user, and you also cannot shorten the retention.
- Batch logs into large objects (for example 64 MB gzip files).
  - Each transition is charged per request.
  - Deep Archive adds about 40 KB of metadata overhead per object.
  - By default, lifecycle rules skip objects smaller than 128 KB.
- Check the checkpoint with tools/verify_retention.py. A delete must fail and the lifecycle rules must be listed.

## Exam notes
- Minimum storage durations:
  - S3: Standard-IA 30 days, Glacier IR 90 days, Glacier Flexible 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days.
  - GCS: Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, Archive 365 days.
  - Azure: Cool 30 days, Cold 90 days, Archive 180 days.
- Equivalent features on other clouds:
  - Azure: lifecycle management policy plus immutable blob storage (a locked time-based retention policy).
  - Google Cloud: Object Lifecycle Management plus Bucket Lock (a locked retention policy).
- Moving 200 TB:
  - Online: DataSync, Storage Transfer Service, AzCopy.
  - Offline: AWS Snow Family, Azure Data Box, Google Transfer Appliance.
  - Choose offline when the link is too slow. Device availability changes, so check the current docs.
- Data residency: keep `region` in the required country (for example ap-south-1 Mumbai).
- Do not replicate to other regions without approval.

## Clean up
In GOVERNANCE mode, delete the test objects with a bypass, then run `terraform destroy`.
In COMPLIANCE mode the data cannot be removed until its lock expires.

"""Steady-state storage per tier for the 7-year log design.
Prices are NOT hard-coded: copy prices.template.json and fill in current values."""
import argparse, json, sys

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--total-tb", type=float, default=200)      # data held at steady state
p.add_argument("--retention-days", type=int, default=2557)
p.add_argument("--hot-days", type=int, default=30)         # matches days_to_glacier_ir
p.add_argument("--deep-days", type=int, default=180)       # matches days_to_deep_archive
p.add_argument("--avg-object-mb", type=float, default=64)
p.add_argument("--prices", help="JSON file with USD per GB-month and per 1000 transitions")
a = p.parse_args()

total_gb = a.total_tb * 1024
daily_gb = total_gb / a.retention_days                    # steady ingest rate
tiers = {
    "STANDARD": daily_gb * a.hot_days,
    "GLACIER_IR": daily_gb * (a.deep_days - a.hot_days),
    "DEEP_ARCHIVE": daily_gb * (a.retention_days - a.deep_days),
}
objects_per_month = daily_gb * 30 * 1024 / a.avg_object_mb
# Deep Archive keeps ~40 KB metadata per object (32 KB billed at archive rate, 8 KB at Standard)
da_objects = tiers["DEEP_ARCHIVE"] * 1024 / a.avg_object_mb
tiers["DEEP_ARCHIVE"] += da_objects * 32 / 1024 / 1024
tiers["STANDARD"] += da_objects * 8 / 1024 / 1024

print(f"Daily ingest: {daily_gb:,.1f} GB, objects/month: {objects_per_month:,.0f}")
for name, gb in tiers.items():
    print(f"{name:13s} {gb:12,.0f} GB ({gb / total_gb:6.1%})")

if not a.prices:
    sys.exit("Add --prices tools/prices.json to see monthly cost.")
prices = json.load(open(a.prices))
if any(v is None for v in prices.values()):
    sys.exit("Fill every null value in the prices file from the official pricing page.")

storage = sum(gb * prices[name] for name, gb in tiers.items())
transitions = objects_per_month / 1000 * (
    prices["transition_per_1000_GLACIER_IR"] + prices["transition_per_1000_DEEP_ARCHIVE"])
baseline = total_gb * prices["STANDARD"]                  # naive: keep everything in Standard
print(f"Tiered design: ${storage + transitions:,.0f}/month (transitions ${transitions:,.0f})")
print(f"All STANDARD:  ${baseline:,.0f}/month")
print(f"Saving:        {1 - (storage + transitions) / baseline:.0%}")

{
  "_note": "Copy to prices.json. Fill USD values for your region from https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/",
  "STANDARD": null,
  "GLACIER_IR": null,
  "DEEP_ARCHIVE": null,
  "transition_per_1000_GLACIER_IR": null,
  "transition_per_1000_DEEP_ARCHIVE": null
}

"""Checkpoint: prove the WORM retention rule and lifecycle tiers are active."""
import os, time
import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

bucket = os.environ["BUCKET_NAME"]                        # from terraform output bucket_name
s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-south-1"))

# 1. Bucket-level Object Lock default
lock = s3.get_object_lock_configuration(Bucket=bucket)["ObjectLockConfiguration"]
print("Default retention:", lock["Rule"]["DefaultRetention"])

# 2. Upload a test log; default retention is applied automatically.
# Uploads to Object Lock buckets need an integrity checksum; recent boto3 adds one by default.
key = f"logs/verify-{int(time.time())}.log"
put = s3.put_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key, Body=b"checkpoint test line\n")
head = s3.head_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)
print("Object lock mode:", head.get("ObjectLockMode"))
print("Retain until:   ", head.get("ObjectLockRetainUntilDate"))

# 3. Try to delete the locked version; it must be refused
try:
    s3.delete_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key, VersionId=put["VersionId"])
    print("FAIL: locked version was deleted")
except ClientError as e:
    print("PASS: delete refused ->", e.response["Error"]["Code"])

# 4. Show the lifecycle tiers that keep cost lowest
rules = s3.get_bucket_lifecycle_configuration(Bucket=bucket)["Rules"]
for r in rules:
    steps = [f"{t['Days']}d->{t['StorageClass']}" for t in r.get("Transitions", [])]
    print(r["ID"], steps, "expire:", r.get("Expiration"))

print("Lab clean-up (GOVERNANCE only): delete with BypassGovernanceRetention=True.")

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the storage and database design objectives on every exam in the path. SAA-C03 and SAP-C02 test cost-optimised and resilient storage, DB and migration choices. AZ-104 tests storage account configuration, and AZ-305 tests data storage design. ACE tests buckets, lifecycle and DB setup, and PCA tests choices in case studies. Questions are mostly scenarios: you get access pattern, retrieval time, retention, budget and residency constraints, and you pick the cheapest option that meets all of them.

compare.a: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval / Azure Cold / any Google Cloud class
compare.b: S3 Glacier Deep Archive / Azure Archive
compare.difference: The first group returns data in milliseconds. Deep Archive and Azure Archive need a restore or rehydration that takes hours, but they are the cheapest per GB.
compare.chooseA: Pick these when data is rarely read but must be available immediately when someone asks, such as audit queries or quarterly reports.
compare.chooseB: Pick these when data is kept only for compliance and a wait of 12–48 hours, or about 15 hours for Azure rehydration, is acceptable.

compare.b: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode (or a locked Azure time-based immutable policy / locked GCS Bucket Lock)
compare.difference: In Governance mode, users with a special permission can bypass the lock. In Compliance mode, no one can shorten or remove the retention, not even the root user.
compare.chooseA: Pick Governance when you want protection against accidental deletion but admins must still be able to override.
compare.chooseB: Pick Compliance or a locked policy when a regulator requires WORM storage and the question says no user, including administrators, can delete the data.

compare.a: Read replicas (Aurora Replicas, Cloud SQL / Azure SQL read replicas)
compare.b: In-memory cache (ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis / Azure Managed Redis, Memorystore)
compare.difference: Replicas are full database copies. They can serve any SQL query and can be promoted for DR. A cache stores hot key-value results for sub-millisecond reads, but the application must manage cache misses and staleness.
compare.chooseA: Pick replicas for read-heavy reporting or analytics queries, or when a standby copy for failover is also needed.
compare.chooseB: Pick a cache for repeated identical reads such as sessions, leaderboards or product pages, when the goal is lowest latency and less load on the DB.

compare.b: Azure Cosmos DB
compare.difference: Spanner is a relational database with SQL and globally strongly consistent transactions. Cosmos DB is a multi-model NoSQL database with five tunable consistency levels and multi-region writes.
compare.chooseA: Pick Spanner for a global relational OLTP workload that needs strong consistency and horizontal write scale, for example financial ledgers or inventory.
compare.chooseB: Pick Cosmos DB for globally distributed NoSQL apps that need low-latency local reads and writes and can tune consistency per request.

compare.a: Online transfer (AWS DataSync, Azure AzCopy / Storage Mover, Google Storage Transfer Service)
compare.b: Offline device (AWS Snowball Edge, Azure Data Box, Google Transfer Appliance)
compare.difference: Online transfer uses your network and also handles ongoing sync. An offline device is shipped physically, which avoids slow or shared links for large one-time bulk moves.
compare.chooseA: Pick online when bandwidth can finish the job in days, or when data changes continuously and must keep syncing.
compare.chooseB: Pick offline when the calculated transfer time is weeks, the link is shared with production, or connectivity is poor.

cues.cue: Unknown or changing access patterns, no retrieval fees wanted
cues.pick: S3 Intelligent-Tiering (AWS) or GCS Autoclass (Google)
cues.why: They move objects between tiers automatically based on access, so you do not need to guess lifecycle rules.

cues.cue: Must not be deleted by anyone, including root or administrators, for N years
cues.pick: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode, a locked Azure immutable policy, or a locked GCS Bucket Lock retention policy
cues.why: Only a locked WORM control enforces retention; lifecycle expiration only deletes data.

cues.cue: Shared POSIX file system for many Linux instances
cues.pick: Amazon EFS / Azure Files (NFS) / Google Filestore
cues.why: Block volumes such as EBS or Persistent Disk are normally attached to one instance, so shared access needs file storage.

cues.cue: Windows SMB shares with Active Directory integration
cues.pick: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server or Azure Files
cues.why: These provide native SMB with AD-based permissions.

cues.cue: Migrate a database with minimal downtime
cues.pick: Database migration service (AWS DMS, Azure Database Migration Service, Google Database Migration Service) with ongoing replication / CDC
cues.why: Change data capture keeps the target in sync until a short cutover.

cues.cue: Heterogeneous migration, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL
cues.pick: Schema conversion first (AWS SCT or DMS Schema Conversion), then DMS for the data
cues.why: DMS moves data, but a schema conversion step is needed to translate schema and code between engines.

cues.cue: Write throughput is the bottleneck
cues.pick: Sharding or a distributed database (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Spanner)
cues.why: Replicas and caches scale reads only; writes need horizontal partitioning.

cues.cue: Data must stay in one country or region
cues.pick: Single-region storage and replicas only; check GRS pairs, multi-region buckets, global tables and cross-region backups
cues.why: Default geo-redundancy or global features can copy data outside the allowed boundary.

scenario.situation: A company ingests about 200 TB of application logs per year in S3 as millions of small JSON files. Security teams query the last 30 days often. Older logs are read only during rare audits, and a 48-hour wait for those is acceptable. Regulation requires seven-year retention, and no one, including administrators, may delete logs early. Which design meets the requirement at the lowest cost?
reasoning: Remove any option that relies only on a lifecycle expiration rule or IAM deny policies for retention. Expiration does not prevent early deletion, and admins can change IAM. The design needs Object Lock in Compliance mode, which requires versioning, with a seven-year retention period.

Remove options that archive millions of tiny files as they are. Per-object transition requests and archive metadata overhead make this costly. Compress and batch logs into large objects first, for example with Firehose buffering or a daily aggregation job.
A 48-hour retrieval tolerance allows the cheapest tier. That rules out Glacier Instant Retrieval and Standard-IA for older data, and points to Glacier Deep Archive with Bulk retrieval.

Keep hot data in S3 Standard for the 30-day query window. Then transition directly to Deep Archive and skip intermediate tiers that add transition requests and minimum-duration charges. Data stays well past the 180-day minimum, so there is no early-deletion fee.
Set expiration just after 2,557 days so storage does not grow forever. Object Lock blocks any deletion before that date.
scenario.answer: Batch and compress the logs, store them in S3 Standard for 30 days, then use a lifecycle rule to move them to Glacier Deep Archive and expire them at about 2,557 days. Protect the bucket with Object Lock Compliance mode and seven-year retention. This is the cheapest tier that meets the retrieval time, and the only design that truly enforces retention.

memoryAids: Minimum storage days per provider: AWS '30-90-90-180' (IA, Instant, Flexible, Deep). Azure '30-90-180' (Cool, Cold, Archive). Google '30-90-365' (Nearline, Coldline, Archive). Google's Archive is the 'whole year' outlier.
Cosmos DB consistency, strongest to weakest: 'Strong Bosses Seldom Consult Everyone' = Strong, Bounded staleness, Session (default), Consistent prefix, Eventual.
'Cache for speed, Replica for reads, Shard for writes' to pick the scaling fix.
cheatSheet: Choose the tier by required retrieval time first, then by price. Hours acceptable means Deep Archive or Azure Archive; instant needed means Glacier Instant Retrieval, Azure Cold or any GCS class.
An S3 object must stay in Standard for at least 30 days before lifecycle can move it to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA. Direct transitions to Glacier classes have no such wait.
One Zone-IA is only for data you can recreate. It is never the answer for compliance or must-survive-AZ-loss data.
Retention = WORM lock (Object Lock Compliance, locked immutable policy, locked Bucket Lock). Cleanup = lifecycle expiration. Exams often need both.
Locking a GCS retention policy or an Azure time-based immutable policy cannot be undone, so set the period carefully.
Azure lifecycle management can tier blobs by last access time if access tracking is enabled. Archive rehydration can use high priority for faster, costlier reads.
Aurora: storage replicated six ways across three AZs; replicas share storage, so lag is low and failover is fast. Aurora Global Database is for cross-region DR and low-latency reads.
Spanner = global relational with strong consistency. Cosmos DB = global NoSQL with tunable consistency. DynamoDB global tables = multi-region active-active NoSQL.
Transfer maths: about 1 TB per 2.3 hours at a fully used 1 Gbps. If the result is more than about a week or the link is shared, ship a device.
Ongoing sync or hybrid access means online tools (DataSync, Storage Transfer Service, AzCopy). A one-time bulk move over a weak link means Snowball Edge, Data Box or Transfer Appliance.
Minimal-downtime DB migration = DMS full load + CDC. Different engines = schema conversion first.
Residency trap: GRS/RA-GRS, multi-region buckets, global tables and cross-region backup copies all move data across regions.
selfCheck: I can pick the cheapest storage class on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud for a given retrieval time and minimum-duration rule, and explain the early-deletion charge.
I can write a lifecycle policy for long-term logs that batches small files, transitions directly to the right archive tier and expires at about 2,557 days.
I can explain why lifecycle expiration is not retention compliance, and choose between Object Lock Governance and Compliance, Azure immutable policies and GCS Bucket Lock.
I can decide between a cache, read replicas and a distributed database (Aurora, Cosmos DB, Spanner, DynamoDB) from the bottleneck described.
I can estimate transfer time from data size and bandwidth and justify online vs offline transfer, plus DMS with CDC for minimal downtime.
I can spot replication, backup or global features in a design that would break a data residency requirement.

objective.question: A company stores 200 TB of application logs in Amazon S3. Logs are queried often for the first 30 days and almost never afterwards. Auditors may ask for old logs, and a 48-hour retrieval time is acceptable. Logs must be kept for seven years and then removed. Which lifecycle design gives the lowest storage cost?
options: Keep logs in S3 Standard for 30 days, transition them to S3 Standard-IA, and expire them at about 2,557 days
Keep logs in S3 Standard for seven years and enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the bucket at year five
Transition logs to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval on day 1 and expire them at 365 days
Keep logs in S3 Standard for 30 days, transition them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and expire them at about 2,557 days
objective.explanation: Deep Archive is the cheapest S3 class, and its Bulk retrieval within 48 hours meets the audit need. Expiring at about 2,557 days matches seven years. Standard-IA and long-term Standard cost far more per GB, and expiring at 365 days breaks the retention rule.

objective.question: An engineer moves an object to S3 Glacier Deep Archive with a lifecycle rule. A second rule deletes the same object 60 days later. How will storage for that object be billed?
options: For 90 days, the Glacier minimum
For 180 days, because Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage duration
No storage charge, because lifecycle deletions are free
Only for the 60 days the object existed
objective.explanation: Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage duration. An object deleted early is charged a pro-rated fee for the remaining days. The 90-day minimum applies to Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval, not to Deep Archive.

objective.question: A team's logging agent writes millions of 20 KB log files a day to S3. Their lifecycle rule moves objects to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days, but most objects never move and costs stay high. What is the best fix?
options: Aggregate and compress the small files into larger objects, for example hourly archives, before they are transitioned
Change the target class to S3 Standard-IA, which has no minimum object size
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Enable S3 Versioning so lifecycle rules can see the small objects
objective.explanation: By default, S3 lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB. Archived objects also carry about 40 KB of metadata overhead each, so batching small files into larger objects is the right fix. Standard-IA also bills a 128 KB minimum object size, and versioning or Transfer Acceleration does not fix this problem.

objective.question: An Azure administrator must give an auditor a blob that is stored in the Archive tier. What must happen first?
options: The storage account must be converted from LRS to GRS
The blob must be copied to Azure Files before it can be read
The blob must be rehydrated to an online tier such as Hot, Cool or Cold, which can take up to about 15 hours at standard priority
Nothing; Archive blobs can be read directly at a higher per-GB cost
objective.explanation: The Azure Archive tier is offline, so a blob must be rehydrated to an online tier before anyone can read it. At standard priority this can take up to about 15 hours. Changing redundancy or copying to Azure Files does not make an archived blob readable.

objective.question: Which statement about the Google Cloud Storage Archive class is correct?
options: It has a 90-day minimum storage duration
It is available only in single-region locations
It gives millisecond access but has a 365-day minimum storage duration and charges retrieval fees
Data must be restored for several hours before it can be read
objective.explanation: All Cloud Storage classes, including Archive, give millisecond access. Archive has a 365-day minimum storage duration and the highest retrieval fees. A 90-day minimum applies to Coldline, and Archive is available in region, dual-region and multi-region locations.

objective.question: A financial regulator requires that trade logs in S3 cannot be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, for seven years. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a seven-year retention period
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period
A bucket policy that denies s3:DeleteObject to all IAM users
An S3 lifecycle expiration rule set to 2,557 days
objective.explanation: Compliance mode prevents any user, including root, from deleting or shortening the retention of a locked object version until the retention period ends. Governance mode can be bypassed by users who have special permissions. A bucket policy can be changed by an administrator, and a lifecycle rule only controls when deletion happens, not whether it is prevented.

objective.question: A company must move 500 TB of archive data from its data centre to the cloud within three weeks. Its 1 Gbps internet link is shared with production traffic. What should the architect recommend?
options: Upgrade the link to 2 Gbps and transfer online
Use an offline transfer device such as AWS Snowball, Azure Data Box or Google Transfer Appliance
Use a database migration service with change data capture
Use an online transfer tool over the existing link, because 500 TB will finish in about five days
objective.explanation: 100 TB takes about 9–10 days on a fully used 1 Gbps link, so 500 TB would take about 45–50 days, or longer on a shared link. Even at 2 Gbps it would take more than three weeks. An offline device is the right choice, and database migration services are built for databases, not bulk file archives.

objective.question: A global payments platform needs a relational database with SQL support, strong consistency across continents and horizontal scaling of writes. It also needs a 99.999% availability SLA. Which service fits best?
options: Cloud Spanner with a multi-region instance configuration
Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with cross-region read replicas
Azure Cache for Redis in front of Azure SQL Database
Amazon Aurora with 15 Aurora Replicas
objective.explanation: Spanner is a globally distributed relational database. It scales writes horizontally, keeps strong consistency, and multi-region instances carry a 99.999% SLA. Read replicas and caches scale reads only, while writes still go to a single primary.

objective.question: Twenty Linux EC2 instances in several Availability Zones must read and write the same set of files at the same time using standard file system semantics. Which storage type should be used?
options: Amazon EFS, a managed NFS file system
EC2 instance store volumes
Amazon S3 mounted as a block device
Amazon EBS gp3 volumes, one per instance
objective.explanation: EFS is shared file storage that many Linux instances across AZs can mount at the same time over NFS. EBS and instance store are block storage tied to single instances in one AZ. S3 is object storage and is not a block device.

objective.question: An engineer applies this S3 lifecycle configuration to a log bucket. What happens?
options: The configuration is accepted, and objects move to Standard-IA after 15 days with no extra charge
The configuration is accepted, but objects are billed for 15 extra days of Standard-IA because of its minimum storage duration
The configuration is rejected, because a single rule cannot transition objects to both Standard-IA and Glacier Deep Archive
The configuration is rejected, because S3 requires objects to stay at least 30 days in their original class before a lifecycle transition to Standard-IA
objective.explanation: S3 lifecycle rules cannot transition objects to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA until they are at least 30 days old, so the PUT fails validation. One rule may contain several transitions, so that distractor is wrong, and the configuration is never applied, so no billing happens.

objective.question: A storage account has the lifecycle policy shown below and was saved two weeks ago. Many blobs in the applogs container have not been read for over 60 days, but none have moved to the Cool tier. What is the most likely cause?
options: The policy must use daysAfterCreationGreaterThan, because modification time is not supported
Lifecycle management only runs on premium block blob storage accounts
Last access time tracking is not enabled on the storage account, so the access-based condition cannot be evaluated
Lifecycle policies cannot move block blobs to the Cool tier, only to Archive
objective.explanation: Conditions based on daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan depend on last access time tracking, which must be turned on for the account. Lifecycle policies do support Cool and Archive for block blobs on standard general-purpose v2 accounts, and modification-time conditions are valid.

objective.question: A compliance team runs these commands on a Cloud Storage bucket that holds audit logs. Which statement describes the result?

code.code:
gcloud storage buckets update gs://acme-audit-logs --retention-period=7y
gcloud storage buckets update gs://acme-audit-logs --lock-retention-period

options: The retention period can now be increased but not reduced or removed, and objects cannot be deleted or replaced until they are seven years old
Only new objects are protected; objects already in the bucket can still be deleted by a storage admin
Objects move to the Archive class after seven years, and the lock prevents any class change before then
Objects are deleted automatically after seven years, and the lock can be removed by a project owner
objective.explanation: Locking a bucket retention policy (Bucket Lock) is permanent. The period can be extended but never shortened or removed, and every object, including existing ones, is protected until it reaches the retention age. A retention policy does not delete or re-tier objects by itself; you add a lifecycle rule for that.

objective.question: An Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL container stores order events with partition key /orderDate and has 50,000 RU/s provisioned. The application receives many HTTP 429 errors during the day, yet total RU consumption across the container stays near 20%. What is the best long-term fix?
options: Change the default consistency level from Session to Eventual to reduce RU cost
Add more read regions to spread the write load
Create a new container with a high-cardinality partition key such as /customerId, and migrate the data
Increase provisioned throughput to 200,000 RU/s
objective.explanation: All of today's writes land on one logical partition (today's date), so that physical partition is throttled while the rest sit idle. That is a hot partition. The partition key cannot be changed in place, so you move the data to a container with a well-distributed key. More RU/s or extra regions do not fix the skew, and weaker consistency only lowers read cost.

objective.question: A company runs a MySQL-compatible Amazon Aurora cluster in eu-west-1. It needs disaster recovery in another Region with an RPO measured in seconds and an RTO of a few minutes. It also wants low-latency reads for users near the second Region. Which solution meets these needs with the least operational effort?
options: Create an Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in the second Region, and promote it during a disaster
Enable Multi-AZ on the Aurora cluster, and add Aurora Replicas in three Availability Zones
Run an AWS DMS task with ongoing replication into a separate Aurora cluster in the second Region
Copy automated snapshots to the second Region every hour, and restore them during a disaster
objective.explanation: Aurora Global Database uses storage-level replication, typically with under a second of lag. Its secondary clusters serve local reads and can be promoted in minutes. Hourly snapshots give an RPO of up to an hour, DMS works but adds tasks to run and monitor, and Multi-AZ protects only within one Region.

objective.question: An engineer tries to save this S3 lifecycle configuration on a log bucket, but S3 rejects it. What is the cause?
options: Objects must be at least 30 days old before a lifecycle rule can move them to STANDARD_IA.
The Expiration value must be a multiple of 365 days.
DEEP_ARCHIVE transitions require at least 180 days in STANDARD_IA first.
Lifecycle rules cannot transition objects to STANDARD_IA and DEEP_ARCHIVE in the same rule.
objective.explanation: S3 needs objects to be at least 30 days old before a lifecycle transition to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA, so Days: 15 is rejected. One rule can hold several transitions. Expiration can be any number of days. The 180-day figure is the Deep Archive minimum storage duration, not a rule about earlier tiers.

objective.question: An Azure storage account holds compliance reports. Each report is read only two or three times a year, but it must open immediately when requested. Reports are kept for two years. Which access tier gives the lowest total cost?
options: Cool
Cold
Archive
Hot
objective.explanation: The Cold tier is an online tier with millisecond access. It has lower storage cost than Cool and a 90-day minimum, which the two-year retention easily meets. Archive is offline and needs rehydration that takes hours, so it fails the immediate-read rule. Hot and Cool cost more to store data that is rarely read.

objective.question: An architect is migrating an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with AWS DMS. What is the correct order of steps?
options: Convert schema with DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT → create replication instance → create and test source and target endpoints → run a full load plus CDC task → validate data, then cut over
Create and test endpoints → cut over the application → run full load → convert schema
Create replication instance → run full load task → convert schema → enable CDC → cut over
Create DMS task → create endpoints → convert schema → create replication instance → cut over
objective.explanation: In a heterogeneous migration, DMS does not convert code objects, so you convert the schema first. Then you create the replication instance and the endpoints, test the connections, and run full load with CDC. You cut over only after validation. The other orders either load data before the target schema exists or cut over before the data is in place.

objective.question: A web app writes a user's profile change to an Aurora MySQL cluster through the writer endpoint. It then reloads the page by reading from the reader endpoint. Sometimes the user briefly sees the old value. What is the cause and the best fix?
options: Aurora Replicas share the cluster storage volume but can still lag slightly behind the writer. Send read-after-write queries for that session to the writer endpoint.
The reader endpoint caches query results. Disable the query cache on the cluster.
The writer commits asynchronously to storage. Enable synchronous commit on the writer.
Aurora Replicas use binlog replication to separate storage volumes. Switch to Multi-AZ DB instances.
objective.explanation: Aurora Replicas read from the shared storage volume, but their in-memory pages are updated asynchronously, so there is a small replica lag. A user who needs to read their own write should read from the writer endpoint. Aurora writes need a storage quorum before they commit, so they are not asynchronous. Replicas do not use binlogs to separate volumes.

objective.question: An Indian fintech uses a DynamoDB global table with replicas in ap-south-1 (Mumbai) and ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) for disaster recovery. A new rule says customer personal data must stay in India. AWS Backup also copies backups to Singapore. What should the architect do?
options: Replace the Singapore replica with one in ap-south-2 (Hyderabad), and change AWS Backup copy rules to keep copies in Indian Regions.
Turn on DynamoDB point-in-time recovery and delete the backup copy rules.
Use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in Mumbai so that reads never reach Singapore.
Keep the Singapore replica but enable encryption with a customer managed KMS key.
objective.explanation: Residency depends on where every copy of the data sits, including replicas and backups. Moving the replica to Hyderabad keeps multi-Region DR inside India, and fixing the backup copy destination closes the second leak. Encryption, PITR alone or a cache still leave data stored in Singapore, or remove DR without fixing the cause.

objective.question: A team wants an Azure Cosmos DB account with write regions in Central India and South India, and Strong consistency for every read. What will happen?
options: It works, but write latency doubles because of synchronous replication.
Strong consistency is only available in the Cosmos DB for MongoDB API.
Strong consistency cannot be used on an account with multiple write regions. They must use a single write region for Strong, or accept a weaker level such as Session.
It works. Strong consistency is the default for multi-region write accounts.
objective.explanation: Cosmos DB does not support Strong consistency on accounts with multiple write regions. You either keep one write region to get Strong, or you choose a weaker level with multi-region writes. Session is the default level, not Strong, and Strong is not limited to the MongoDB API.

objective.question: A company must copy 50 TB from an Amazon S3 bucket to Cloud Storage. After that, it must sync new objects every night, with no servers to manage. Which Google Cloud option fits best?
options: BigQuery Data Transfer Service
A Compute Engine VM running gcloud storage rsync from cron
Storage Transfer Service with an S3 source and a daily schedule
Transfer Appliance
objective.explanation: Storage Transfer Service is a managed service. It supports Amazon S3 as a source, runs scheduled incremental transfers and needs no infrastructure. Transfer Appliance is for offline transfer from your own premises. BigQuery Data Transfer Service loads data into BigQuery, not Cloud Storage. A cron VM works but adds servers to manage.

objective.question: A set of Windows Server application servers on EC2 needs a shared SMB file share. Access must be controlled with Active Directory users and NTFS ACLs. Which storage should the architect choose?
options: EBS io2 volumes with Multi-Attach
Amazon S3 mounted with Mountpoint for Amazon S3
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EFS
objective.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed SMB shares with Active Directory integration and NTFS ACLs. EFS is NFS-based and aimed at Linux. EBS Multi-Attach is block storage, not an SMB share, and it needs a cluster-aware file system. Mountpoint for S3 is not an SMB file system with ACLs.

objective.question: A Cloud Spanner table receives about 100,000 log inserts per second, but throughput stays far below what the node count should allow. What is the most likely problem?
options: allow_commit_timestamp makes every write a cross-region transaction.
Spanner needs a secondary index on EventTime before it can spread writes.
The primary key starts with a monotonically increasing timestamp, so all new rows land in the same split and create a hotspot. Lead with a well-distributed key such as a UUIDv4 or a hash shard.
STRING(MAX) columns cannot be written at high rates.
objective.explanation: Spanner splits data by primary-key range. A leading timestamp key sends every insert to the end of the key space, which is one split on one server. A distributed leading key, such as a UUIDv4, a hash prefix or a bit-reversed sequence, spreads the writes. A secondary index on the timestamp would have the same hotspot problem.

objective.question: An Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance runs at 95% CPU. About 90% of its statements are INSERT and UPDATE. Users report slow checkouts. What is the best immediate action?
options: Send part of the traffic to the Multi-AZ standby instance.
Scale the DB instance up to a larger instance class, then plan write scaling such as sharding or a different engine if growth continues.
Put ElastiCache for Redis in front of the database.
Add three read replicas and spread traffic across them.
objective.explanation: The bottleneck is writes, and read replicas or a cache only offload reads. In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby does not serve traffic. Scaling the writer up fixes the problem now, and sharding or a write-scalable database is the longer-term answer.

subjective.question: Design storage tiers and a lifecycle policy for 200 TB of logs that must be kept for seven years at the lowest cost. Explain your choices.
subjective.answer: First I confirm the access pattern. Usually logs are queried for 30 days, rarely after that, and a retrieval time of one to two days is acceptable for audits. On AWS, I would land logs in S3 Standard. A pipeline batches and compresses small files into large objects, for example hourly gzip or Parquet files, because objects under 128 KB do not transition by default and each archived object adds about 40 KB of overhead. After 30 days, a lifecycle rule moves objects to Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest class. Its 180-day minimum is no problem because we keep the data for years. Expiration is set at about 2,557 days, or just after, to match seven years including leap days. If deletion must be prevented, I add Object Lock in compliance mode. On Azure, the equivalent is Hot then Archive with an immutability policy. On Google Cloud, it is Standard then Archive with Bucket Lock.
keyPoints: Confirm the access pattern and retrieval SLA before choosing tiers
Batch and compress small log files before archiving
Transition to the coldest tier whose minimum duration and retrieval time fit
Expire at about 2,557 days and add WORM if deletion must be blocked
Map the design to Azure and Google Cloud equivalents

subjective.question: Explain the difference between object, block and file storage, with a cloud example and a typical use for each.
subjective.answer: Block storage gives a raw volume split into blocks that one server formats with a file system. Examples are Amazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks and Google Persistent Disk. It offers low latency and suits boot disks and databases, but a volume is usually attached to one VM in one zone. File storage gives a shared, hierarchical file system over protocols such as NFS or SMB. Examples are Amazon EFS or FSx, Azure Files and Google Filestore. Many servers can mount it at once, so it suits shared content, home directories and lift-and-shift apps. Object storage keeps data as objects with metadata in a flat namespace, accessed over HTTP APIs. Examples are S3, Azure Blob Storage and Cloud Storage. It scales almost without limit, is cheapest per GB, supports tiers and lifecycle rules, and suits logs, backups, media and data lakes.
keyPoints: Block: low-latency volumes for single VMs, such as boot disks and databases
File: shared POSIX or SMB access for many clients
Object: API access, massive scale, tiers and lifecycle rules
Name one service per type on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud

subjective.question: What is a minimum storage duration, and how should it shape a lifecycle policy? Compare AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
subjective.answer: A minimum storage duration is the shortest time you are billed for in a colder tier. If you delete, overwrite or move an object earlier, you pay an early-deletion charge for the remaining days. On AWS, Standard-IA and One Zone-IA have 30 days, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval have 90 days, and Deep Archive has 180 days. On Azure, Cool is 30 days, Cold is 90 days and Archive is 180 days. On Google Cloud, Nearline is 30 days, Coldline is 90 days and Archive is 365 days. In design terms, only move data to a tier if it will stay there at least that long. Avoid chains of short hops that add transition fees and early-deletion charges. Do not archive data you plan to delete soon. Also factor in retrieval fees and retrieval time, because a cheap tier can become expensive if data is read often.
keyPoints: Definition and the early-deletion charge
Correct minimums for each provider
Only tier down if the data will stay at least the minimum
Account for transition fees, retrieval fees and access frequency

subjective.question: When would you use a cache, a read replica, or sharding or a distributed database? Give an example of each.
subjective.answer: I use a simple rule. A cache cuts read latency. A read replica scales reads and helps with DR. Sharding or a distributed database scales writes. A cache such as ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis or Memorystore suits hot, repeated reads, like a product catalogue or session data. It returns results in sub-milliseconds and removes load from the database, but you must handle invalidation and stale data. A read replica suits read-heavy workloads such as reporting or a global read audience. Aurora supports up to 15 replicas, and a cross-region replica can be promoted during a disaster. Replication is asynchronous, so reads can lag slightly behind writes. When a single primary cannot absorb the write volume, I shard or use a natively distributed database, such as DynamoDB, Cosmos DB or Spanner, which partition data and spread writes across nodes.
keyPoints: Cache lowers latency for hot, repeated reads
Replicas scale reads and can be promoted for DR
Writes scale only through partitioning or distributed databases
Mention trade-offs: staleness, replica lag, partition key design

subjective.question: Describe how Amazon Aurora achieves high durability and availability.
subjective.answer: Aurora separates compute from a distributed storage layer. The storage keeps six copies of the data across three Availability Zones, two in each AZ. Writes use a quorum, so Aurora can lose an entire AZ and still serve data. Storage grows automatically and repairs itself. On the compute side there is one writer instance and up to 15 Aurora Replicas that share the same storage volume. Because replicas read the shared storage, replica lag is usually very low. If the writer fails, Aurora promotes a replica, typically within about a minute or less, and the cluster endpoint points to the new writer. Applications should use the cluster endpoint for writes and the reader endpoint for reads. For regional disasters, Aurora Global Database replicates to other Regions, and a secondary Region can be promoted.
keyPoints: Six copies across three AZs with quorum writes
Shared storage volume with up to 15 replicas
Automatic failover through the cluster endpoint
Global Database for cross-region DR

subjective.question: Explain Cosmos DB consistency levels and why Session is the default.
subjective.answer: Cosmos DB offers five consistency levels, from strongest to weakest: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix and Eventual. Stronger levels give fresher reads but cost more in latency, throughput and availability, especially across regions. Weaker levels are faster and cheaper but may return older data. Session is the default because it fits most applications. Within one client session, it guarantees that you read your own writes, that reads move forward in time, and that writes stay in order. Other sessions may see slightly older data. This gives users a correct experience, such as seeing the order they just placed, without paying the global coordination cost of Strong. I would choose Strong only when every reader must always see the latest committed write, and Eventual for things like counters or likes where order does not matter.
keyPoints: Names all five levels in order
Trade-off between consistency and latency, throughput and availability
Session gives read-your-writes within a session
When to pick Strong or Eventual instead

subjective.question: A customer says personal data must stay in India. How do you design and enforce data residency in the cloud?
subjective.answer: First I clarify the rule. Which data is covered, may backups or support access leave the country, and does it apply to processing or only to storage? Then I choose Indian regions, such as the Mumbai and Hyderabad regions on AWS, Azure India regions or Google Cloud Mumbai and Delhi, and use them for primary data and DR. I enforce this with guardrails, not just good intentions. On AWS, I use SCPs that deny actions outside allowed regions. On Azure, I use the Allowed locations policy. On Google Cloud, I use the resource locations organization policy. I check that replication, backups, global databases, CDN caches and logging sinks do not copy data outside the boundary, for example by choosing in-country replication pairs. I add encryption with customer-managed keys held in-region, then audit continuously with policy compliance reports.
keyPoints: Clarify the scope of the residency requirement
Pick in-country regions for primary and DR
Enforce with SCPs, Azure Policy or organization policies
Check replication, backups, logs and global services
Use in-region keys and continuous audit

subjective.question: How do you decide between online and offline data transfer for a large migration? Show your reasoning with numbers.
subjective.answer: I start with the data size, usable bandwidth and deadline. A fully used 1 Gbps link moves about 10.8 TB a day, so 100 TB takes about 9–10 days. Real links are rarely fully available, so if the link is shared I might plan for half that speed. My rule of thumb is this. If the online transfer would take more than about a week, or would hurt production traffic, I consider an offline device such as AWS Snowball, Azure Data Box or Google Transfer Appliance. For 300 TB on a shared 1 Gbps link, online would take about two months, so offline is better. For a few terabytes, online tools such as DataSync, AzCopy or Storage Transfer Service are simpler. A common pattern is offline for the bulk copy, then online sync for changes made while the device was in transit.
keyPoints: Calculate time from size and usable bandwidth
About 9–10 days per 100 TB at a full 1 Gbps
Offline if more than about a week or the link is shared
Hybrid pattern: bulk offline, then incremental online
Name the tools on each provider

subjective.question: How would you migrate a production Oracle or MySQL database to the cloud with minimal downtime using a database migration service?
subjective.answer: I would use AWS DMS, Azure Database Migration Service or Google Database Migration Service. First I assess the source. For a heterogeneous move such as Oracle to PostgreSQL, I convert the schema with a tool like AWS Schema Conversion Tool and fix the code it cannot convert. For a homogeneous move such as MySQL to MySQL, native tooling is often enough. Next I create the target, set up network connectivity through VPN or a dedicated link, and run a full load. Then I enable change data capture, which reads the source logs and keeps the target in sync while the application stays live. I validate row counts and data, and test the application against the target. At cutover, I stop writes, let CDC catch up, switch connection strings, and keep a rollback plan. Downtime then drops to minutes.
keyPoints: Assess the source and convert the schema for heterogeneous moves
Full load, then change data capture
Validate data and test before cutover
Short cutover window with a rollback plan

subjective.question: Six months after enabling a lifecycle rule that expires log objects after 90 days, a FinOps report shows that S3 storage cost for the log bucket keeps growing. Versioning is enabled, and the logging tool uploads large files using multipart upload. How do you troubleshoot and fix this?
subjective.answer: First, I check the bucket in S3 Storage Lens or with an S3 Inventory report. I look at the split between current versions, noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads. In a versioned bucket, the Expiration action does not delete data. It only adds a delete marker, and the old data stays as a noncurrent version that is still billed. So I add a NoncurrentVersionExpiration action, for example after 1 to 7 days, or I move noncurrent versions to a cheaper class if they must be kept. I also add an ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker cleanup, so that empty delete markers do not pile up. Next, I add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload, for example after 7 days. Parts from failed uploads are billed but invisible in a normal listing. Finally, I confirm that the rule's prefix or tag filter really matches the objects. Then I watch Storage Lens for a few weeks to see the cost flatten.
keyPoints: In versioned buckets, Expiration creates delete markers, and noncurrent versions are still billed
Add NoncurrentVersionExpiration and clean up expired delete markers
Add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload for orphaned upload parts
Use Storage Lens or S3 Inventory to find where the bytes are, and verify rule filters

subjective.question: Review this cache-aside code for a product catalogue that uses Redis in front of a relational database. What problems do you see, and how would you fix them?
subjective.answer: The read path is classic cache-aside, but there are three problems. First, no TTL is set. Keys never expire, so memory grows and stale data can live forever; I would use redis.set with ex=300 or a value that suits the business, plus some random jitter. Second, update_price changes the database but not the cache. Users will see the old price until the key is evicted. After a successful commit, I would delete the key (redis.delete). Deleting is safer than writing the new value, because it avoids race conditions between concurrent writers. Third, nothing protects against a stampede. When a hot key expires, many requests hit the database at once. A short lock, request coalescing or early refresh helps here. I would also cache 'not found' results briefly to stop repeated misses, and handle Redis being unavailable by falling back to the database. For read-heavy load that still needs SQL, read replicas can sit behind the cache too.
keyPoints: Missing TTL leads to stale data and unbounded memory use
Writes must invalidate (delete) the cache key after the DB commit
Protect hot keys from cache stampede with locks, jittered TTLs or early refresh
Fall back gracefully when the cache is unavailable

subjective.question: Compare S3 Object Lock governance mode, compliance mode and legal hold. How do the Azure Blob and Google Cloud Storage equivalents map to them, and which would you choose for logs that a regulator says must be kept for seven years?
subjective.answer: S3 Object Lock needs versioning and applies WORM protection to each object version. In governance mode, users with the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can shorten the retention or delete the version, so it is good for testing or internal policy. In compliance mode, nobody can delete the version or shorten its retention until the date passes, not even the root user. A legal hold has no end date. It stays until someone with permission removes it, and it is used for litigation. In Azure, a time-based retention policy can be unlocked while you test and then locked for compliance. Azure also has legal holds, set at container or version level. Google Cloud Storage uses a bucket retention policy that becomes permanent once you lock it with Bucket Lock. It also offers event-based and temporary holds, and object retention lock for per-object rules. For a regulator's seven-year rule, I would choose compliance mode, a locked Azure policy or a locked GCS bucket. I would test in governance or unlocked mode first, because a lock cannot be undone.
keyPoints: Governance mode can be bypassed with a special permission; compliance mode cannot, even by root
Legal hold has no expiry and is removed manually
Azure: unlocked vs locked time-based retention plus legal hold; GCS: Bucket Lock plus holds
Regulatory retention needs the locked or compliance option; test first because locks are irreversible

subjective.question: An AWS DMS task migrating an on-premises MySQL database to Aurora finished its full load. During the CDC phase, the CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget metrics keep rising, and cutover is blocked. How do you diagnose and fix this?
subjective.answer: First, I check which metric is rising. If CDCLatencySource is high, DMS cannot read changes fast enough from the source. I check binlog settings: binlog_format should be ROW, and retention must be long enough. I also check network bandwidth and VPN throughput to the replication instance, and source load. If only CDCLatencyTarget is high, the problem is applying changes on Aurora. Typical causes are tables without primary keys (each update becomes a full scan), secondary indexes or triggers slowing writes, large LOB columns in full LOB mode, or an undersized Aurora writer. Next, I check the replication instance's CPU, memory, swap and disk queue. If it is saturated, I scale it up. I can turn on batch apply for high-volume tables, and I can split large or busy tables into separate tasks. I add any missing primary keys, use limited LOB mode where possible, and read the task logs for errors or table suspensions. Once latency is near zero and validation passes, I stop writes and cut over.
keyPoints: Separate source-side latency from target-side latency
Source: binlog ROW format and retention, network bandwidth, source load
Target: primary keys, indexes and triggers, LOB mode, writer size, batch apply
Scale the replication instance, split tasks, and validate before cutover

subjective.question: A company runs a transactional database on self-managed VMs and is choosing block storage. It needs steady 40,000 IOPS, sub-millisecond latency and very high durability. It also has a scratch workload that needs fast temporary disk. Compare your options on AWS and Azure, and say how you would choose.
subjective.answer: On AWS, gp3 lets you provision IOPS and throughput separately from size, but its per-volume IOPS ceiling may be too low for this workload. I would check the current limit against the 40,000 target. io2 Block Express is built for demanding databases. It offers higher provisioned IOPS, very low latency and higher durability than gp3, so it fits the main database. I would also make sure the EC2 instance type supports the EBS bandwidth and IOPS needed, because the instance can become the bottleneck. On Azure, Premium SSD v2 lets you set IOPS and throughput independently and is cost-effective for databases. Ultra Disk gives the highest performance and can be tuned without downtime. VM-level disk limits still apply. For scratch data, I would use EC2 instance store or the Azure temporary disk or local NVMe. These are fast and cheap, but data is lost when the VM stops or moves, so never put the database there. For backups, I would use snapshots copied to another Region.
keyPoints: gp3 decouples IOPS from size; io2 Block Express for high, consistent IOPS and durability
Azure Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disk for tunable high-performance database disks
Instance or VM limits can cap disk performance
Instance store and temp disks are ephemeral, so use them only for scratch data

subjective.question: A data platform stores 2 PB of objects. Some are read daily and others are untouched for years, and nobody can predict which. Compare S3 Intelligent-Tiering, fixed lifecycle rules and Google Cloud Storage Autoclass for this case. Which would you pick, and when would you not?
subjective.answer: Fixed lifecycle rules work when access follows age, like logs. Here access is unpredictable, so age-based rules would either move hot data to a cold tier and pay retrieval fees, or leave cold data in Standard. S3 Intelligent-Tiering watches access per object and moves it between Frequent, Infrequent and Archive Instant Access tiers. It charges no retrieval fees but adds a small per-object monitoring fee. Objects under 128 KB are not monitored and stay in the Frequent tier. The optional Archive and Deep Archive Access tiers must be enabled and are not instant. GCS Autoclass does the same per bucket. It has a management fee and no early-deletion or retrieval charges. I would pick auto-tiering here. I would avoid it when objects are tiny and numerous, because the fees and lack of monitoring cancel the benefit. I would also avoid it when the access pattern is clearly age-based, since cheap lifecycle rules then do the job better.
keyPoints: Lifecycle rules suit age-based access; auto-tiering suits unknown access
Intelligent-Tiering has per-object monitoring fees and no retrieval fees
Small objects under 128 KB are not auto-tiered
Autoclass is set per bucket, with no early-deletion or retrieval charges
Archive tiers in Intelligent-Tiering are opt-in and not instant

subjective.question: An auditor needs a 4 GB blob from the Azure Archive tier within four hours. The administrator started a rehydration with Set Blob Tier to Hot eight hours ago, and the blob is still not readable. What went wrong, what can be done now, and how should the design change?
subjective.answer: The rehydration was most likely started at Standard priority, which can take up to 15 hours. High priority can finish in under an hour for blobs smaller than 10 GB, though it costs more. You can raise a pending rehydration from Standard to High priority, so I would do that now. Another way is to use Copy Blob to a new blob in an online tier at High priority. That leaves the archived original untouched, which also helps with early-deletion charges. You can track progress through the blob's archive status property, or with an Event Grid event when rehydration completes. For the design, if auditors regularly need data within hours, Archive is the wrong tier for that window. Keep the recent years in Cold, which has millisecond reads and a 90-day minimum, and archive only older data. Also write down the expected retrieval time and cost in the audit runbook.
keyPoints: Standard priority can take up to 15 hours; High priority is often under 1 hour for blobs under 10 GB
A pending rehydration can be raised to High priority
Copy Blob to an online tier is another option
Monitor through archive status or Event Grid
Use the Cold tier when data needs quick audit access

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this proposed design for regulated trade logs that must be kept for seven years, cannot be deleted, and must stay in India.

code.code:
Bucket: trade-logs (ap-south-1), versioning ON
Object Lock: default retention GOVERNANCE mode, 1 year
Replication: CRR to us-east-1 bucket for DR
Lifecycle:
  - Day 0: write 50 million raw 5 KB JSON files per day
  - Day 30: transition to GLACIER_IR
  - Day 60: transition to DEEP_ARCHIVE
  - Day 120: expire (cost saving on old data)
Auditor SLA: any log within 12 hours

subjective.answer: There are five problems. First, Governance mode lets users with the bypass permission delete objects, so the regulator's rule needs Compliance mode. Second, the retention period is one year, not seven. Third, cross-region replication to us-east-1 breaks the India residency rule. For DR, replicate to ap-south-2 (Hyderabad) instead. Fourth, expiring at day 120 deletes data that must be kept, and an object moved to Deep Archive at day 60 and removed at day 120 is still billed for the 180-day minimum. Object Lock would block the deletion anyway, so the rule conflicts with the retention requirement. Fifth, 50 million 5 KB files a day means huge transition request charges and per-object archive metadata overhead. Compress and batch them into larger objects first. The Glacier Instant Retrieval step at day 30 followed by Deep Archive at day 60 also triggers the IR 90-day minimum charge. Deep Archive standard retrieval fits the 12-hour SLA. A cleaner flow is Standard, then Deep Archive at around 30 to 90 days, then expiry after seven years.
keyPoints: Use Compliance mode with seven-year retention, not one-year Governance
Cross-region copy to the US breaks residency; use Hyderabad
Expiry at day 120 conflicts with retention and minimum durations
Batch tiny files before archiving
Avoid short hops between tiers that each have a minimum duration

subjective.question: You must move 300 TB of on-premises files to Cloud Storage using Transfer Appliance. Users keep changing the files during the move, and the final cutover must lose no data. Put the procedure in order and explain each step briefly.
subjective.answer: Step one: size the data, choose the bucket location and class, and order an appliance with enough capacity. Step two: set up the target bucket, IAM and encryption keys in advance. Step three: when the appliance arrives, connect it on the local network and copy the data, which the appliance encrypts. Note the copy start time, because that becomes the baseline. Step four: ship the appliance back. Google uploads the data into your bucket, and you check object counts and checksums. Step five: run an online delta sync of files changed since the baseline. You can use Storage Transfer Service with an on-premises agent, or gcloud storage rsync, over your link. Repeat the sync until the delta is small. Step six: freeze writes, run a final sync, validate it, and switch applications to Cloud Storage. Step seven: securely retire the appliance data and the source copies according to policy. The offline bulk copy plus online delta pattern is what prevents data loss.
keyPoints: Prepare the bucket, IAM and keys before the appliance arrives
Record a baseline timestamp during the offline copy
Validate counts and checksums after the upload
Use online incremental sync for changes made after the baseline
Freeze writes, run a final sync, then cut over

subjective.question: A global retailer needs a shopping-cart store that accepts writes in Mumbai, Frankfurt and Virginia at the same time with low local latency. It must survive a full Region outage, and eventual consistency between Regions is acceptable. Compare Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, Cosmos DB multi-region writes and Cloud Spanner, and pick one.
subjective.answer: Aurora Global Database has one primary writer Region. Secondary Regions are read-only, and write forwarding still sends writes to the primary. Writes from Mumbai would therefore have cross-continent latency, so it does not meet the requirement. Spanner gives strong external consistency with multi-region configurations, but a write must reach quorum across Regions. That adds latency the cart does not need. It is the right choice when strong global consistency is the requirement. DynamoDB global tables and Cosmos DB with multi-region writes both accept local writes in every Region and replicate asynchronously. They are active-active by design, and they resolve conflicts, for example last writer wins. Both fit the requirement. I would choose based on the platform: DynamoDB global tables on AWS, or Cosmos DB on Azure with Session consistency. I would model the cart as a key-value document keyed by user ID, so that conflicts are rare.
keyPoints: Aurora Global has a single writer Region; write forwarding does not give local writes
Spanner suits strong global consistency at the cost of write latency
DynamoDB global tables and Cosmos DB multi-write are active-active
Understand conflict resolution such as last writer wins
Key the data by user to reduce conflicts

subjective.question: An RDS for MySQL read replica used for reporting shows ReplicaLag climbing to several hours every night during a batch job, then slowly recovering. How do you troubleshoot and fix it?
subjective.answer: First, I confirm the timing in CloudWatch by comparing ReplicaLag with the primary's write IOPS and the replica's CPU and IOPS. Common causes are as follows. The batch job runs very large transactions, and the replica applies each one only after it commits. The replica's SQL apply thread is single-threaded, so it cannot keep up with a parallel write load. The replica is a smaller instance class or has less storage performance than the primary. Long reporting queries on the replica compete with apply or block it. To fix it, I would break the batch into smaller transactions. I would enable multi-threaded replication by setting replica parallel workers in the parameter group. I would size the replica to match the primary, including storage IOPS, and move heavy reports out of the batch window. If reports must stay fresh during the batch, a reader on Aurora, which has lower replica lag, or a separate analytics copy may be better. Finally, I would alarm on lag so it is caught early.
keyPoints: Correlate ReplicaLag with write load and replica resources
Large transactions and single-threaded apply cause lag
Match the replica's instance class and IOPS to the primary
Enable parallel replication and split batches into smaller transactions
Set alarms on lag; consider Aurora or a separate analytics store

subjective.question: A German hospital on Azure must store 1 PB of medical images for ten years. Images must be readable within seconds for the first year and rarely after that. They must be tamper-proof, stay in Germany, and survive a regional outage. Design the storage.
subjective.answer: I would use Blob Storage in Germany West Central with GRS. Its paired Region is Germany North, so geo-replicated copies stay in Germany. Archive is supported only on LRS, GRS and RA-GRS, not on ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS, so this choice also keeps archiving possible. For tamper-proofing, I would apply a time-based immutability policy of ten years and lock it. Locked policies cannot be shortened or removed, and changing a blob's tier is still allowed under immutability. Lifecycle management would move blobs from Hot to Cool after about 30 days. I would move them to Cold after about 180 days and still within the first year, because Cold keeps millisecond reads. Archive would follow only after year one. Each move must respect the minimum durations: 30 days for Cool, 90 for Cold and 180 for Archive. I would bundle small files where possible, and define rehydration expectations for old studies. Finally, I would add an Azure Policy that denies resources outside the German Regions.
keyPoints: The GRS pair stays inside Germany, which meets residency
Archive is not supported on ZRS or GZRS redundancy
Use a locked time-based immutability policy for ten years
Stay on online tiers during year one and archive only after
Respect minimum durations and enforce Regions with Azure Policy

subjective.question: Find the mistakes in these commands, which are meant to create an audit-log bucket for an Indian bank. The data must stay in India, be kept for seven years, and the last 30 days are queried daily.

code.code:
gcloud storage buckets create gs://bank-audit-logs \
  --location=US --default-storage-class=ARCHIVE

gcloud storage buckets update gs://bank-audit-logs \
  --retention-period=7y

# lifecycle.json: {"rule":[{"action":{"type":"Delete"},
#                  "condition":{"age":365}}]}
gcloud storage buckets update gs://bank-audit-logs \
  --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json

subjective.answer: There are four mistakes. First, --location=US is a US multi-region, which breaks residency. Use asia-south1 (Mumbai) or asia-south2 (Delhi), or the asia1-style dual-region if your pairing needs it, but check that every location is in India. Second, setting Archive as the default class for data that is queried daily is costly. Archive has the highest retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum. Keep new objects in Standard and use a SetStorageClass lifecycle rule to move them to Archive after 30 days. Third, the retention policy is set but not locked. Without locking, an admin can reduce or remove it, so run the update with --lock-retention-period once it is tested. Locking is permanent. Fourth, the Delete rule at age 365 conflicts with the seven-year rule. The retention policy will block those deletes, but the rule is still wrong. Set the Delete age to about 2,557 days, which covers seven years including leap days, so cleanup happens only after retention ends.
keyPoints: The US multi-region breaks India residency
Recent logs that are queried daily belong in Standard, not Archive
The retention policy must be locked to be WORM
The Delete age must match seven years
Locking a retention policy is irreversible, so test first

subjective.question: Auditors are expected to retrieve about 5% of 200 TB of archived logs each year. Without using memorised prices, explain how you would compare S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive for total cost, and what usually decides the answer.
subjective.answer: I would build a simple yearly model for each class. Storage cost is the stored GB multiplied by the price per GB-month, multiplied by 12. Retrieval cost is the retrieved GB multiplied by the per-GB retrieval fee, plus request fees for those objects. Transition cost is the number of objects moved multiplied by the per-request transition fee. I would also add the minimum-duration risk: 90 days for Instant Retrieval, 90 for Flexible and 180 for Deep Archive. Prices come from the current pricing page for the Region, here ap-south-1. With only 5%, or about 10 TB a year, retrieved, storage dominates. Deep Archive's much lower storage price usually wins, as long as its retrieval time of up to 12 hours for standard, or longer for bulk, meets the audit SLA. Instant Retrieval only wins if reads must take milliseconds or if retrievals are frequent, because it has higher retrieval fees and higher storage cost. Object count matters too, so batching files reduces the transition and request terms.
keyPoints: Total cost = storage + retrieval + requests + transitions
Account for minimum storage duration risk
Low retrieval rates favour the cheapest storage class
The retrieval-time SLA can rule out Deep Archive
Batching reduces per-object fees

subjective.question: A Linux build farm uses an Amazon EFS file system of about 100 GB in Bursting throughput mode. It was fast for the first weeks, but now builds crawl every afternoon. Diagnose the cause and recommend a fix.
subjective.answer: In Bursting mode, baseline throughput scales with the amount of data stored. A 100 GB file system has a low baseline and depends on burst credits. Heavy afternoon builds use up the credits, and throughput then drops to the baseline. I would check the BurstCreditBalance metric falling to near zero, and PercentIOLimit and throughput metrics against the permitted throughput. The best fix for spiky, unpredictable load is to switch to Elastic throughput. It scales automatically and you pay for what you use. Provisioned throughput suits steady, known demand, where you pay for a fixed level. Do not pad the file system with dummy data to raise the baseline, as that is a wasteful workaround. Also check the build pattern. Many tiny files cause metadata-heavy I/O, so caching dependencies on local instance storage or EBS for scratch work can reduce load on EFS. Keep the General Purpose performance mode for its lower latency.
keyPoints: Bursting baseline throughput scales with stored size
Exhausted burst credits cause afternoon slowdowns
Check BurstCreditBalance and PercentIOLimit
Use Elastic for spiky load and Provisioned for steady load
Move scratch and metadata-heavy work to local or EBS storage

steps.overview: This step teaches you to turn business targets (RPO and RTO) into a disaster recovery design and a budget. You will compare the four standard DR strategies, decide between multi-zone and multi-region, wire up health checks and DNS failover, and prove the plan works with game days. Every architect exam on this path has scenario questions that ask for the cheapest design that still meets a stated RPO and RTO.
objectives: Explain RPO and RTO and translate them into replication, backup and automation choices.
Select the cheapest DR strategy (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active) that meets a given RPO and RTO.
Distinguish failures that multi-zone designs handle from those that need multi-region designs.
Configure health checks and DNS failover routing for a primary and a DR site.
Plan and run a chaos experiment or game day that measures the real RPO and RTO.

concepts.explanation: The maximum amount of data loss the business accepts, measured in time before the disaster. A 15-minute RPO means you may lose at most the last 15 minutes of writes. RPO is driven by how often and how continuously data is copied: nightly backups give about 24 hours, while asynchronous replication gives seconds to minutes.

The maximum time allowed between the outage and the service being usable again. It covers detection, decision, infrastructure start-up, data restore or promotion, and DNS changes. RTO is driven by how much infrastructure is already running and how automated the failover is.

The cheapest strategy: data is backed up (often copied to another region) and infrastructure is rebuilt from code only after a disaster. RPO and RTO are typically hours, because restoring large databases and building stacks takes time. Use it for internal or non-critical systems, or when RTO is measured in hours or days.

Core data is replicated continuously to the DR region (for example a cross-region database replica), but application servers are off or scaled to zero. On failover you promote the database and start compute from templates or images. RPO is seconds to minutes and RTO is typically tens of minutes, at low steady-state cost.

A smaller but fully working copy of the whole stack runs in the DR region all the time, with data replicated continuously. On failover you scale it up and shift traffic. RTO is minutes, and the DR site can be tested any time because it already serves requests.

Two or more regions serve production traffic at full scale at the same time. Failover is just removing the failed region from routing, so RTO is near zero and RPO is near zero (depending on the data replication model). It is the most expensive option and needs care with write conflicts and data consistency.

Availability zones (AWS AZs, Azure availability zones, Google Cloud zones) are separate data centres in one region with low-latency links, so synchronous replication and load balancing across them protect against data-centre failures. A multi-region design protects against a whole-region outage, bad regional deployments or data residency needs, but replication is usually asynchronous so RPO is not zero. High availability is usually multi-zone; disaster recovery is usually multi-region.

A health checker probes an endpoint (for example HTTPS /health) from several locations. When it fails a set number of times, DNS stops returning the primary record and returns the secondary. Examples: Amazon Route 53 failover routing, Azure Traffic Manager priority routing or Azure Front Door, and Google Cloud DNS routing policies with health checks or a global load balancer.

Chaos engineering injects controlled faults (stop instances, add latency, block an AZ) to check that the system behaves as designed. A game day is a scheduled, team-wide exercise that runs a full DR scenario and times every step. Tools include AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), Azure Chaos Studio, and scripted tests on Google Cloud. An untested DR plan should be treated as not working.

Cloud providers offer services that cut RPO and RTO without custom scripting. Examples: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (block-level replication of servers), Aurora Global Database, Azure Site Recovery for VM replication, and Google Cloud Backup and DR Service. Exams favour these managed options over hand-built scripts when they meet the requirement.

keyFacts: Typical AWS DR guidance: backup and restore = hours; pilot light = tens of minutes; warm standby = minutes; multi-site active/active = near zero RPO and RTO. Cost rises in the same order.
Decision rule: list the strategies from cheapest to dearest and pick the first one whose realistic RPO and RTO both meet the targets.
A 15-minute RPO rules out daily snapshots; you need continuous or frequent replication such as cross-region read replicas, Aurora Global Database or log shipping.
Aurora Global Database usually replicates to secondary regions with lag of under one second and supports cross-region failover in minutes.
S3 Replication Time Control is designed to replicate 99.99% of objects within 15 minutes and is backed by an SLA.
Route 53 health checks run every 30 seconds by default, or 10 seconds as a fast option; the default failure threshold is 3 consecutive failures.
DNS failover time = detection time + TTL of cached records; keep TTLs low (for example 60 seconds) on failover records.
RDS automated backups allow point-in-time restore, usually to within about the last 5 minutes, but a restore creates a new instance and can take a long time for large databases.
Synchronous replication across zones (for example RDS Multi-AZ, zone-redundant Azure SQL, Cloud SQL HA) gives near-zero RPO for zone failure but does not protect against region failure.

example.caption: Route 53 failover for the e-commerce app: primary in Mumbai (ap-south-1), pilot-light DR in Hyderabad (ap-south-2). Data uses an Aurora cross-region replica (RPO seconds) and DR compute scales from 0 on failover (RTO well under 1 hour).
