AWS uses gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and interface endpoints via PrivateLink; Azure uses Private Endpoints with Private DNS zones; Google uses Private Google Access, Private Service Connect and VPC Service Controls perimeters to stop data exfiltration. Combine with resource policies, such as aws:SourceVpce, so access only works through the endpoint.

All audit logs flow to one dedicated log account, subscription or project that workload teams cannot administer. AWS uses an organization trail in CloudTrail to an S3 bucket with Object Lock and log file validation; Azure uses diagnostic settings and Activity Log to a central Log Analytics workspace and immutable storage; Google uses aggregated organization log sinks to a locked Cloud Storage bucket or locked log bucket. This is the checkpoint requirement: admin actions logged where developers cannot change them.

Threat detection finds active bad behaviour: Amazon GuardDuty, Microsoft Defender for Cloud workload protections with Microsoft Sentinel as SIEM, and Google Security Command Center threat detection. Posture management (CSPM) finds misconfigurations against benchmarks: AWS Security Hub with AWS Config, Defender for Cloud secure score, and Security Command Center findings. Exam tip: GuardDuty detects threats, Config records configuration, Security Hub aggregates findings.

ISO 27001 is a certifiable information security management system (ISMS) standard with Annex A controls. SOC 2 is an auditor's attestation report against Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). PCI DSS (current version 4.0.1) applies to cardholder data, and India's DPDP Act 2023 governs digital personal data of individuals. Under the shared responsibility model, the provider's certificates cover the cloud itself, but you must still configure and prove your own controls.

keyFacts: S3 encrypts all new objects by default with SSE-S3 (since January 2023); use SSE-KMS when you need key policy control and CloudTrail records of key use.
AWS KMS key deletion has a mandatory waiting period of 7 to 30 days (default 30); disable a key instead if you might need it again.
AWS KMS automatic rotation for customer managed symmetric keys is optional; the default period is one year. AWS managed keys rotate automatically every year.

Azure Key Vault soft delete is always on, with 7 to 90 days retention (default 90); purge protection blocks permanent deletion during that period and is required for many customer-managed key scenarios.
CloudTrail Event history shows 90 days of management events free per Region; for longer retention, organisation-wide coverage and tamper evidence you need a trail to S3 with log file validation.
AWS Shield Standard is automatic and free; Shield Advanced adds DDoS response team support, cost protection and advanced metrics, and is a paid subscription.
Google VPC Service Controls create a service perimeter that stops data exfiltration from services like Cloud Storage and BigQuery, even for users with valid IAM permissions.
Decision rule: 'customer must control or revoke keys' means CMK/CMEK; 'keys must never leave our premises' means external key store (AWS XKS, Google EKM) or a dedicated HSM.

India's DPDP Act 2023, with the DPDP Rules notified in 2025, requires consent-based processing, reasonable security safeguards, and breach notification to the Data Protection Board and affected users; penalties can reach INR 250 crore per breach.
Central audit logs should use write-once storage: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, Azure immutable blob storage, or a locked retention policy on a Cloud Storage bucket.

example.caption: AWS CLI: customer-managed key, organisation-wide encrypted audit trail, threat detection and posture dashboard. Run in the log-archive or delegated admin context. The bucket policy and key policy must allow cloudtrail.amazonaws.com.
example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
BUCKET=acme-org-log-archive

# 1. Customer-managed KMS key with rotation
KEY_ID=$(aws kms create-key --description "Org audit log key" \
  --query KeyMetadata.KeyId --output text)
aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/org-audit --target-key-id "$KEY_ID"
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id "$KEY_ID"

# 2. Default SSE-KMS encryption on the log bucket
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration \
  '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"aws:kms","KMSMasterKeyID":"alias/org-audit"},"BucketKeyEnabled":true}]}'

# 3. Organisation trail, all Regions, tamper-evident digests
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name org-trail \
  --s3-bucket-name "$BUCKET" \
  --is-organization-trail --is-multi-region-trail \
  --enable-log-file-validation --kms-key-id "$KEY_ID"
aws cloudtrail start-logging --name org-trail

# 4. Threat detection and posture dashboard
aws guardduty create-detector --enable
aws securityhub enable-security-hub --enable-default-standards

pitfalls: Choosing SSE-S3 or platform-managed keys when the question says the company must control, audit or revoke the key; that needs a customer-managed key.
Storing central logs in the same account or subscription as the workload, so a compromised admin can delete them; always use a separate log archive with immutability and restricted access.
Thinking a WAF stops all DDoS attacks; WAF handles layer 7 rules, while network-layer floods need Shield, Azure DDoS Protection or Cloud Armor at the edge.
Creating a private endpoint but forgetting private DNS, so clients still resolve and use the public endpoint.
Assuming the provider's ISO 27001, SOC 2 or PCI DSS certificate makes your application compliant; it covers only the provider's side of the shared responsibility model.
Scheduling deletion of a KMS key or purging a Key Vault key that still protects data; the data becomes permanently unreadable.

workflow.title: Secure the landing zone: encryption, edge, logging and posture

steps.label: Classify data and pick key model
steps.detail: Tag each data store by sensitivity and decide provider-managed or customer-managed keys based on compliance needs.

steps.label: Create keys and enforce encryption
steps.detail: Create CMKs in KMS, Key Vault or Cloud KMS with rotation, and use policies to deny unencrypted storage and non-TLS access.

steps.label: Lock down network access
steps.detail: Use private endpoints or VPC Service Controls for data services and remove public access.

steps.label: Put WAF at the edge
steps.detail: Attach managed WAF rule sets and rate limits to the CDN or load balancer, with DDoS protection enabled.

steps.label: Centralise immutable audit logs
steps.detail: Send organisation-wide audit logs to a separate log account or project with write-once retention and read-only access for developers.

steps.label: Enable detection and posture tools
steps.detail: Turn on GuardDuty and Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, or Security Command Center across all accounts and review findings.

steps.label: Map controls to frameworks
steps.detail: Link each control to ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS or DPDP requirements and keep evidence for audits.

project.title: lz-security-baseline
project.summary: This Terraform project adds a security baseline to an AWS landing zone account. It creates customer-managed KMS keys, encrypted S3 and DynamoDB data stores, a WAF with managed rules and rate limiting, a multi-Region CloudTrail into a locked log archive bucket, and GuardDuty, AWS Config and Security Hub CSPM as the posture dashboard. Files: main.tf holds providers and variables, encryption.tf holds keys and data stores, logging.tf holds the tamper-resistant audit trail, waf.tf holds edge protection, posture.tf holds threat detection and posture, and scripts/checkpoint.py checks the step's checkpoint.
project.run:
terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan -var="prefix=mc-lz" -var="alb_arn="
terraform apply tfplan
pip install boto3
PREFIX=mc-lz AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 python scripts/checkpoint.py

files.code:
# lz-security-baseline (Step 8: Security architecture and compliance)

Adds encryption, a WAF, central audit logs and a posture dashboard to one
landing zone account in ap-south-1 (Mumbai).

## Files
- main.tf: provider, variables, outputs
- encryption.tf: two CMKs (data, logs), encrypted S3 bucket and DynamoDB table
- logging.tf: CloudTrail to a log archive bucket with S3 Object Lock (WORM)
- waf.tf: AWS WAF web ACL (managed rules + rate limit) with logs
- posture.tf: GuardDuty, AWS Config and Security Hub CSPM (FSBP standard)
- scripts/checkpoint.py: proves the checkpoint and exits non-zero on failure

## Run
1. terraform init && terraform apply (set alb_arn to attach the WAF to an ALB)
2. PREFIX=mc-lz AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 python scripts/checkpoint.py
3. Open Security Hub in the console. This is your posture dashboard.
   Controls appear only after AWS Config has recorded resources.

## Checkpoint
Every data store is encrypted with a CMK. Every admin (management) API call
is written by CloudTrail to a bucket that developers cannot change:
- Object Lock blocks delete or overwrite during the retention period.
- Log file validation shows if a log file was edited.
- In a real landing zone, put this bucket in a separate Log Archive account.
  Add an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail.

## Notes
- The lab uses object_lock_mode = GOVERNANCE, so you can clean up. Production
  should use COMPLIANCE. In that mode, nobody (not even root) can delete logs early.
- In transit: both bucket policies deny requests that do not use TLS
  (aws:SecureTransport = false).
- If Control Tower already enables AWS Config, remove the Config resources
  from posture.tf to avoid conflicts.
- Shield Standard is automatic. Shield Advanced is a paid opt-in.

## Same idea on other clouds
| AWS | Azure | Google Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| KMS CMK | Key Vault / Managed HSM (CMK) | Cloud KMS (CMEK) |
| AWS WAF + Shield | Front Door / App Gateway WAF + DDoS Protection | Cloud Armor |
| CloudTrail + Object Lock | Activity Log to immutable storage | Cloud Audit Logs + locked bucket |
| GuardDuty, Security Hub | Defender for Cloud | Security Command Center |

## Compliance mapping (high level, not legal advice)
- ISO 27001 Annex A: cryptography, logging and monitoring controls.
- SOC 2: Security (Common Criteria) for access, monitoring and change logs.
- PCI DSS: protect stored account data, and log and monitor all access.
- DPDP Act 2023: reasonable security safeguards for personal data and
  evidence for breach reporting to the Data Protection Board.

"""Checkpoint: every data store is encrypted and admin actions are logged immutably.
Usage: PREFIX=mc-lz AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 python scripts/checkpoint.py"""
import os
import boto3

region = os.environ.get("AWS_REGION", "ap-south-1")
prefix = os.environ.get("PREFIX", "mc-lz")  # must match var.prefix in main.tf
session = boto3.Session(region_name=region)
account = session.client("sts").get_caller_identity()["Account"]
s3 = session.client("s3")
results = []


def check(name, ok, detail=""):
    results.append(bool(ok))
    print(f"[{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name} {detail}")


# 1. Encryption at rest with the customer-managed key
for bucket in (f"{prefix}-app-data-{account}", f"{prefix}-log-archive-{account}"):
    rule = s3.get_bucket_encryption(Bucket=bucket)["ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration"]["Rules"][0]
    algo = rule["ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault"]["SSEAlgorithm"]
    check(f"S3 {bucket} uses SSE-KMS", algo == "aws:kms", algo)

table = session.client("dynamodb").describe_table(TableName=f"{prefix}-orders")["Table"]
sse = table.get("SSEDescription", {})
check("DynamoDB orders uses KMS CMK", sse.get("SSEType") == "KMS" and sse.get("Status") == "ENABLED")

# 2. Admin actions logged where developers cannot change them
ct = session.client("cloudtrail")
trail = ct.get_trail(Name=f"{prefix}-trail")["Trail"]
check("CloudTrail is logging", ct.get_trail_status(Name=f"{prefix}-trail")["IsLogging"])
check("Trail is multi-Region", trail["IsMultiRegionTrail"])
check("Log file validation enabled", trail["LogFileValidationEnabled"])
check("Trail encrypted with KMS", "KmsKeyId" in trail)

lock = s3.get_object_lock_configuration(Bucket=trail["S3BucketName"])["ObjectLockConfiguration"]
mode = lock.get("Rule", {}).get("DefaultRetention", {}).get("Mode")
check("Log archive has Object Lock", lock.get("ObjectLockEnabled") == "Enabled" and mode, mode)

# 3. Threat detection and posture
gd = session.client("guardduty")
ids = gd.list_detectors()["DetectorIds"]
check("GuardDuty enabled", ids and gd.get_detector(DetectorId=ids[0])["Status"] == "ENABLED")

sh = session.client("securityhub")
filters = {
    "ComplianceStatus": [{"Value": "FAILED", "Comparison": "EQUALS"}],
    "RecordState": [{"Value": "ACTIVE", "Comparison": "EQUALS"}],
}
counts = {}
for page in sh.get_paginator("get_findings").paginate(Filters=filters):
    for finding in page["Findings"]:
        label = finding["Severity"]["Label"]
        counts[label] = counts.get(label, 0) + 1
print("Security Hub failed controls by severity:", counts or "none yet")
check("No CRITICAL posture findings", counts.get("CRITICAL", 0) == 0)

raise SystemExit(0 if all(results) else 1)  # non-zero exit fails a CI pipeline

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the security domains of every exam on the path: 'Design Secure Architectures' in SAA-C03, 'Design for new solutions' and organisational complexity in SAP-C02, 'Implement and manage storage/identities' in AZ-104, 'Design identity, governance and monitoring' and data storage in AZ-305, and 'Ensuring security and compliance' in the Google Professional Cloud Architect exam. Questions are almost always scenario-based. You get a compliance or control requirement, such as 'must revoke', 'cannot be deleted', 'no public internet' or 'detect threats'. You must pick the managed service and configuration that meets it with the least effort and the least privilege.

compare.b: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (CMK/CMEK)
compare.difference: Provider-managed keys give encryption with zero control. A customer-managed key gives you a key policy, separation of duties, per-use audit logs and the ability to disable the key and cut off access.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question only says 'encrypt at rest' and stresses lowest cost or lowest operational overhead.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when the question mentions controlling, auditing, rotating on your own schedule, or revoking access to the key.

compare.a: AWS WAF / Azure WAF / Cloud Armor WAF rules
compare.b: AWS Shield Advanced / Azure DDoS Protection / Cloud Armor network-level protection
compare.difference: WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests at layer 7, such as SQL injection, XSS, bad bots and rate limits per IP. DDoS protection absorbs volumetric and protocol floods at layers 3 and 4, and the paid tiers add response teams and cost protection.
compare.chooseA: Pick WAF when the threat is malicious web requests, OWASP Top 10 attacks, geo-blocking or per-IP rate limiting.
compare.chooseB: Pick DDoS protection when the threat is large traffic floods, or when the business needs DDoS cost protection and expert support.

compare.a: Azure service endpoint / Google Private Google Access
compare.b: Azure Private Endpoint (Private Link) / Google Private Service Connect / AWS interface endpoint
compare.difference: Service endpoints and Private Google Access keep traffic on the provider backbone, but the service still uses its public IP. Private endpoints place a private IP for the service inside your VNet or VPC, so it is reachable from on-premises and the public endpoint can be disabled.
compare.chooseA: Pick the service endpoint option when you only need subnet-level access to a PaaS service from inside the cloud network at no extra cost.
compare.chooseB: Pick private endpoints when the question says private IP, access from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute or Interconnect, or 'disable public network access'.

compare.a: Threat detection (Amazon GuardDuty, Microsoft Defender for Cloud workload plans, Security Command Center threat detection)
compare.b: Posture and configuration management (AWS Config and Security Hub, Defender CSPM and Secure Score, SCC misconfiguration findings)
compare.difference: Threat detection looks for active malicious behaviour in logs and traffic, such as stolen credentials, crypto-mining or calls to known bad IPs. Posture tools check whether resources are configured against a standard, such as public buckets or unencrypted disks.
compare.chooseA: Pick threat detection when the question says unusual API calls, compromised instance, malware or anomalous behaviour.
compare.chooseB: Pick posture tools when the question says compliance score, benchmark such as CIS or PCI, misconfiguration, or a dashboard across accounts or subscriptions.

compare.a: Multi-tenant KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault Standard/Premium, Cloud KMS)
compare.b: Dedicated or external HSM (AWS CloudHSM or XKS, Azure Managed HSM or Dedicated HSM, Google Cloud HSM or Cloud EKM)
compare.difference: Multi-tenant KMS is fully managed and integrates natively with storage and databases. Single-tenant or external options give exclusive control of the HSM or keep the keys outside the provider, at higher cost and with more operational effort.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for most customer-managed key needs, because it gives native service integration and the lowest overhead.
compare.chooseB: Pick it only when the question demands a single-tenant HSM, sole customer control of the HSM, or keys held outside the cloud provider.

cues.cue: Logs must be retained for years and no one, including root or admins, can delete them
cues.pick: Separate log archive account or subscription with WORM storage in compliance mode or a locked policy
cues.why: Governance mode and unlocked policies can be bypassed by privileged users, so they fail an 'anyone' requirement.

cues.cue: Prevent member accounts from disabling CloudTrail or leaving the organisation
cues.pick: An organisation trail plus a Service Control Policy that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and DeleteTrail
cues.why: SCPs are guardrails that even an account's admins cannot override.

cues.cue: Find PII or card numbers stored in buckets or datasets
cues.pick: Amazon Macie, Google Sensitive Data Protection, or Microsoft Purview
cues.why: These services discover and classify sensitive data; GuardDuty and Defender for Cloud detect threats, not data types.

cues.cue: EC2 or VM must reach S3 or DynamoDB without internet, NAT or cost
cues.pick: VPC gateway endpoint with an endpoint policy
cues.why: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB carry no hourly charge, while interface endpoints and NAT gateways do.

cues.cue: Stop data being copied out of BigQuery or Cloud Storage even by authorised users
cues.pick: VPC Service Controls perimeter
cues.why: IAM decides who can act, while the perimeter decides where data can go.

cues.cue: Rotate database passwords automatically and remove secrets from code
cues.pick: AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault secrets with managed identity, or Google Secret Manager
cues.why: Secrets belong in a secrets store accessed by workload identity, not in a KMS key or environment variables.

cues.cue: Encrypt traffic in transit to a public website with minimal certificate management
cues.pick: Managed TLS certificates on the load balancer or CDN (AWS Certificate Manager, App Service or Front Door managed certs, Google-managed SSL certs)
cues.why: Managed certificates renew automatically and terminate TLS at the edge.

cues.cue: Single view of findings and compliance across many accounts or subscriptions
cues.pick: Security Hub with a delegated administrator, Defender for Cloud at management-group scope, or Security Command Center at organisation level
cues.why: Central aggregation at organisation scope is the posture-dashboard answer.

scenario.situation: An Indian payments start-up runs on AWS Organizations and must pass a PCI DSS audit. Auditors want every API action in every account recorded for seven years. The logs must be provably untampered, and no workload account administrator must be able to alter or delete them. The security team wants the least operational overhead. What should the architect do?
reasoning: Remove CloudTrail Event history. It only covers recent management events in one Region and has no long-term retention.
Remove options that write a trail to a bucket in each workload account. The local admin could delete the bucket or stop the trail, even with MFA Delete enabled.
Remove S3 Object Lock in governance mode. Users with bypass permissions can remove objects early, so it fails the 'no admin can delete' rule.

Keep the option that creates an organisation trail delivering to a central bucket in a dedicated log archive account. That bucket should have Object Lock compliance mode, a seven-year retention period, log file validation and SSE-KMS. An SCP should block trail changes.
scenario.answer: Create an organisation-wide CloudTrail trail to an S3 bucket in a separate log archive account. Enable log file validation, SSE-KMS, Object Lock in compliance mode with seven-year retention, and an SCP that denies stopping or deleting the trail. This one managed design covers every account, proves integrity, and cannot be undone by workload admins.

memoryAids: Key choice ladder 'P-C-H-X': Provider-managed (just encrypt), Customer-managed (control and revoke), HSM dedicated (single tenant), eXternal (keys stay outside the cloud). Climb only as far as the question forces you.
Log safety 'SAIL': Separate account, Append-only or WORM storage, Integrity validation, Locked guardrails (SCP or Azure Policy or Org Policy).
Edge stack 'D-W-A': DDoS protection absorbs floods, WAF filters requests, App authenticates users. Each layer stops a different attack.
cheatSheet: The answer with the most control is not always correct; pick the least-effort option that meets the stated requirement.
'Revoke access to data quickly' means disable the customer-managed key or remove its grant, not delete the key.
Envelope encryption: a data key encrypts the data, the KMS key encrypts the data key, and the root key never leaves the HSM.
Azure customer-managed keys for Storage or SQL need soft delete and purge protection on the vault, plus a managed identity with key permissions.
Google CMEK means the Cloud KMS key is in your project; it must be in a location compatible with the resource, and the service agent needs the encrypter/decrypter role.
Private endpoint answers need private DNS too: a Route 53 private hosted zone, an Azure Private DNS zone such as privatelink.blob.core.windows.net, or Cloud DNS private zones.
Cloud Armor is Google's WAF and DDoS layer for external Application Load Balancers; Azure WAF runs on Application Gateway or Front Door.
Azure central logs: diagnostic settings and the Activity Log go to a central Log Analytics workspace, with Microsoft Sentinel for SIEM.
Google central logs: aggregated log sinks at organisation or folder level go to a bucket in a dedicated logging project.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, GuardDuty detects threats, Macie finds sensitive data, Config tracks configuration drift, and Security Hub aggregates findings.
Compliance reports such as AWS Artifact, Microsoft Service Trust Portal and Google Compliance Reports Manager prove the provider's side only.
DPDP Act maps to consent records, data minimisation, encryption and access control as 'reasonable safeguards', logging, and a tested breach-notification runbook.
selfCheck: I can say when a question needs provider-managed, customer-managed, dedicated HSM or external keys, and justify the choice in one line.
I can design a tamper-proof central audit log on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, naming the storage lock and the guardrail policy for each.
I can explain why a WAF alone does not stop a volumetric DDoS attack, and name the matching DDoS service on each cloud.
I can configure private access to a PaaS service end to end, including DNS, and disable its public endpoint.
I can match GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Config, Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, Sentinel and Security Command Center to the right question cue.
I can explain the shared responsibility split for ISO 27001, SOC 2, PCI DSS and DPDP, and list the controls my team still owns.

objective.question: A company stores customer files in Amazon S3. Auditors now require two things: the security team must control who can use the encryption key through a policy, and every use of the key must be recorded in CloudTrail. What is the most suitable change?
options: Switch the bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS using a customer managed KMS key
Turn on S3 Versioning so every object change is logged
Enable client-side encryption with keys stored in the application code
Keep the default SSE-S3 encryption because it already encrypts all new objects
objective.explanation: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives a key policy you control, and each KMS API call is logged in CloudTrail. SSE-S3 encrypts by default but gives no key policy control or per-use audit trail. Keys in code are insecure, and Versioning is not an encryption or key-audit control.

objective.question: A team no longer uses a customer managed AWS KMS key. However, some old backups encrypted with it may need to be restored next year. What should the architect recommend?
options: Schedule the key for deletion with the default 30-day waiting period
Delete the key immediately because AWS keeps a hidden copy for recovery
Disable the key so it cannot be used now but can be re-enabled later
Schedule the key for deletion with a 7-day waiting period
objective.explanation: Disabling a key stops its use but keeps it, so the old backups can still be decrypted after re-enabling. Once deletion completes after the 7–30 day waiting period, data encrypted under the key cannot be recovered. AWS does not keep a recoverable copy, and KMS has no immediate deletion option.

objective.question: You are configuring an Azure Storage account to use customer-managed keys stored in Azure Key Vault. The configuration fails validation. Which Key Vault setting must you enable?
options: Azure RBAC permission model
Public network access from all networks
Key auto-rotation policy
Purge protection
objective.explanation: Customer-managed key scenarios such as Azure Storage require soft delete and purge protection on the vault. Soft delete is always on, so purge protection is the setting you add. RBAC, public access and auto-rotation are useful but are not the blocking requirement.

objective.question: A bank regulator states that encryption keys protecting cloud data must never leave the bank's own premises. The bank wants to keep using native AWS service encryption for S3 and EBS. Which option meets this requirement?
options: AWS KMS keys with imported key material
An AWS KMS external key store (XKS) backed by the bank's on-premises HSM
AWS managed keys, because AWS rotates them every year
AWS KMS customer managed keys with automatic rotation enabled
objective.explanation: An external key store keeps key material in the customer's own key manager or HSM outside AWS, while KMS-integrated services still work. Imported key material is stored inside AWS KMS after import, so the key does leave the premises. Customer managed and AWS managed keys are also held in AWS KMS.

objective.question: On Google Cloud, a data analyst with valid IAM permissions copied a BigQuery dataset to a project owned by another organisation. Security wants to stop this kind of data exfiltration, even for users who hold correct IAM roles. What should you implement?
options: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) on the dataset
Remove the BigQuery Data Viewer role from all analysts
VPC Service Controls with a service perimeter around the projects
Firewall rules that deny egress on port 443
objective.explanation: VPC Service Controls create a perimeter that blocks data from moving to resources outside it, even when IAM allows the action. Firewall rules do not control Google API calls this way. CMEK controls encryption, not where data can be copied, and removing roles would stop legitimate work.

objective.question: An organisation with 40 AWS accounts must keep a record of all management API activity for 7 years. The record must be tamper-evident and must not be deletable by anyone in workload accounts, including administrators. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Create an organisation trail to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account, with log file validation and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode
Send CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs in each account with a 7-year retention setting
Create a trail in each account that writes to a local S3 bucket with versioning enabled
Rely on CloudTrail Event history in each account and Region
objective.explanation: An organisation trail covers all accounts, log file validation gives tamper evidence, and Object Lock compliance mode stops deletion even by root users until retention ends. Event history keeps only 90 days. Per-account buckets and log groups can be changed by local administrators.

objective.question: A public e-commerce site runs behind Amazon CloudFront and an Application Load Balancer. The company wants to block SQL injection attacks and also wants access to the AWS Shield Response Team and protection from scaling charges during a DDoS attack. What should the architect use?
options: Security groups and network ACLs on the load balancer subnets
Amazon GuardDuty with automated remediation
AWS WAF with managed rules, plus a Shield Advanced subscription
Shield Standard only, because it is automatic and free
objective.explanation: AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks SQL injection, while Shield Advanced adds response team support, cost protection and advanced metrics. Shield Standard does not include these features or layer 7 request inspection. Security groups do not inspect request content, and GuardDuty detects threats rather than blocking web attacks.

objective.question: Which statement correctly describes envelope encryption as used by AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and Google Cloud KMS?
options: The master key is sent to the application, which uses it to encrypt large files locally
Data is encrypted only while in transit, inside a TLS envelope
The data is encrypted with a data encryption key, and that data key is encrypted with a key held in the key management service
Data is encrypted twice with the same master key for extra strength
objective.explanation: In envelope encryption, a data encryption key encrypts the data, and a key encryption key in the KMS wraps that data key. The master key never leaves the service and large data never needs to be sent to it. It is an at-rest pattern, not TLS.

objective.question: A company must make sure an Azure Storage account and an Azure SQL database can be reached only from a private IP address inside its hub-and-spoke virtual networks, with no public endpoint. What should you configure?
options: An Azure Firewall rule allowing traffic from the VNet address space to the public endpoint
A network security group that denies Internet outbound traffic
Private endpoints (Azure Private Link) with private DNS zones, and disable public network access
Service endpoints on the subnets, keeping public network access enabled
objective.explanation: Private endpoints give the service a private IP in your VNet, private DNS resolves the name to it, and disabling public access removes the public path. Service endpoints still use the service's public endpoint. Firewall and NSG rules alone do not remove public exposure of the service.

objective.question: A security team attaches this bucket policy to an Amazon S3 bucket. What is the effect?
options: It blocks public access but still allows HTTP requests from IAM users in the same account.
It denies all access to the bucket, because Principal "*" with Deny overrides every Allow.
It forces all new objects to be encrypted at rest with SSE-KMS.
It rejects any request to the bucket or its objects that is not made over HTTPS (TLS), for all principals.
objective.explanation: aws:SecureTransport is false only when the request uses plain HTTP, so the Deny enforces encryption in transit for everyone. It says nothing about encryption at rest. It does not block HTTPS requests, because the condition does not match them.

objective.question: You create a Cloud Storage bucket in the asia-south1 region and set a Cloud KMS key as the default CMEK. Uploads fail with a permission error on the key. The key ring is in asia-south1. What is the most likely fix?
options: Grant the project's Cloud Storage service agent the roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter role on the key.
Move the key ring to the global location so all services can use it.
Enable uniform bucket-level access on the bucket.
Grant the user who uploads the roles/cloudkms.admin role on the key ring.
objective.explanation: With CMEK, Cloud Storage calls Cloud KMS through its service agent, not as the end user. So the service agent needs Encrypter/Decrypter on the key. The key location must match the bucket location, so a global key would fail. KMS admin on the user and uniform bucket-level access do not fix the service agent's missing permission.

objective.question: A company runs 30 Azure subscriptions under one management group. Every new and existing Key Vault, storage account and SQL database must send its diagnostic logs to a central Log Analytics workspace in the security subscription. Teams must not need to do anything. What should you implement?
options: A Microsoft Sentinel analytics rule that alerts when diagnostic settings are missing.
A resource lock of type ReadOnly on every resource group.
An Azure Policy initiative with the DeployIfNotExists effect at the management group, with a managed identity, plus a remediation task for existing resources.
An Azure Policy assignment with the Audit effect at each subscription.
objective.explanation: DeployIfNotExists creates the diagnostic settings automatically. It needs a managed identity with rights to deploy, and it needs a remediation task to fix resources that already exist. Audit only reports the gap. A Sentinel rule only alerts. A ReadOnly lock would block changes, not configure logging.

objective.question: An architect must share an encrypted EBS snapshot from a production account with a separate disaster recovery account. The snapshot was encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/ebs. Sharing fails. What should the architect do?
options: Create a KMS grant on aws/ebs for the DR account root user.
Share the snapshot publicly for a short time, then copy it in the DR account.
Copy the snapshot and re-encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key. Allow the DR account in that key's policy, then share the copy.
Edit the key policy of aws/ebs to allow the DR account.
objective.explanation: You cannot change the key policy of an AWS managed key, so snapshots encrypted with it cannot be shared across accounts. Re-encrypting with a customer managed key lets you grant the DR account access through the key policy. Encrypted snapshots cannot be made public at all, and making backups public would break security in any case.

objective.question: A team placed Azure Application Gateway WAF v2 with the OWASP managed rule set in front of a web app. A penetration test shows SQL injection attempts reaching the backend. The WAF logs show matching rule hits for these requests. What is the most likely cause?
options: Azure DDoS Network Protection is not enabled on the virtual network.
The backend pool uses HTTPS, so the WAF cannot inspect the traffic.
The managed rule set does not include SQL injection rules.
The WAF policy is in Detection mode, so matching requests are logged but not blocked.
objective.explanation: In Detection mode the WAF records rule matches but lets the requests through. Prevention mode is needed to block them. The logged rule hits show that the rules exist and inspection works, because Application Gateway terminates TLS. DDoS protection does not filter application-layer attacks such as SQL injection.

objective.question: An Azure hub-and-spoke network uses custom DNS servers (Windows Server VMs in the hub) that forward all queries to on-premises DNS. You create a private endpoint for a storage account and link the private DNS zone privatelink.blob.core.windows.net to the hub VNet. Spoke VMs still resolve the storage account to its public IP. What is the most likely cause?
options: Public network access on the storage account must be disabled before private DNS records are returned
The custom DNS servers do not forward privatelink queries to Azure-provided DNS (168.63.129.16), so the private DNS zone is never consulted
The private endpoint must be created in each spoke VNet, not in the hub
A network security group on the spoke subnet is blocking traffic to the private endpoint
objective.explanation: Private DNS zones are only answered by Azure-provided DNS, so custom DNS servers need a conditional forwarder for the storage zone to 168.63.129.16, or you can use Azure DNS Private Resolver. An NSG does not change name resolution. Disabling public access does not change DNS answers. One private endpoint in the hub works for peered spokes.

objective.question: On-premises servers connect to an AWS VPC over Direct Connect. They must upload to Amazon S3 privately, without using the internet. The team created an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and updated the route tables, but on-premises traffic still goes over the public path. What should the architect do?
options: Attach the gateway endpoint to the virtual private gateway
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) and have on-premises clients use its endpoint-specific DNS names
Add the on-premises CIDR to the gateway endpoint policy
objective.explanation: A gateway endpoint only works through VPC route tables, so on-premises networks cannot reach it over Direct Connect or VPN. An S3 interface endpoint has private IPs in the VPC that on-premises clients can reach. Endpoint policies and Transfer Acceleration do not change this routing limit.

objective.question: A data lake bucket holds billions of small objects. It uses this default encryption. The monthly KMS bill is high, and Athena jobs sometimes fail with KMS ThrottlingException. Security requires the customer managed key to stay in use. What is the best change?
options: Set BucketKeyEnabled to true so S3 uses a bucket-level key and makes far fewer calls to KMS
Create a multi-Region replica of the key in ap-south-2
Enable automatic key rotation on the KMS key
Switch the default encryption to SSE-S3
objective.explanation: S3 Bucket Keys let S3 create data keys from a short-lived bucket-level key. This sharply reduces KMS requests, cost and throttling, and the same customer managed key stays in use. SSE-S3 breaks the requirement. Rotation and multi-Region keys do not reduce the number of requests.

objective.question: A Lambda function in account 222222222222 reads S3 objects in account 111111111111. The objects are encrypted with this customer managed key. The Lambda role's IAM policy allows kms:Decrypt on the key ARN, and the bucket policy allows the role to call s3:GetObject. Reads fail with an AccessDenied error from KMS. What is the fix?
options: Enable automatic rotation on the key so that the new key material is shared
Create an alias for the key in account 222222222222
Re-encrypt the objects with the AWS managed key aws/s3 so that any account can read them
Add a key policy statement in account 111111111111 that allows the account 222222222222 principal (or the Lambda role) to call kms:Decrypt
objective.explanation: Cross-account KMS use needs two permissions: the key policy in the owning account must trust the other account, and an IAM policy in the calling account must allow the action. This key policy trusts only account 111111111111. AWS managed keys cannot be used across accounts, and rotation and aliases do not grant access.

objective.question: A Compute Engine VM has only an internal IP address and there is no Cloud NAT. It must call the Cloud Storage and BigQuery APIs. What is the simplest way to allow this?
options: Enable Private Google Access on the VM's subnet
Create a Private Service Connect endpoint for every bucket
Create VPC peering with the Google APIs network
Give the VM an external IP address
objective.explanation: Private Google Access is turned on per subnet. It lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Private Service Connect is an option for custom endpoints, but it is not created per bucket and it is not the simplest choice. An external IP breaks the private design.

objective.question: An Azure Storage account uses a customer-managed key in Key Vault through its system-assigned managed identity. It worked with vault access policies. An admin then switched the vault's permission model to Azure role-based access control, and the storage account can no longer reach its key. What should you do?
options: Assign the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role to the storage account's managed identity on the key or the vault
Disable purge protection and re-create the key
Assign the Key Vault Contributor role to the storage account's managed identity
Assign the Key Vault Reader role to the storage account's managed identity
objective.explanation: After the switch to Azure RBAC, the old access policies no longer apply. The identity needs a data-plane role that allows get, wrapKey and unwrapKey, which is what Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User grants. Key Vault Reader and Key Vault Contributor are management-plane roles and cannot use keys.

objective.question: A security team runs this command to collect audit logs from the whole Google Cloud organisation into a central log bucket. Org-level IAM changes appear in the bucket, but Admin Activity logs from projects are missing. What is the cause?

code.code:
gcloud logging sinks create org-audit-sink \
  logging.googleapis.com/projects/sec-logging/locations/asia-south1/buckets/org-audit \
  --organization=123456789012 \
  --log-filter='logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com"'

options: Data Access audit logs are not enabled in the projects
Log buckets must be in the global location to receive organisation logs
The sink was created without --include-children, so it only captures the organisation resource's own logs
The sink's writer identity has not been granted roles/logging.bucketWriter on the destination
objective.explanation: An aggregated sink needs --include-children to pull logs from all folders and projects under the organisation. A missing writer permission would stop all logs, including the org-level ones that do arrive. Admin Activity logs are always on, and regional log buckets are supported.

objective.question: A CloudTrail log archive bucket must keep every log object for 7 years. No user, including the account root user, may delete or overwrite an object during that period. Which S3 setting meets this requirement?
options: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year default retention
Versioning with MFA Delete enabled
A lifecycle rule that moves objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 7-year default retention
objective.explanation: In compliance mode, no user, including root, can delete a protected object version or shorten its retention. In governance mode, users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can delete objects. MFA Delete and lifecycle rules do not give a fixed retention guarantee.

objective.question: An auditor preparing your company's SOC 2 report asks for AWS's own SOC 2 Type 2 report and PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance. Where do you download them?
options: AWS Artifact
AWS Security Hub
AWS Config conformance packs
AWS Audit Manager
objective.explanation: AWS Artifact gives on-demand access to AWS's compliance reports. The equivalents are the Service Trust Portal on Azure and Compliance Reports Manager on Google Cloud. Audit Manager, Config and Security Hub help you collect evidence and check your own side of the shared responsibility model.

objective.question: AWS WAF is attached to a CloudFront distribution in front of an internet-facing Application Load Balancer. The ALB security group is shown below. A penetration tester sends SQL injection payloads straight to the ALB's DNS name, and they reach the application. What is the best fix?

code.code:
resource "aws_security_group_rule" "alb_https" {
  type              = "ingress"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  protocol          = "tcp"
  cidr_blocks       = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
}

options: Allow only the CloudFront origin-facing managed prefix list in the ALB security group, and require a secret custom header in an ALB listener rule (or use CloudFront VPC origins with an internal ALB)
Add a rate-based rule to the CloudFront web ACL
Associate the web ACL with the Route 53 hosted zone
Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced so the ALB is protected
objective.explanation: The WAF only inspects traffic that passes through CloudFront, and this security group lets anyone reach the ALB directly. Locking the origin to CloudFront closes the bypass. Shield Advanced and rate-based rules do not stop a direct-to-origin bypass, and AWS WAF cannot be attached to Route 53.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between encryption at rest and encryption in transit. How would you enforce each one on cloud storage?
subjective.answer: Encryption at rest protects data stored on disks, object storage, databases and backups, so a stolen disk or snapshot is unreadable. Encryption in transit protects data moving over the network, usually with TLS, so it cannot be read or changed on the wire. All three major clouds now encrypt storage at rest by default with provider-managed keys. For example, S3 has applied SSE-S3 to all new objects since January 2023. To enforce stronger at-rest control, I set default encryption to a customer managed key and use policy to block unencrypted resources. Examples are AWS Config rules, Azure Policy and Google organisation policy constraints for CMEK. For in transit, I add an S3 bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. On Azure I enable secure transfer required and set a minimum TLS version. I also use HTTPS listeners on load balancers. Both layers are needed, because each protects against a different threat.
keyPoints: At rest protects stored data; in transit protects data on the network (TLS)
Default provider encryption exists, e.g. SSE-S3 since January 2023
Enforce CMK use with Config, Azure Policy or organisation policy
Enforce TLS with aws:SecureTransport deny, secure transfer required, minimum TLS version

subjective.question: What is envelope encryption and why do cloud key management services use it?
subjective.answer: Envelope encryption uses two layers of keys. A data encryption key (DEK) encrypts the actual data locally, inside the storage service or the application. The DEK is then encrypted, or wrapped, by a key encryption key that lives inside AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault or Google Cloud KMS. The wrapped DEK is stored next to the data. To read the data, the service asks the KMS to unwrap the DEK, which happens only if IAM and the key policy allow it. This design has several benefits. Large data never travels to the KMS, so it is fast and cheap. The master key never leaves the service or HSM. Every unwrap call is logged, which gives an audit trail. Rotating or disabling the master key controls access to all data under it without re-encrypting terabytes. That is why revoking a CMK can make data unreadable almost instantly.
keyPoints: DEK encrypts data; KEK in KMS wraps the DEK
Master key never leaves the KMS/HSM; bulk data never sent to KMS
Each decrypt/unwrap is authorised and logged
Rotation or disabling the KEK controls access without re-encrypting all data

subjective.question: A client asks whether they should use provider-managed keys, customer-managed keys or external keys. How do you decide?
subjective.answer: I start from the requirement wording. If the client only needs data encrypted at rest, provider-managed keys are enough. They are free to operate, rotated by the provider, and need no key management work. If the client says they must control, audit, rotate or revoke the key, I recommend customer-managed keys: AWS KMS customer managed keys, Azure Key Vault CMK, or Google Cloud KMS CMEK. These give a key policy, separation of duties, and logs of every key use, but the team now owns rotation and deletion risk. On AWS, rotation for customer managed keys is optional, with a default period of one year. Deletion has a 7–30 day waiting period, and deleting a key makes its data unrecoverable. If the client says keys must never leave their premises, I recommend an external key store such as AWS XKS or Google Cloud EKM, or a dedicated HSM. I also warn them that this adds latency and availability dependencies.
keyPoints: Encryption only: provider-managed keys
Control, revoke or audit: CMK/CMEK with key policy and logging
Keys never leave premises: external key store (XKS, EKM) or dedicated HSM
CMK brings ownership of rotation and deletion risk; external keys add availability risk

subjective.question: Design central audit logging for a multi-account or multi-subscription landing zone so that every admin action is logged where developers cannot change it.
subjective.answer: First, I collect logs at the organisation level, not per account. On AWS, that means an organisation trail in CloudTrail. On Azure, I use diagnostic settings for the Activity Log, applied by Azure Policy across management groups. On Google Cloud, I use an aggregated log sink at the organisation level. Second, I send the logs to a dedicated log archive account, subscription or project. Only the security team can access it, and developers have no write or delete rights. Third, I make the storage write-once. I use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on AWS, immutable blob storage with a locked policy on Azure, and a locked retention policy on a Cloud Storage bucket. On AWS I also enable CloudTrail log file validation for tamper evidence, and I can encrypt the logs with a KMS key owned by security. Fourth, I use service control policies or Azure Policy to deny anyone from stopping trails or deleting diagnostic settings. This matters because CloudTrail Event history alone keeps only 90 days.
keyPoints: Organisation-wide collection: org trail, policy-driven diagnostic settings, aggregated sink
Separate log archive account with restricted access
Write-once storage: Object Lock compliance, immutable blob, locked bucket retention
Guardrails (SCP, Azure Policy) stop logging being disabled; log file validation

subjective.question: What does zero trust mean in a cloud architecture, and how would you apply it in practice?
subjective.answer: Zero trust means no user, device or network is trusted by default, even inside the corporate network. Every request is verified explicitly, given least privilege, and designed as if a breach has already happened. In practice, I make identity the main perimeter. I use single sign-on with MFA and conditional access, for example Microsoft Entra Conditional Access. I give short-lived, role-based credentials instead of long-lived keys, and just-in-time admin access such as Entra Privileged Identity Management. For network, I segment workloads and use private endpoints for PaaS services. I avoid exposing management ports, using services like Azure Bastion, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or Google Identity-Aware Proxy. I encrypt traffic everywhere, including east-west traffic. Finally, I log every access centrally and watch it with threat detection, so suspicious behaviour is caught quickly. Zero trust is a set of principles, not a single product.
keyPoints: Verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach
Identity as perimeter: SSO, MFA, conditional access, short-lived credentials
Just-in-time admin and no open management ports (Bastion, Session Manager, IAP)
Segmentation, private access, encryption everywhere, continuous monitoring

subjective.question: Compare the main options for private access to managed services on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
subjective.answer: The goal is to reach managed services without going over the public internet, and ideally to remove public endpoints. On AWS, gateway VPC endpoints serve S3 and DynamoDB through route tables. Interface endpoints, using AWS PrivateLink, place an ENI with a private IP in your subnet for many other services. Endpoint policies can restrict which buckets or actions are allowed. On Azure, service endpoints extend the VNet identity to the service, but the service keeps its public endpoint. Private endpoints, using Private Link, give the resource a private IP. You then need private DNS zones and should disable public network access. On Google Cloud, Private Google Access lets VMs without external IPs reach Google APIs. Private Service Connect gives private endpoints for Google APIs and producer services. VPC Service Controls add a perimeter against data exfiltration. For exam scenarios, the key phrase
keyPoints: AWS: gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and interface endpoints via PrivateLink with endpoint policies
Azure: service endpoints vs private endpoints; private DNS and disable public access
Google: Private Google Access, Private Service Connect, VPC Service Controls
DNS resolution is a common failure point with private endpoints

subjective.question: What is the difference between threat detection and security posture management? Name the native tools on each cloud.
subjective.answer: Posture management answers a simple question: is my environment configured safely? It continuously checks resources against benchmarks such as the CIS benchmarks. Typical findings are public buckets, unencrypted disks, missing MFA or open ports. Threat detection answers a different question: is someone attacking or misusing my environment right now? It analyses logs, DNS queries, network flows and API calls to find things like crypto-mining, credential theft or unusual data access. On AWS, AWS Config and Security Hub handle posture, GuardDuty handles threat detection, and Amazon Detective helps with investigation. On Azure, Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides both a secure score for posture and workload protection plans for threats. Microsoft Sentinel is the SIEM. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center covers posture findings and threat detection. In the landing zone, I enable these organisation-wide. I aggregate findings in the security account and build the posture dashboard there. I also route high-severity findings to alerts or automated remediation.
keyPoints: Posture = misconfiguration against benchmarks; threat detection = active malicious behaviour
AWS: Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty, Detective
Azure: Defender for Cloud (secure score and protection plans), Sentinel as SIEM
Google: Security Command Center; enable organisation-wide and aggregate centrally

subjective.question: How would you map a cloud platform to ISO 27001, SOC 2 and PCI DSS at a high level?
subjective.answer: First, I explain what each one is. ISO 27001 is a certifiable standard for an information security management system, with risk assessment and Annex A controls. SOC 2 is an independent attestation report against the Trust Services Criteria, such as security and availability. PCI DSS is a mandatory standard for anyone who stores, processes or transmits cardholder data. Then I apply the shared responsibility model. The cloud provider's own certifications cover the physical and infrastructure layers, and auditors can get these from AWS Artifact, the Microsoft Service Trust Portal or the Google Cloud compliance reports. My company still owns configuration, identity, data and application controls. I map each control to concrete evidence. For example, encryption maps to KMS and CMK settings, logging to immutable audit logs, access control to IAM and MFA, and vulnerability management to scanning. I use the compliance standards in posture tools, such as Security Hub, Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance and Security Command Center. For PCI, I reduce scope by isolating the cardholder data environment in separate accounts or networks.
keyPoints: ISO 27001 = ISMS certification; SOC 2 = attestation report; PCI DSS = card data standard
Shared responsibility: provider reports via Artifact, Service Trust Portal, Google compliance reports
Map controls to technical evidence (encryption, logs, IAM, scanning)
Use posture tool compliance dashboards; reduce PCI scope by isolation

subjective.question: An Indian fintech is moving customer data to the cloud. What does India's DPDP Act mean for the architecture?
subjective.answer: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 has operational DPDP Rules, which were notified in 2025, and many obligations phase in over a transition period. The fintech acts as a Data Fiduciary. Processing must be based on valid consent or a permitted legitimate use. So the platform needs consent records, purpose tagging and the ability to erase data when the purpose ends or consent is withdrawn. The Act requires reasonable security safeguards. Architecturally, that means encryption at rest with controlled keys, TLS in transit, least-privilege access, and immutable audit logs that show who accessed personal data. Processors such as SaaS vendors must be bound by contract. In a breach, the company must notify the Data Protection Board and affected individuals, and the Rules set a timeline for a detailed report to the Board. So threat detection, logging and an incident runbook must be ready in advance. Penalties can reach INR 250 crore for failing to apply security safeguards. Cross-border transfer is allowed unless the government restricts specific countries, but sector regulators such as RBI may still require data to stay in India.
keyPoints: Consent-based processing: consent records, purpose limitation, erasure
Reasonable security safeguards: encryption, access control, immutable logs
Breach notification to Data Protection Board and affected users; detection and runbooks needed
Penalties up to INR 250 crore; sector rules like RBI localisation still apply

subjective.question: Explain what this AWS KMS key policy statement does. Why is it useful for an S3 data key, and what must you check before applying it?
subjective.answer: This statement lets app-role encrypt, decrypt and generate data keys with this KMS key. It allows this only when the request comes through Amazon S3 in ap-south-1 on behalf of account 111122223333. The role cannot call kms:Decrypt directly from a laptop or script to unwrap data keys. It can only read objects through S3, where bucket policies, VPC endpoint policies and S3 logging also apply. This is least privilege for the key. Because Resource is "*" inside a key policy, it refers only to this key. Before applying it, I check three things. First, other statements must not grant the role wider KMS access, because Allows add up. Second, the key administrator statement must stay in place so the key cannot become unmanageable. Third, no other service, such as Lambda or Glue, needs the key directly. If one does, it needs its own scoped statement. I would also confirm that S3 Bucket Keys are enabled, because they reduce KMS request cost.
keyPoints: kms:ViaService limits key use to requests made through S3 in one Region
Blocks direct Decrypt calls outside the service path
Key policy Allows are additive, so check other grants
Keep the key administrator statement to avoid an unmanageable key
Consider S3 Bucket Keys to cut KMS calls and cost

subjective.question: A public web application on Google Cloud sits behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Design its WAF and DDoS protection with Google Cloud Armor, and explain how you would roll out rules without breaking real users.
subjective.answer: The global external Application Load Balancer already absorbs volumetric layer 3 and 4 DDoS attacks at Google's edge. I attach a Cloud Armor backend security policy to the backend service for layer 7 protection. In that policy I add preconfigured WAF rules based on the OWASP Core Rule Set, for example SQL injection, XSS, LFI and RCE. I add rate-limiting or rate-based ban rules on sensitive paths such as login. If needed, I add geo or IP allow and deny lists. I enable Adaptive Protection, which learns normal traffic and suggests rules during layer 7 floods. For a critical site, Cloud Armor Enterprise adds DDoS response support and bill protection. For rollout, I first put new rules in preview mode. Cloud Armor then logs what it would block without blocking it. I review the request logs in Cloud Logging and tune sensitivity levels or exclude specific fields to remove false positives. After that I switch the rules to enforce. I also lock backends so traffic reaches them only through the load balancer.
keyPoints: Load balancer edge absorbs L3/L4 DDoS; Cloud Armor handles L7
Preconfigured OWASP-based WAF rules plus rate limiting
Adaptive Protection for L7 attack detection
Preview mode and log review before enforcing
Restrict backends so traffic cannot bypass the load balancer

subjective.question: An auditor asks how key rotation works for your customer-managed keys on AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault and Google Cloud KMS. Does rotation re-encrypt existing data? What would you do if a key were suspected compromised?
subjective.answer: On all three clouds, rotation creates new key material, but the key keeps the same identity. In AWS KMS, automatic rotation for symmetric customer managed keys keeps the same key ID and ARN and keeps the old backing keys so old ciphertext still decrypts. In Azure Key Vault, a rotation policy creates a new key version. Services such as Storage can follow the latest version automatically if they reference the key without a version. In Cloud KMS, a rotation period creates a new primary key version, and old versions stay enabled. Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data. New data keys are wrapped with the new material, and old data stays readable with the old versions. Envelope encryption makes this cheap. If a key is suspected compromised, rotation alone is not enough. I would create a new key or version and re-encrypt the data, or copy it re-encrypted, for example with S3 batch copy or an EBS snapshot copy. I would review the key's audit logs, then disable the old key and later destroy it.
keyPoints: Rotation adds new key material and keeps old versions for decryption
Existing data is not re-encrypted by rotation
Azure versionless key references allow automatic version uptake
A compromise needs re-encryption, not just rotation
Review audit logs, then disable and later destroy the old key

subjective.question: Explain what this service control policy does in an AWS Organization, why it supports the checkpoint 'admin actions are logged where developers cannot change it', and what gaps remain.
subjective.answer: Attached to workload OUs, this SCP denies everyone in member accounts, including the root user and administrators, the right to stop or change CloudTrail, remove GuardDuty or stop AWS Config. The only exception is the SecurityBreakGlass role. An SCP sets the maximum permissions, so even AdministratorAccess cannot override it. Developers therefore cannot switch off the audit trail or the detective controls. Some gaps remain. First, SCPs do not apply to the management account, so access to that account must be tightly controlled. Second, SCPs do not affect service-linked roles. Third, the policy protects the logging services but not the log data itself. I would also deliver an organization trail to a separate Log Archive account, with S3 Object Lock, CloudTrail log file validation and a restrictive bucket policy. Fourth, the break-glass role needs MFA, alerting on every use and protection so it cannot be created in any account. Fifth, GuardDuty's delegated administrator should manage member detectors, and Security Hub or Config rules should flag drift.
keyPoints: SCPs cap permissions even for admins and root in member accounts
Protects CloudTrail, GuardDuty and Config from being disabled
Management account and service-linked roles are not restricted
Log data needs Object Lock and validation in a separate Log Archive account
The break-glass exception needs MFA, alerting and tight control

subjective.question: Your checkpoint says every data store must be encrypted. How would you prove this continuously across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and stop non-compliant stores from being created?
subjective.answer: I use two layers on each cloud: preventive guardrails and continuous detection. On AWS, S3 now encrypts new objects by default, and I enable EBS encryption by default in each Region. SCPs or IaC checks block unencrypted RDS instances. Where CMKs are required, bucket policies demand SSE-KMS. AWS Config managed rules such as rds-storage-encrypted, encrypted-volumes and S3 encryption checks run in an organization conformance pack, and Security Hub aggregates the findings. On Azure, platform encryption is always on. To require customer-managed keys, I assign built-in Azure Policy definitions with the Deny effect at the management group. Defender for Cloud and Policy compliance reports show the status. On Google Cloud, data is encrypted by default. Where CMEK is required, the organization policy constraint gcp.restrictNonCmekServices forces it, and Security Command Center reports findings. In CI, Checkov or a similar tool scans Terraform before deployment. The evidence for auditors is the posture dashboard plus compliance history, not screenshots.
keyPoints: Defaults: S3/Azure/Google encrypt at rest; turn on EBS default encryption
Preventive: SCPs, Azure Policy Deny, Google org policy for CMEK
Detective: AWS Config/Security Hub, Defender for Cloud, Security Command Center
Shift left with IaC scanning in CI
Compliance history is the audit evidence

subjective.question: A bucket has held millions of objects encrypted with SSE-S3 for three years. Compliance now requires all data, old and new, to use a customer managed KMS key. List, in order, the steps you would take, and explain the common mistake teams make.
subjective.answer: First, create the customer managed key. Write a key policy that keeps key administrators separate from key users, and grant the application roles kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt. Second, change the bucket's default encryption to SSE-KMS with this key and enable S3 Bucket Keys to control cost. Third, optionally add a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests that name a different key. The common mistake is stopping at this point. Default encryption applies only to new writes, so existing objects stay on SSE-S3. Fourth, generate an S3 Inventory report, then run an S3 Batch Operations Copy job that copies every object in place with the new KMS key. Fifth, if versioning is on, the old SSE-S3 copies remain as noncurrent versions. Expire them with a lifecycle rule once retention rules allow it. Finally, check the encryption status field in a fresh Inventory report, and confirm through CloudTrail that KMS calls are coming from S3.
keyPoints: Create the CMK with a key policy that separates administrators from users
Default encryption affects only new objects
Use S3 Inventory plus a Batch Operations copy to re-encrypt existing data
Handle noncurrent versions that still use SSE-S3
Verify with Inventory encryption status and CloudTrail

subjective.question: After the team moved its AMIs and EBS volumes to a customer managed KMS key, the Auto Scaling group's new instances go to terminated almost immediately. The activity history shows the error below. Launching the same AMI by hand works. What is the cause and how do you fix it?

code.code:
Launching a new EC2 instance: i-0abc123. Status Reason:
Client.InternalError: Client error on launch.

subjective.answer: This error usually means EC2 Auto Scaling cannot use the KMS key that encrypts the EBS volumes. A manual launch works because it runs with my own IAM permissions. Auto Scaling, however, launches instances through its service-linked role, AWSServiceRoleForAutoScaling, and the new customer managed key's policy does not trust that role. The fix is to add a key policy statement that allows the service-linked role to call kms:Encrypt, kms:Decrypt, kms:ReEncrypt*, kms:GenerateDataKey* and kms:DescribeKey. Add a second statement that allows kms:CreateGrant with the condition kms:GrantIsForAWSResource set to true. If the key is in another account, the key policy must also trust that account, and a grant must be created for the service-linked role in the Auto Scaling account. I would then test a scale-out, check CloudTrail for KMS AccessDenied events, and record this in the landing zone's key policy template.
keyPoints: Auto Scaling launches through its service-linked role, not the user's role
The key policy must allow the role to call Decrypt, GenerateDataKey* and DescribeKey
CreateGrant is needed, with the GrantIsForAWSResource condition
Cross-account keys also need a grant
Confirm the fix using CloudTrail KMS events

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this Terraform for a CloudTrail organisation trail destination bucket. The comment says where it is deployed. Explain how you would fix each one.
subjective.answer: There are several mistakes. First, the bucket is in a workload account, so that account's administrators can delete the logs. Move it to a dedicated Log Archive account that only the security team can access. Second, versioning is suspended and there is no Object Lock. Enable versioning, then enable Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention that matches the audit requirement. Third, the policy grants s3:* to the whole account, which includes delete and policy changes. Replace it with the standard CloudTrail statements: allow the cloudtrail.amazonaws.com principal to call s3:GetBucketAcl and to call s3:PutObject on the AWSLogs prefix, with aws:SourceArn or aws:SourceOrgID conditions. Add explicit denies for object deletes and for non-TLS requests. Fourth, there is no SSE-KMS with a customer managed key and no block public access. Add both, and turn on CloudTrail log file validation. Finally, use an SCP so that member accounts cannot stop or delete the trail.
keyPoints: Keep logs in a separate Log Archive account
Enable versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode
Use a least-privilege CloudTrail service principal policy, not s3:*
Add SSE-KMS, block public access and deny non-TLS requests
Enable log file validation and protect the trail with an SCP

subjective.question: Compare Azure Key Vault Standard, Key Vault Premium and Azure Key Vault Managed HSM, and map them to their AWS and Google Cloud equivalents. Which would you choose for a payments company that needs single-tenant HSMs, and why?
subjective.answer: Key Vault Standard protects keys in software and also stores secrets and certificates. Premium adds HSM-backed keys in a multi-tenant HSM service. Managed HSM is a single-tenant, fully managed HSM pool with a higher FIPS validation level. Each pool has its own security domain, and you control it through local RBAC. The closest AWS match is AWS KMS for the first two, and CloudHSM, or a KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM, for single-tenant needs. On Google Cloud, Cloud KMS offers software and HSM protection levels, Cloud HSM uses Google-managed HSMs, and Cloud External Key Manager keeps keys outside Google. For a payments company that needs single-tenant HSMs, I would choose Managed HSM. It still works with Azure Storage, SQL and Disk encryption as customer-managed keys. The trade-offs are higher cost, and the team must back up the security domain safely, because losing it means losing the keys.
keyPoints: Standard uses software keys; Premium uses multi-tenant HSM-backed keys
Managed HSM is single-tenant, with its own security domain and local RBAC
Equivalents: KMS/CloudHSM on AWS; Cloud KMS/Cloud HSM/EKM on Google Cloud
Choose based on the tenancy and validation level the regulator requires
Managed HSM adds cost and security-domain backup responsibility

subjective.question: A developer cannot SSH to a private VM using Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding. The command and error are shown. The VM has no external IP. What is failing, and what would you check in order?

code.code:
gcloud compute ssh app-vm-1 --zone=asia-south1-a --tunnel-through-iap
# ERROR: Error while connecting [4003: 'failed to connect to backend']

subjective.answer: Error 4003 means IAP accepted the user, but IAP could not open a TCP connection to the VM. It is a network problem, not an IAM problem; an IAM failure shows as 4033. First, I check the VPC firewall rules. There must be an ingress rule that allows TCP 22 from IAP's range, 35.235.240.0/20, to the VM, for example by network tag or service account. Many landing zones deny all ingress by default and forget this rule. Second, I confirm that the SSH daemon is running on port 22 and that the guest OS firewall allows it, using the serial console if needed. Third, I confirm that the zone and instance name are correct. If the error changes to 4033, I would check that the user has roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor, plus OS Login roles if OS Login is enforced. The VM does not need an external IP. This is the zero trust pattern of identity-aware access with no open bastion.
keyPoints: 4003 means a backend connection failure, not an authorisation failure
The firewall must allow 35.235.240.0/20 on port 22
Check sshd and the guest OS firewall
4033 points to roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor or OS Login roles
No external IP or bastion is needed

subjective.question: Your Application Load Balancer terminates TLS and sends plain HTTP to EC2 targets. A zero trust review flags this. Compare re-encrypting at the ALB with TLS passthrough on a Network Load Balancer. Which is better here, and why?
subjective.answer: With re-encryption, the ALB terminates the client TLS session, inspects the request, and opens a new HTTPS connection to each target. This keeps layer 7 features: AWS WAF, path-based routing, authentication with Cognito or OIDC, and access logs. The targets need certificates, which can be private or self-signed because the ALB does not validate them strictly. With NLB TLS passthrough, the encrypted stream goes to the targets unchanged, so TLS runs end to end and the targets hold the only private key. However, you lose WAF inspection and HTTP routing at the load balancer, and certificates must be managed on every instance. For a public web application that must also block OWASP attacks, I would choose ALB re-encryption, because the WAF must see plaintext. Passthrough fits non-HTTP protocols, or cases where the client uses mutual TLS with the backend and no intermediary may see the data. In both cases, enforce TLS 1.2 or higher with a modern security policy.
keyPoints: Re-encryption keeps WAF and layer 7 features
Passthrough gives true end-to-end TLS but loses inspection
Weigh certificate management on targets
The WAF requirement usually decides the choice
Enforce a minimum TLS version policy

subjective.question: Case study: An Indian health-tech start-up is building on Azure. Requirements: patient data stays in India; the company can revoke access to its encryption keys; the public API is protected from OWASP attacks and large DDoS floods; every admin action is kept tamper-proof for audits; developers have no standing access to production data. Propose an architecture.
subjective.answer: I would use a management group hierarchy with Azure Policy that allows only Central India and South India and denies public network access on data services. Data would live in Azure SQL and Storage, encrypted with customer-managed keys in a Premium Key Vault. The vault would have purge protection and soft delete, and the keys would sit in a security subscription. Disabling the key or removing the managed identity's role revokes access. Storage and SQL would be reached only through private endpoints with linked private DNS zones. Public traffic would enter through Azure Front Door Premium with WAF managed rules, in prevention mode after tuning, and Azure DDoS Protection would cover the virtual network's public IPs. Activity logs and diagnostic logs would be sent by policy to a central Log Analytics workspace and to an immutable storage account in a separate subscription. Microsoft Sentinel would provide detection and Defender for Cloud would track posture. Developers would get access only through Entra PIM, which is time-bound and approved. These controls support DPDP Act duties, but legal processes such as consent and breach notice are still required.
keyPoints: Region restriction and deny-public policies at the management group
CMK in Key Vault with purge protection gives the ability to revoke
Private endpoints, Front Door WAF and DDoS Protection
Central, immutable logs in a separate subscription, with Sentinel and Defender for Cloud
PIM for just-in-time access; DPDP duties extend beyond technical controls

subjective.question: An e-commerce company on AWS wants the smallest possible PCI DSS scope. How would you design the platform to reduce scope, and what remains the company's responsibility?
subjective.answer: The biggest reduction comes from never touching card data. I would use a PCI-compliant payment provider's hosted payment page or iframe. The card number then goes straight from the browser to the provider, and the company stores only tokens. If card data must be handled, I would isolate the cardholder data environment in dedicated AWS accounts under a separate OU. It would get its own VPCs, strict security groups, no peering to non-PCI workloads, and SCPs that limit Regions and services. Inside it, data would be encrypted with customer managed KMS keys, TLS 1.2 or higher would be required, CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs would go to the log archive, and GuardDuty and Config rules would run. AWS's PCI attestation in Artifact covers only the infrastructure. The company remains responsible for its own code, secure development, access reviews, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, log review and the security of its web pages, including protecting the payment page scripts.
keyPoints: Hosted payment pages and tokenisation remove card data from scope
Isolate the CDE in separate accounts with SCPs and network segmentation
Use encryption, logging and detection inside the CDE
The provider's attestation covers only its side
The customer still owns application, access, scanning and testing

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to roll out Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub across a 60-account AWS Organization, so that new accounts are covered automatically. Explain why the order matters.
subjective.answer: First, in the management account, register a dedicated security tooling account as the delegated administrator for GuardDuty and for Security Hub. The management account should not run day-to-day security work. Second, do this in every Region the organisation uses, because GuardDuty is a Regional service. Third, from the delegated administrator, turn on auto-enable for all existing and new member accounts, and choose the protection plans you need, such as S3 and EKS protection.
