files.code:
# landing-zone-iac

Step 9 sample: a landing zone as Terraform modules, with plan review on every pull request.

## Layout
- `modules/network/` - reusable VPC module (inputs in variables.tf, resources in main.tf).
- `envs/dev/` - one environment. It sets the remote state, the provider and the module inputs.
- `policy/plan.rego` - OPA policy. Conftest runs it against the JSON plan.
- `.github/workflows/terraform-plan.yml` - runs fmt, validate, plan and policy, then comments the plan on the PR.

## One-time setup
1. Create a versioned S3 bucket for state (see the run commands). Use your own account ID in the name.
2. Create an IAM role that GitHub can assume through OIDC. Give it read-only rights for plan.
3. Save the role ARN as the repo secret `AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN`.

## Key ideas
- Declarative and idempotent: running `apply` twice makes no second change.
- State: S3 backend with `use_lockfile = true` (native S3 locking, Terraform 1.10+). No DynamoDB table is needed.
- One state file per environment. A small blast radius per apply.
- Policy as code: the pipeline fails if a VPC has no `cost-centre` tag or a rule opens SSH to the internet.
- Apply happens only after review and merge. Use a separate apply job with a protected GitHub environment.

## Checkpoint: new environment in under an hour
1. `cp -r envs/dev envs/test`
2. In `envs/test/main.tf` change the state `key`, `environment` and `cidr` (for example 10.20.0.0/16).
3. Open a PR, read the posted plan, merge, then apply.

Same idea in other clouds: CloudFormation or CDK on AWS, Bicep on Azure, Terraform or Infrastructure Manager on Google Cloud.

# Policy as code for Terraform plans. Run with:
#   conftest test --policy policy envs/dev/plan.json
# Input is the output of `terraform show -json tfplan`.
package main

import rego.v1

# Resources being created or changed in this plan.
changed contains rc if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	some action in rc.change.actions
	action in {"create", "update"}
}

# Rule 1: every VPC must carry a cost-centre tag (FinOps showback).
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in changed
	rc.type == "aws_vpc"
	not rc.change.after.tags_all["cost-centre"]
	msg := sprintf("%s must have a cost-centre tag", [rc.address])
}

# Rule 2: no SSH open to the whole internet.
deny contains msg if {
	some rc in changed
	rc.type == "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule"
	rc.change.after.cidr_ipv4 == "0.0.0.0/0"
	rc.change.after.from_port <= 22
	rc.change.after.to_port >= 22
	msg := sprintf("%s opens SSH to 0.0.0.0/0", [rc.address])
}

# Rule 3: warn (not fail) when anything will be destroyed, so reviewers look twice.
warn contains msg if {
	some rc in input.resource_changes
	"delete" in rc.change.actions
	msg := sprintf("%s will be destroyed", [rc.address])
}

# On every pull request: fmt, validate, plan, post the plan as a comment, then check policy.
name: terraform-plan

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["envs/**", "modules/**", "policy/**"]

permissions:
  id-token: write       # OIDC to AWS, no long-lived keys
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write  # to post the plan comment

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: envs/dev
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ secrets.AWS_PLAN_ROLE_ARN }} # read-only plan role
          aws-region: ap-south-1

      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with:
          terraform_wrapper: false # clean stdout for show -json

      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive ../..
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -no-color -out=tfplan
      - run: |
          terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt
          terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json

      - name: Post plan on the PR
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require('fs');
            const plan = fs.readFileSync('envs/dev/plan.txt', 'utf8').slice(0, 60000);
            const body = '#### Terraform plan: envs/dev\n<details><summary>Show plan</summary>\n\n```\n' + plan + '\n```\n</details>';
            await github.rest.issues.createComment({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              body
            });

      - name: Policy check (OPA / Conftest)
        working-directory: .
        run: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/project" openpolicyagent/conftest test --policy policy envs/dev/plan.json

revision.examFocus: This step maps to deployment and governance objectives across the path. SAA-C03 and SAP-C02 cover CloudFormation, StackSets, SCPs and multi-account rollout. AZ-104 and AZ-305 cover ARM/Bicep, what-if, Azure Policy and management groups. Google ACE and PCA cover Terraform-based provisioning and Organization Policy. Exams rarely ask for syntax. They give a scenario (many accounts, drift, a compliance rule, a safe rollout) and ask for the native tool or control with the least effort and the smallest blast radius.

compare.a: AWS SCP (or Azure Policy / GCP Organization Policy)
compare.b: IAM policy / Azure RBAC role assignment
compare.difference: Guardrails only limit what is possible, or which resource properties are allowed. IAM/RBAC actually grant a principal the right to act. An action needs an allow from IAM/RBAC and no deny from the guardrail.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question says 'prevent across all accounts/subscriptions', 'even administrators', or 'only allowed Regions/SKUs'.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when a user or pipeline 'cannot perform' an action and nothing in the question says a guardrail blocks it.

compare.b: CloudFormation drift detection
compare.difference: A change set previews what your new template will do before deployment. Drift detection compares live resources with the last deployed template to find manual edits.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for 'review changes before updating the stack' or 'see if a resource will be replaced'.
compare.chooseB: Pick it for 'someone changed resources in the console' or 'find out-of-band modifications'.

compare.b: Azure Policy effect DeployIfNotExists / Modify
compare.difference: Deny blocks a non-compliant create or update. DeployIfNotExists and Modify fix compliance automatically, and existing resources need a remediation task. Both of these effects need a managed identity on the assignment.
compare.chooseA: Pick Deny when the requirement is 'must never be created', such as public IPs or disallowed Regions.
compare.chooseB: Pick DeployIfNotExists/Modify when the requirement is 'ensure every resource gets diagnostics, tags or an agent automatically'.

compare.b: Native IaC (CloudFormation/CDK, Bicep)
compare.difference: With Terraform you run and protect state yourself, but one workflow covers many providers and SaaS. Native tools have provider-managed state and support on day one for new services, but they work in one cloud only.
compare.chooseA: Pick Terraform for multi-cloud, hybrid, third-party providers (DNS, monitoring), or one team standard across clouds.
compare.chooseB: Pick native IaC for a single-cloud shop that wants no state backend, automatic rollback (CloudFormation) or tight portal integration.

compare.b: Single CloudFormation stack in a pipeline
compare.difference: StackSets deploy the same template to many accounts and Regions. With service-managed permissions through AWS Organizations, they can also auto-deploy to new accounts in an OU.
compare.chooseA: Pick StackSets for 'baseline in every account', 'new accounts automatically get' or 'multiple Regions at once'.
compare.chooseB: Pick a single stack for one application in one account and Region.

cues.cue: New accounts added to the OU must automatically get the baseline
cues.pick: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment (or Control Tower customisations)
cues.why: They target OUs, not fixed account lists, so new accounts are covered with no manual step.

cues.cue: Preview changes to an Azure resource group before deploying Bicep
cues.pick: az deployment group what-if
cues.why: It is the native dry run for ARM/Bicep, the Azure version of terraform plan.

cues.cue: Block a non-compliant Terraform change before apply
cues.pick: Policy as code on the plan JSON (Sentinel in HCP Terraform, or OPA/Conftest on 'terraform show -json' output)
cues.why: Checking the plan catches violations in the pipeline, before anything is created in the cloud.

cues.cue: Restrict resource locations for every project in the organisation (Google Cloud)
cues.pick: Organization Policy Service constraint (resource locations) at the organisation or folder node
cues.why: Org policies inherit down the hierarchy, like SCPs or management-group policy assignments.

cues.cue: Run Terraform as a managed Google Cloud service
cues.pick: Infrastructure Manager
cues.why: It is Google's managed Terraform service and replaces the deprecated Deployment Manager, so do not pick Deployment Manager for new designs.

cues.cue: Stop the database being lost when the stack is deleted or the resource replaced
cues.pick: DeletionPolicy: Retain or Snapshot (plus UpdateReplacePolicy)
cues.why: Without these, CloudFormation deletes stateful resources along with the stack.

cues.cue: Developers need self-service, approved infrastructure without learning IaC
cues.pick: Golden path: AWS Service Catalog products, Azure template specs / deployment stacks, or an IDP portal such as Backstage backed by versioned modules
cues.why: Platform teams publish vetted templates and developers consume them with guardrails built in.

cues.cue: Rename or move a Terraform resource without recreating it
cues.pick: moved block
cues.why: It updates the state address and leaves the real resource alone, so there is no destroy and create.

scenario.situation: A company runs 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. Security requires that no account can disable CloudTrail, and that every account, including future ones, gets a standard IAM role and a set of AWS Config rules. The platform team wants the least operational overhead. Engineers in member accounts have AdministratorAccess. What should the architect implement?
reasoning: Split the requirement in two: something must be prevented (disabling CloudTrail), and something must be deployed everywhere (role plus Config rules).
Prevention that must beat AdministratorAccess points to an SCP on the OU or root. IAM permission boundaries need per-account work and admins can change them.

Deployment to all current and future accounts points to StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment on the OU. A script looping over accounts adds overhead and misses new accounts.
Reject 'AWS Config remediation only' for CloudTrail. It detects and fixes after the event but does not prevent it.
Remember the SCP does not cover the management account, so keep workloads out of it.
scenario.answer: Attach an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail to the workload OUs. Deploy the IAM role and Config rules with a service-managed CloudFormation StackSet that has automatic deployment turned on for those OUs.

memoryAids: GRANT vs GUARD: IAM/RBAC GRANT access. SCP, Azure Policy and Org Policy only GUARD it. A guard never opens a door.
Preview twins: plan (Terraform) = change set (CloudFormation) = what-if (Bicep). Drift twins: refresh-only plan (Terraform) = drift detection (CloudFormation).
State splits by 'E-L': split by Environment and by Layer, so each plan stays small and safe.
cheatSheet: Prevent = SCP / Deny policy / Org Policy constraint. Detect = AWS Config / Audit. Auto-fix = Config remediation / DeployIfNotExists or Modify.
DeployIfNotExists and Modify need a managed identity. Existing non-compliant resources need a remediation task.
An Azure Policy initiative is a group of policies. Assign it at a management group so it inherits to all subscriptions.
CDK synthesises to CloudFormation. 'cdk diff' previews changes, and CloudFormation still owns state and rollback.
A failed CloudFormation update rolls back automatically. Terraform has no automatic rollback, so you fix forward or re-apply the previous code.
Terraform 'plan -refresh-only' shows drift without changing infrastructure. Run it on a schedule for drift alerts.
Share outputs between Terraform layers with remote state outputs or data sources, and keep each layer's state separate.
Pipeline pattern: PR runs fmt, validate, plan, policy check and posts the plan. Merge runs an approval gate, then applies the saved plan.
Use OIDC federation from CI (GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, GitLab) to cloud roles instead of long-lived access keys.
Bicep modules can be shared through template specs or a private Bicep registry in Azure Container Registry.
Google Cloud: Infrastructure Manager for managed Terraform, Config Connector to manage resources as Kubernetes objects. Deployment Manager is deprecated.
Terraform 'workspaces' share one backend config, so for strong isolation between prod and non-prod prefer separate state and credentials.
selfCheck: I can pick Terraform, CloudFormation/CDK or Bicep for a scenario and justify it in one sentence.
I can tell whether a requirement needs a grant (IAM/RBAC), a preventive guardrail, a detective control or auto-remediation.
I can design a Terraform state layout by environment and layer, with a remote, locked, encrypted backend and least-privilege plan and apply roles.
I can explain how StackSets, management-group policy assignments and Org Policy reach accounts or subscriptions that do not exist yet.
I can refactor or adopt resources with moved and import blocks without destroying anything, and detect drift on a schedule.
I can build a PR pipeline that posts the plan, runs a policy check and applies only the reviewed plan after approval.

objective.question: A team runs 'terraform plan' in a pull request and a reviewer approves it. Two hours later the pipeline runs 'terraform apply' and changes a resource nobody reviewed, because the code on main changed in between. What is the best fix?
options: Save the plan with 'terraform plan -out=tfplan' and apply exactly that file with 'terraform apply tfplan'
Run 'terraform refresh' before every apply
Run 'terraform validate' in the apply stage
Run 'terraform apply -auto-approve' immediately after the plan step
objective.explanation: A saved plan file locks in the exact changes that were reviewed, and apply executes only those changes. Auto-approve removes the review gate. Refresh and validate do not tie the apply to the reviewed plan.

objective.question: Two engineers ran 'terraform apply' at the same time against the same S3 remote state and corrupted it. The team uses a recent Terraform version and wants the simplest supported fix. What should they do?
options: Enable S3 versioning only
Set use_lockfile = true in the S3 backend configuration to enable native S3 state locking
Switch to local state and share the file over a network drive
Store state in Git so changes are versioned
objective.explanation: Recent Terraform versions support native S3 locking through use_lockfile, which stops concurrent applies. Older setups used a DynamoDB table for this. Versioning helps recovery but does not lock, and state must never live in Git or on shared local files.

objective.question: A CloudFormation stack contains a production Amazon RDS database. The team must make sure the data survives if someone deletes the stack. What should they add to the database resource?
options: A stack policy that denies Update:Replace
DependsOn to the VPC resource
Termination protection on the EC2 instances
DeletionPolicy: Snapshot (or Retain)
objective.explanation: DeletionPolicy: Snapshot takes a final snapshot on stack delete, and Retain keeps the resource. A stack policy guards against updates, not stack deletion. The other two options do not protect RDS data.

objective.question: A company using AWS Organizations must deploy the same AWS Config rules and IAM roles to every account in three Regions. New accounts must get them automatically. Which approach needs the least operational effort?
options: Use CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to an OU
Use CloudFormation change sets in the management account
Write a Lambda function that calls CreateStack in every account
Run a CloudFormation stack by hand in each account
objective.explanation: StackSets deploy one template across many accounts and Regions. With service-managed permissions and automatic deployment, new accounts in the target OU get the stack automatically. Change sets only preview changes to a single stack.

objective.question: An Azure engineer moving from Terraform to Bicep asks where to store the Bicep state file and how to preview changes before deployment. What is the correct answer?
options: Bicep has no state file because Azure Resource Manager tracks deployed resources; preview with 'az deployment group what-if'
Store state in Key Vault and preview with 'az deployment group validate'
Bicep keeps state in the .bicepparam file; preview with 'bicep plan'
Store state in an Azure Storage blob with a lease lock and preview with 'bicep build'
objective.explanation: Bicep compiles to ARM templates, and ARM itself knows the current resource state, so no state file is needed. The what-if operation shows the creates, changes and deletes. 'bicep build' only compiles, and 'validate' checks syntax and rules without showing a change preview.

objective.question: An organisation needs every new Azure storage account across 40 subscriptions to automatically get diagnostic settings that send logs to a central Log Analytics workspace. Which approach should it use?
options: An Azure Policy with the DeployIfNotExists effect assigned at the management group, with a managed identity for remediation
An Azure Policy with the Deny effect assigned at the subscription level
A resource lock on each subscription
An Azure Policy with the Audit effect assigned to each resource group
objective.explanation: DeployIfNotExists deploys the missing configuration and needs a managed identity to do it. Assigning at the management group covers all child subscriptions. Audit only reports, Deny blocks creation, and locks do not configure anything.

objective.question: A security team attaches an SCP to the root of AWS Organizations that denies ec2:RunInstances outside ap-south-1. A developer in a member account has an IAM policy allowing ec2:* everywhere. An admin in the management account also launches an instance in us-east-1. What happens?
options: The developer is blocked in us-east-1; the management account admin is not affected by the SCP
Both succeed because the IAM policies allow ec2:*
The developer succeeds because IAM allow overrides SCP deny
Both launches are blocked
objective.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for member accounts, and an explicit deny there wins over any IAM allow. SCPs never grant permissions and do not affect the management account, which is why workloads should not run in it.

objective.question: You refactor Terraform by moving 'aws_vpc.main' into a new module called 'network'. The plan now shows the VPC will be destroyed and recreated. How do you keep the existing VPC with the least risk?
options: Add a moved block with from = aws_vpc.main and to = module.network.aws_vpc.main
Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } and apply
Delete the state file and use an import block
Run 'terraform state rm aws_vpc.main' and re-run apply
objective.explanation: A moved block tells Terraform the resource address changed, so it updates state without destroying anything, and it is reviewable in code. prevent_destroy only makes the plan fail. State rm and deleting state are risky manual steps.

objective.question: A company runs workloads on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. It wants one IaC language, one review workflow and shared modules for all three. Which tool fits best?
options: Terraform
AWS CDK
Azure Bicep
AWS CloudFormation
objective.explanation: Terraform uses providers for all major clouds with one workflow (init, plan, apply) and one module system. CloudFormation and CDK target AWS, and Bicep targets Azure, so they suit single-cloud work.

objective.question: A team creates subnets with the code below. They remove "10.0.2.0/24" from the list. The plan shows that the third subnet will be destroyed and recreated, and the second subnet will get a new CIDR. What change best prevents this behaviour in the future?
options: Switch to for_each over a map keyed by a stable name (for example "app-a"), so each subnet's address does not depend on its list position
Run 'terraform apply -refresh-only' before every change to the list
Wrap the resource in a module and call the module three times with count
Add lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true } to the subnet resource
objective.explanation: With count, resources are addressed by index, so removing a middle element shifts every later index and forces changes. for_each uses stable keys, so only the removed subnet is affected. create_before_destroy only changes the order of replacement, a refresh-only apply does not change addressing, and module count has the same index problem.

objective.question: A company standardises on Terraform. On Google Cloud it wants a managed service that runs Terraform plans and applies inside Google Cloud, stores the state for them, and runs under a specified service account. The team does not want to run its own runners. Which service should it use?
options: Infrastructure Manager
Cloud Build with a gcloud deployment-manager step
Config Connector installed on a GKE cluster
Cloud Deployment Manager with Jinja templates
objective.explanation: Infrastructure Manager is Google Cloud's managed service for Terraform. It runs plans and applies, manages state, and uses a service account you choose. Deployment Manager uses its own template format and Google has deprecated it. Config Connector manages resources as Kubernetes objects, not Terraform.

objective.question: In HCP Terraform, a platform team writes a Sentinel policy that blocks any run that opens SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0. In rare incidents, the security lead must be able to approve an exception for a single run without editing the policy. Which enforcement level should the policy use?
options: soft-mandatory
hard-mandatory
Disable the policy set for that workspace during incidents
advisory
objective.explanation: With soft-mandatory, a failing run is blocked, but a user with override permission can approve it, and the override is logged. Advisory only shows a warning and never blocks. Hard-mandatory cannot be overridden. Turning off the policy set removes the control and leaves no proper audit trail of the exception.

objective.question: A pipeline runs 'terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json' and then 'conftest test plan.json' with the policy below. Which statement about this policy is correct?

code.code:
package main

import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  "create" in rc.change.actions
  not rc.change.after.tags.CostCenter
  msg := sprintf("%s is missing CostCenter tag", [rc.address])
}

options: It fails the check only for S3 buckets that this plan will create without a CostCenter key in their tags; existing buckets being updated are not checked
It fails the check for any resource type in the plan that is missing a CostCenter tag
It automatically adds a CostCenter tag to new buckets before apply
It fails the check for every S3 bucket in the AWS account that has no CostCenter tag, including buckets Terraform does not manage
objective.explanation: The rule reads only the plan JSON. It matches resource_changes of type aws_s3_bucket whose actions include "create" and whose planned tags have no CostCenter key. It cannot see the live account, it never changes the plan, and it filters on one resource type. Note that it checks 'tags', not 'tags_all', so a tag supplied only through provider default_tags would still fail.

objective.question: A developer runs 'cdk deploy' for a stack that uses file assets. The first deployment to a new account and Region in ap-south-1 fails with an error saying the environment does not appear to be bootstrapped. What should the developer do?
options: Run 'cdk bootstrap aws://ACCOUNT_ID/ap-south-1' to create the CDKToolkit stack, including the staging bucket and deployment roles, then deploy again
Enable CloudFormation StackSets trusted access in AWS Organizations
Add the ap-south-1 Region to the 'env' property and run 'cdk diff'
Run 'cdk synth' and upload the template manually in the CloudFormation console
objective.explanation: CDK needs each account and Region pair to be bootstrapped. Bootstrapping creates the CDKToolkit stack with the asset bucket, an ECR repository and the IAM roles that deployments use. A manual upload skips the asset publishing, cdk diff only shows changes, and StackSets trusted access is not related to CDK bootstrapping.

objective.question: A GitHub Actions run was cancelled halfway through 'terraform apply'. Every later run now fails with the error below. What should the engineer do?

code.code:
Error: Error acquiring the state lock

Lock Info:
  ID:        7c1e2f4a-91b3-4d2e-a0c1-5e9f3b7d8a21
  Path:      tf-state-prod/network/terraform.tfstate
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       runner@gh-actions
  Version:   1.9.5

options: Confirm that no run is still active, then run 'terraform force-unlock' with the lock ID.
Run 'terraform init -reconfigure' to clear the lock and reset the backend.
Add '-lock=false' to every apply in the pipeline so stale locks cannot block it again.
Delete the state file from the bucket and run apply again so Terraform rebuilds it.
objective.explanation: A cancelled run can leave a stale lock behind. Once you have confirmed that nothing is still writing, 'terraform force-unlock <ID>' removes it safely. Deleting state loses the record of every resource, '-lock=false' brings back the clashing-apply problem, and 'init -reconfigure' does not release locks.

objective.question: An engineer wants one Terraform configuration to use a different state bucket for each environment. 'terraform init' fails with 'Variables may not be used here'. What is the correct fix?
options: Use partial backend configuration: leave bucket and key out of the block and pass them with 'terraform init -backend-config=env/prod.hcl'.
Set the values with TF_VAR_state_bucket and TF_VAR_env environment variables before running init.
Remove 'use_lockfile', because S3 locking requires a DynamoDB table when variables are used.
Replace the variables with locals, because backends can read locals but not input variables.
objective.explanation: Backend blocks are processed before variables are evaluated, so they cannot reference variables or locals. Partial configuration through -backend-config files or flags is the supported pattern. TF_VAR_ values are still variables, so they fail for the same reason, and S3 native locking with use_lockfile does not need DynamoDB.

objective.question:
You must bring an existing, hand-built Azure virtual network under Terraform 1.5 or later with no downtime, using config generation. Which order of steps is correct?
P: Run 'terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf'.
Q: Add an 'import' block with 'to' and 'id'.
R: Run 'terraform apply' to record the resource in state.
S: Tidy the generated config and re-plan until it shows only the import and no changes.
options: P, Q, R, S
Q, R, P, S
Q, P, R, S
Q, P, S, R
objective.explanation: The import block tells Terraform what to import, and plan with -generate-config-out writes starter HCL. You review and clean that HCL until the plan shows a pure import, and only then apply. Applying before the review risks changing the live resource, and generating config before the import block exists produces nothing to import.

objective.question: A CloudFormation template sets an explicit TableName on a DynamoDB table. An engineer changes the table's KeySchema, and the stack update fails with: 'CloudFormation cannot update a stack when a custom-named resource requires replacing.' What is the cause?
options: DynamoDB tables cannot be changed by CloudFormation after creation and must be managed outside the stack.
The stack has termination protection enabled, which blocks any replacement.
Changing KeySchema requires replacement. CloudFormation creates the new table before deleting the old one, and the fixed name would collide.
The IAM role used by CloudFormation lacks dynamodb:UpdateTable permission.
objective.explanation: CloudFormation replaces resources by creating the new one first, and a hard-coded physical name cannot exist twice. You must change or remove the custom name and plan the data migration. Missing permissions or termination protection produce different errors, and DynamoDB tables are fully manageable by CloudFormation.

objective.question: A plan fails with 'Invalid for_each argument ... depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply'. What is the best fix?
options: Change for_each to count, because count accepts unknown values.
Wrap the expression in nonsensitive() so Terraform can read the IDs during plan.
Drive both resources from keys known at plan time, for example 'for_each = toset(var.app_names)' on the instances, then 'for_each = aws_instance.app' on the records.
Use '-target=aws_instance.app' on every run so the instance IDs always exist first.
objective.explanation: for_each keys must be known at plan time, and instance IDs only exist after apply. Keys taken from configuration, such as names, are known during plan and also give stable addresses. Routine -target is an anti-pattern, count also needs a known number and causes index shifting, and nonsensitive() has nothing to do with unknown values.

objective.question: This Bicep file is deployed with 'az deployment group create' and fails. What is the mistake?
options: Bicep cannot create resource groups at all. They must be created with the Azure CLI first.
The location parameter must be passed in the module's name property.
Resource groups are a subscription-level resource. The file needs targetScope = 'subscription' and must be deployed with 'az deployment sub create'.
Modules cannot take a resource group symbolic name as scope. It must be scope: resourceGroup('fixed-name').
objective.explanation: The default targetScope is resourceGroup, and you cannot create a resource group from inside a resource-group deployment. Setting targetScope = 'subscription' and using a subscription deployment fixes it, and 'scope: rg' is valid Bicep for placing the module in the new group. Bicep can create resource groups, and location has nothing to do with the module name.

objective.question: Every resource in your Azure landing zone must carry a 'costCentre' tag. If a resource lacks the tag, it should be copied automatically from its resource group, and this must also apply to resources that already exist. Which Azure Policy approach fits?
options: A Modify effect that adds the tag from the resource group, with a remediation task that uses the assignment's managed identity for existing resources.
An Azure RBAC custom role that requires the tag before resource creation.
An Audit effect, with owners fixing non-compliant resources by hand.
A Deny effect on resources without the tag, plus a weekly script that adds tags.
objective.explanation: Modify is the effect designed to add or change tags at create or update time. Existing resources are fixed through a remediation task that runs as the assignment's managed identity. Deny blocks deployments instead of fixing them, Audit only reports, and RBAC controls who can act, not resource properties.

objective.question: A public repository runs Terraform plan for pull requests, including PRs from forks, with this workflow. What is the main security mistake?

code.code:
on:
  pull_request_target:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/tf-plan
          aws-region: ap-south-1
      - run: terraform init && terraform plan

options: The job should use 'contents: write' so it can post the plan as a comment.
OIDC tokens do not work with pull_request_target, so the plan will fail authentication.
terraform init must run in a separate job from terraform plan.
pull_request_target runs with the base repository's privileges. Checking out the untrusted PR head lets a fork run arbitrary code, such as an external data source, with cloud credentials.
objective.explanation: pull_request_target gives the job secrets and OIDC permissions, and here it executes code chosen by whoever opened the PR. A plan can run code through data sources and providers, so credentials can leak. Use the pull_request trigger, which withholds secrets from forks, or gate fork runs behind approval.

objective.question: A company must make sure that no Google Cloud resources are created outside asia-south1 and asia-south2 in any project, including future projects. Which control should it use?
options: A VPC Service Controls perimeter around all projects.
A Cloud Billing budget alert for spend in other regions.
An Organization Policy using the resource locations constraint (gcp.resourceLocations), set at the organization node.
An IAM deny policy on the compute.instances.create permission.
objective.explanation: The resource locations constraint limits where location-based resources can be created, and setting it at the organization node means every current and future project inherits it. IAM deny controls who can call APIs, not where resources go. VPC Service Controls protect against data exfiltration, and budgets only alert.

objective.question: A production RDS resource in Terraform has 'lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }'. A developer opens a PR that deletes the entire resource block. Which statement is correct?
options: prevent_destroy only works while the block is in the configuration. With the block gone, the plan will propose destroying the database, so also enable RDS deletion_protection and add a policy check that blocks delete actions.
Terraform will automatically remove the database from state without destroying it.
The plan will fail because RDS resources cannot be destroyed by Terraform.
Terraform will refuse the plan, because prevent_destroy is stored in state and keeps protecting the resource.
objective.explanation: prevent_destroy is read from the configuration, so deleting the block removes the protection along with it. Defence in depth is needed: cloud-side deletion protection makes the API call fail, and a policy-as-code rule in CI flags delete actions on critical resources. Terraform never removes resources from state silently.

subjective.question: Explain declarative infrastructure as code and idempotency. Why do they matter in a real platform team?
subjective.answer: Declarative IaC means I describe the end state I want, such as a VPC with three subnets, and the tool works out the steps to reach it. I do not write the step-by-step commands myself. Idempotency means running the same code many times gives the same result. If nothing has changed, the second run makes no changes. This matters in real work for three reasons. First, environments become reproducible, so dev, test and prod match. Second, the tool can compare desired and actual state and show a diff before changing anything. Terraform does this with plan, CloudFormation with change sets, and Bicep with what-if. Third, re-running a pipeline after a failure is safe. Scripts that run 'create' commands are not idempotent. A second run fails or creates duplicates, which leads to drift and outages.
keyPoints: Declarative describes the desired end state, not the steps
Idempotent: repeated runs converge with no extra changes
Enables diff previews: plan, change sets, what-if
Reproducible environments and safe pipeline retries

subjective.question: How would you structure your landing zone as Terraform modules so that a new environment can be created from code in under an hour?
subjective.answer: I would split the landing zone into small, focused modules: network (VPC or VNet, subnets, routing, hub connectivity), identity and IAM roles, logging and monitoring, security baseline (guardrails, encryption keys), and shared services such as DNS. Each module has clear input variables and outputs. Modules do not reach into each other's internals. They are versioned in their own repository and called with pinned refs like ?ref=v1.2.0. Above them sits a thin environment root module per environment, such as dev or prod. It only composes modules and sets variables through tfvars. Each environment has its own remote state with locking. I keep the blast radius small by splitting state per layer, for example network separate from apps. A new environment then means copying a small root folder, setting a few variables, and letting the pipeline run plan and apply. Pinned provider versions make it reproducible.
keyPoints: Small single-purpose modules with clear inputs and outputs
Thin per-environment root modules that only compose
Pinned module and provider versions
Separate remote state with locking per environment and layer
Pipeline-driven creation for speed and repeatability

subjective.question: Describe a CI/CD pipeline for Terraform that posts the plan on each pull request and applies safely.
subjective.answer: On every pull request, the pipeline runs terraform fmt -check, init, validate, linting and security scanning such as tflint or Checkov, and policy checks. Then it runs terraform plan -out=tfplan and posts a readable plan summary as a PR comment, so reviewers can see the creates, changes and destroys. Branch protection requires approval from code owners, and stricter approval for prod. After merge, the apply stage applies that saved plan file, or re-plans and stops if the plan differs from what was approved. This means only reviewed changes go live. The pipeline authenticates with short-lived credentials through OIDC federation instead of stored access keys, and with least-privilege roles per environment. Remote state with locking stops concurrent runs. I would also add manual approval gates for production and a scheduled plan job to detect drift.
keyPoints: fmt, validate, lint, security and policy scans on the PR
plan -out and post the plan as a PR comment
Apply the reviewed plan after approval and merge
OIDC short-lived credentials and least privilege
State locking, prod gates and scheduled drift checks

subjective.question: How do you handle secrets and Terraform state securely?
subjective.answer: State can hold sensitive values in plain text, such as database passwords and keys. So I never commit state or secrets to Git, and I add *.tfstate and .terraform to .gitignore. State lives in a remote backend such as S3, Azure Storage or a GCS bucket. The backend has encryption at rest, versioning for recovery, strict access control and locking. Secrets are not hard-coded in tfvars. They are created or read at deploy time from AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault or Google Secret Manager. Where possible I let the service generate and manage them, for example RDS managed master passwords. I mark outputs and variables as sensitive so they do not print in logs or PR comments. Note that sensitive hides values from output but they still exist in state, so state access must stay tight. Pipelines use OIDC rather than long-lived keys.
keyPoints: Never commit state or secrets to Git
Encrypted, versioned, locked remote backend with tight access
Fetch secrets from Secrets Manager, Key Vault or Secret Manager
sensitive = true hides output but values remain in state
OIDC instead of long-lived credentials

subjective.question: Compare OPA, Sentinel and cloud-native policy such as Azure Policy and AWS SCPs. How would you layer them?
subjective.answer: OPA is an open-source policy engine that uses the Rego language. Tools like Conftest evaluate Terraform plan JSON with it in the pipeline, before anything is deployed. Sentinel is HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework, used in HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise, which can enforce rules between plan and apply. These are preventive checks at deploy time, but only for changes that go through the pipeline. Cloud-native policy works at the API level, so it also catches console or CLI changes. Azure Policy effects include Deny, Audit, Modify, Append, DeployIfNotExists and AuditIfNotExists, and I assign them at the management group level. AWS SCPs set maximum permissions for member accounts and never grant any. I layer them: pipeline policy gives fast developer feedback in the PR. Cloud-native guardrails are the hard backstop that no one can bypass. Audit-mode findings feed compliance reports.
keyPoints: OPA/Rego and Sentinel check plans in the pipeline
Cloud-native policy enforces at API level and catches out-of-band changes
Azure Policy effects and management group scope
SCPs limit permissions and never grant; management account is exempt
Layered approach: early feedback plus a hard backstop

subjective.question: What are golden paths and an internal developer platform (IDP)? How do they relate to IaC?
subjective.answer: A golden path is the supported, opinionated and easiest way to do a common task, such as creating a new service with a repository, a CI/CD pipeline, an account or project, networking, monitoring and security already set up. An internal developer platform is the self-service layer that offers these paths, often through a portal like Backstage, templates or a simple API. IaC is the engine underneath. Each golden path calls versioned Terraform, CDK or Bicep modules that include the organisation's standards, such as tagging, encryption, logging and policy. Developers fill in a few inputs and get a compliant environment in minutes, without filing tickets. The platform team treats it as a product. They measure adoption and lead time, and they keep the path optional but attractive. Good paths reduce cognitive load, cut ticket queues, and make security and cost controls the default rather than an afterthought.
keyPoints: Golden path: paved, opinionated, supported way for common tasks
IDP: self-service portal or API, for example Backstage
Built on versioned IaC modules with standards included
Platform run as a product with metrics
Compliance, tagging and cost controls by default

subjective.question: What is drift? How do you detect and handle it in Terraform, CloudFormation and Bicep?
subjective.answer: Drift is when real infrastructure differs from the code, usually because someone changed it by hand in the console. In Terraform, a plan compares state and the real resources with the code, so a scheduled plan job in the pipeline reports drift. terraform plan -refresh-only shows the changes without proposing fixes. In CloudFormation, drift detection compares stack resources with the template and flags modified or deleted resources. In Bicep, running what-if against the current deployment shows the differences, because ARM tracks resources. To handle drift, I first decide whether the change was a valid hotfix. If it was, I update the code to match. If not, I re-apply the code to restore the desired state. To prevent drift, I limit console write access, use cloud-native policy and SCPs, and route all changes through the PR pipeline.
keyPoints: Drift: real resources differ from code
Terraform scheduled plan and -refresh-only
CloudFormation drift detection; Bicep what-if
Decide: codify the change or re-apply
Prevent by limiting manual access and using policy

subjective.question: Your company has hundreds of resources created by hand in the console. How do you bring them under Terraform without downtime?
subjective.answer: I would work in small batches, starting with low-risk shared resources, and freeze manual changes for each batch. For each resource, I write an import block with the to address and the cloud ID. Then I run terraform plan with -generate-config-out to draft the configuration, or I write it myself using existing modules. The terraform import CLI also works, but import blocks are better because they go through PR review. I clean up the generated code into modules and run plan until it shows zero changes. That proves the code matches reality. Only then do I apply, which just records the resources in state. If I later reorganise code into modules, I use moved blocks so Terraform updates addresses instead of destroying and recreating. I pin provider versions and add prevent_destroy on critical data stores like databases as a safety net.
keyPoints: Incremental batches with a change freeze
Import blocks (reviewable) or terraform import CLI
-generate-config-out to draft code
Iterate until plan shows no changes, then apply
moved blocks for refactors; prevent_destroy on critical data

subjective.question: How would you choose between Terraform, CloudFormation/CDK, Bicep and Google Cloud's native options for a new project?
subjective.answer: My decision rule is simple. If the organisation is multi-cloud or wants one workflow and module ecosystem across providers, including SaaS like DNS or monitoring, I choose Terraform. If it is AWS-only and wants managed state, native rollback, StackSets and day-one service support, I choose CloudFormation. I choose CDK on top if developers prefer TypeScript or Python with loops and abstractions, since CDK synthesises CloudFormation. For Azure-only native work, Bicep is clean, has no state file because ARM tracks resources, and supports what-if previews. On Google Cloud, the strategic path is Terraform, with Infrastructure Manager available as a managed service that runs Terraform. Deployment Manager is legacy and being retired, so I would not start new work on it. I also weigh team skills, existing modules, policy tooling and support needs before deciding.
keyPoints: Multi-cloud or one workflow: Terraform
AWS-only: CloudFormation, or CDK for programming languages
Azure-only: Bicep, no state file, what-if
Google Cloud: Terraform or Infrastructure Manager; avoid legacy Deployment Manager
Consider team skills and existing ecosystem

subjective.question: Your Azure team deploys landing zone resources with 'az deployment group create' using Bicep. Resources removed from the template stay in Azure, and engineers sometimes change resources by hand in the portal. How would deployment stacks help? Explain what the command below does.

code.code:
az stack group create \
  --name lz-network \
  --resource-group rg-network-prod \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters prod.bicepparam \
  --action-on-unmanage deleteResources \
  --deny-settings-mode denyWriteAndDelete \
  --deny-settings-excluded-principals <pipeline-sp-object-id>

subjective.answer: A normal Bicep deployment in incremental mode only adds or updates resources. It never removes resources you delete from the template, so orphans build up. A deployment stack is an Azure resource that tracks the set of resources it manages. This command creates or updates the stack 'lz-network' from main.bicep with prod parameters. '--action-on-unmanage deleteResources' means that if a resource is removed from the template, Azure deletes it on the next update instead of just detaching it. '--deny-settings-mode denyWriteAndDelete' applies deny assignments to the managed resources, so even Owners cannot change or delete them in the portal. The excluded principal is the pipeline's service principal, so code stays the only way to change these resources. This reduces drift and orphans. Use deleteResources carefully on stateful resources. Detaching first is safer while you are migrating to stacks.
keyPoints: Incremental deployments do not remove resources dropped from the template
A deployment stack tracks its managed resources; action-on-unmanage controls whether they are detached or deleted
Deny settings block manual writes and deletes, which prevents drift
Exclude the pipeline identity so changes still flow through code
Take care with deleteResources on stateful resources such as databases

subjective.question: Your GitHub Actions pipeline for Terraform uses an IAM user access key stored as a repository secret. Security wants no long-lived keys and wants plan jobs to be unable to change anything. Design the authentication, and explain the trust policy condition below.
subjective.answer: I would replace the access key with OIDC federation. GitHub issues a short-lived signed token for each job. AWS trusts the GitHub OIDC provider, and the job calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to get temporary credentials, so there is no stored secret. I would create two roles. The plan role has read-only permissions plus access to state, and pull request jobs can assume it. The apply role has write permissions, and its trust policy is restricted, as shown here. The 'aud' condition checks that the token was issued for AWS STS. The 'sub' condition allows only jobs in the acme/landing-zone repository that run in the GitHub 'prod' environment. That environment can require reviewers and only allow the main branch. Forks and other branches cannot assume the role. Azure and Google Cloud work the same way, through workload identity federation.
keyPoints: OIDC federation gives short-lived credentials with no stored keys
Separate a read-only plan role from a write apply role
The aud condition checks the token audience; the sub condition pins the repository and environment or branch
GitHub environment protection rules add human approval before apply
Azure and Google Cloud offer the same pattern through workload identity federation

subjective.question: Every 'terraform plan' for an Auto Scaling group shows a change to desired_capacity, even though nobody edited the code. Applying it disrupts scaling. Why does this happen, and how would you fix it properly?
subjective.answer: This is a perpetual diff. Another controller, the scaling policy, changes desired_capacity at runtime. When Terraform refreshes, it sees the live value, say 6, and plans to set it back to 2. Applying that change would scale the group in and could cause an outage. The fix shown here is lifecycle ignore_changes on desired_capacity. Terraform sets the value at creation and then leaves it alone, while min_size and max_size stay managed in code. Use ignore_changes only for attributes that something else is meant to own, such as autoscaling counts or tags added by an external tagging tool. Do not use it to hide real drift. Document why each ignored attribute is there. For the general case, make sure only one system owns each attribute, and run scheduled drift-detection plans so that unexpected diffs are investigated, not ignored.
keyPoints: A perpetual diff happens when another system changes an attribute Terraform manages
Applying the diff can undo autoscaling and cause an outage
lifecycle ignore_changes hands ownership of that attribute to the external controller
Each attribute should have one owner; ignore_changes must not be used to hide real drift
Scheduled drift detection catches unexpected changes

subjective.question: Your landing zone is one Terraform root module with about 2,000 resources across networking, identity, logging and shared services. A plan takes 20 minutes, and a typo in a tag change once put the transit gateway at risk. How would you restructure the state, and how do the separate parts share values?
subjective.answer: I would split the single state into several root modules, each with its own state, divided by layer and by rate of change. For example: organisation and identity, networking per Region, central logging, and shared services per environment. Each state then has a smaller blast radius, faster plans, separate locks and its own permissions. The networking pipeline can need approval from the network team, while application stacks change daily. For sharing values, lower layers publish outputs. Upper layers read them with terraform_remote_state, provider data sources, or a parameter store such as SSM Parameter Store. Data sources and parameters avoid giving read access to the whole state file. I would move resources between states with terraform state mv or import and removed blocks, testing in a non-production copy first. Dependency order is documented, and the pipeline applies layers in sequence for a new environment.
keyPoints: Split state by layer, ownership and rate of change to reduce blast radius
Smaller states mean faster plans, separate locking and per-team permissions
Share values through outputs, remote state, data sources or a parameter store
Migrate with state mv, import and removed blocks, and test first
Apply layers in a defined order when building a new environment

subjective.question: Ten product teams consume your shared Terraform modules. A change to the VPC module recently broke three teams' pipelines overnight. How would you version and release modules and providers so that teams upgrade safely?
subjective.answer: First, modules must never be consumed from a moving branch. I would publish each module to a private registry, or as tagged Git releases, using semantic versioning. A major version means a breaking change, a minor version adds a feature, and a patch is a fix. Consumers pin a version constraint such as '~> 3.2', so they get patches but never an unplanned major version. Each module has examples, a README listing inputs and outputs, and automated tests such as terraform validate, tflint, and terraform test or Terratest that run in CI before a release. Breaking changes come with release notes and moved blocks where addresses change. For providers, I commit .terraform.lock.hcl so every run uses the same provider builds. A bot such as Renovate or Dependabot opens pull requests for new module and provider versions, and the plan in that pull request shows each team the exact impact before merge.
keyPoints: Publish modules to a registry or as tagged releases using semantic versioning
Consumers pin versions with constraints and never use a branch reference
Test modules in CI and document breaking changes, adding moved blocks where addresses change
Commit .terraform.lock.hcl so provider builds stay the same across runs
Use automated upgrade pull requests where the plan shows the impact

subjective.question: Case study: An Indian fintech regulated by RBI must keep all customer data in India. It wants a multi-account AWS landing zone built from code. New environments must take under an hour, every change must be auditable, and product teams want self-service. Outline your design.
subjective.answer: I would use AWS Organizations with OUs for security, infrastructure, non-prod and prod. Accounts would be vended from code, either with Control Tower and Account Factory for Terraform or with our own Terraform account module. An SCP at the root denies actions outside ap-south-1 and ap-south-2, with exceptions for global services, and blocks disabling CloudTrail or Config. An organisation trail goes to a locked log-archive account. Terraform state is split per account and layer in an encrypted, versioned S3 bucket with locking. Every change goes through a pull request: plan with a read-only OIDC role, OPA checks on the plan JSON, a human review, then an apply of the saved plan behind an environment approval. For self-service, teams request an environment through a template in the IDP. That pre-composes VPC, logging, IAM and baseline modules, so a new environment is a short PR and finishes inside an hour.
keyPoints: Region-restricting SCP enforces data residency, with global-service exceptions
Account vending from code (AFT or a custom module) plus a central log archive
State split per account and layer, in an encrypted, locked backend
PR workflow: read-only plan role, policy checks, approved apply of the saved plan
IDP template gives self-service within the one-hour target

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: 'terraform plan' on an engineer's laptop shows no changes. The same commit in CI shows every resource as 'will be created'. What are the likely causes, and how do you diagnose them?
subjective.answer: 'Everything will be created' means Terraform thinks it manages nothing. Either it is reading an empty state, or it cannot see the real resources. First, check the backend. CI may have run init without the right -backend-config, so it uses a different key or bucket, or it fell back to a local backend. Next, check the workspace: the laptop may be on 'prod' while CI is on 'default'. 'terraform workspace show' and 'terraform state list' in both places reveal this fast. Third, check credentials. If CI assumes a role in the wrong account or Region, refresh finds nothing, and resources drop out of the plan as missing. 'aws sts get-caller-identity' or the Azure and gcloud equivalents confirm this. Never apply such a plan, because it would create duplicates or fail on name clashes. Fix the config, then pin backend and provider settings in versioned files.
keyPoints: Empty or wrong state: backend key, bucket, or a missing -backend-config
Workspace mismatch between laptop and CI
Wrong account, subscription or project credentials make refresh find nothing
Use state list, workspace show and identity checks to compare
Never apply such a plan; fix the configuration first

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this reusable Terraform module that teams call for databases. How would you fix each one?
subjective.answer: First, the module declares its own provider block with a hard-coded Region. Reusable modules should only declare required_providers with version constraints and let the caller pass providers. Otherwise the module cannot be used with count or for_each, and the Region choice is taken from the caller. Second, the password is hard-coded, so it sits in Git and in state. Use manage_master_user_password = true so RDS keeps it in Secrets Manager, or read it from a secrets store. Third, the output exposes the password. Remove it, or at least mark it sensitive. Fourth, publicly_accessible = true and skip_final_snapshot = true are unsafe defaults. Default to private, take a final snapshot, and enable storage_encrypted and deletion_protection. Finally, 'name' has no type, description or validation, and instance_class and storage are fixed. Expose them as typed variables with sensible defaults.
keyPoints: No provider blocks inside reusable modules; use required_providers only
No hard-coded secrets; use managed master password or a secrets store
Do not output secrets, or mark them sensitive
Secure defaults: private, encrypted, final snapshot, deletion protection
Typed and validated variables instead of hard-coded sizes

subjective.question: Comparison: For dev, staging and prod, which is better: Terraform CLI workspaces with one configuration, or separate root directories, each with its own backend? Why?
subjective.answer: For long-lived environments with different risk levels, I prefer separate root directories, or separate stacks per environment, each with its own backend and credentials. They call the same versioned modules. Each environment then has its own state location, its own pipeline role and its own approval gates. A prod plan can only run with prod credentials, and differences between environments are visible in code instead of hidden behind terraform.workspace conditionals. CLI workspaces share one backend configuration, and usually one credential set. It is easy to be on the wrong workspace and apply to prod by mistake, and you cannot easily put prod state in a different, more locked-down account. Workspaces do suit short-lived copies of the same thing, such as per-PR preview environments or identical test stacks. Note that HCP Terraform 'workspaces' are a different concept: each one has its own variables, permissions and state, so they map well to environments.
keyPoints: Separate roots give separate state, credentials and approvals per environment
CLI workspaces share the backend and risk wrong-workspace applies
Environment differences stay explicit in code, not in conditionals
Workspaces suit identical, short-lived copies such as PR previews
HCP Terraform workspaces differ from CLI workspaces

subjective.question: Ordering: A team kept Terraform state locally and committed it to Git. List the steps, in order, to move it to a secure remote backend and clean up safely.
subjective.answer: 1. Freeze changes: pause the pipeline and tell the team not to apply. 2. Back up the current terraform.tfstate outside Git. 3. Create the backend through a small bootstrap configuration: an S3 bucket, Azure storage account or GCS bucket with versioning, encryption, public access blocked and tight IAM, plus locking. 4. Add the backend block, or partial configuration, to the code. 5. Run 'terraform init -migrate-state' and confirm the copy. 6. Verify: 'terraform state list' matches, and 'terraform plan' shows no changes. 7. Delete local state files, add *.tfstate and .terraform/ to .gitignore, and remove state from Git history. 8. Rotate any secrets that appeared in the old state, because history and clones may still hold them. 9. Unfreeze, and let only the pipeline write state from now on.
keyPoints: Freeze applies and back up state first
Bootstrap a versioned, encrypted, locked backend
terraform init -migrate-state, then verify with a no-change plan
Remove state from the repo and from Git history; update .gitignore
Rotate any secrets that were exposed in the state

subjective.question: Explain AWS CDK L1, L2 and L3 constructs. Which would you use to build a golden path for your developers, and why?
subjective.answer: L1 constructs, named Cfn*, map one-to-one to CloudFormation resources and expose every property with no defaults. L2 constructs are curated, intent-based classes such as s3.Bucket. They add sensible defaults, helper methods like grantRead and type-safe properties. L3 constructs, or patterns, combine several resources into a solution, such as a load-balanced Fargate service. For a golden path, I would publish our own L3 constructs in an internal package. An example is 'CompanyService', which wires up the VPC lookup, an encrypted bucket, logging, alarms, tags and least-privilege roles. Internally it uses L2s, and L1 escape hatches where L2 lacks a setting. Developers get one simple, typed API with our standards built in, and we version it like any library. We would add cdk-nag or CDK Aspects for compliance checks, and run 'cdk diff' in PRs so reviewers see the synthesised changes.
keyPoints: L1 = raw CloudFormation, L2 = curated defaults, L3 = multi-resource patterns
Golden path = internal, versioned L3 constructs with standards built in
Use escape hatches to L1 when L2 lacks a property
Aspects or cdk-nag for policy checks
cdk diff in PRs for review

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: A CloudFormation stack update failed. During rollback, a resource could not be returned to its old state because someone had deleted it manually, and the stack is now in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. How do you recover?
subjective.answer: UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED means CloudFormation could not restore one or more resources to their previous state. The stack is stuck, and you cannot update it until the rollback finishes. First, read the stack events to find the failing resource and the reason, here the manually deleted resource. If you can fix the cause, for example by recreating the dependency or restoring permissions, do that and run 'continue-update-rollback'. If you cannot, run continue-update-rollback with the resources-to-skip option for that logical ID. CloudFormation then marks it as rolled back, the stack reaches UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, and you can deploy again. Skipped resources may now differ from the template, so run drift detection and fix them through code or by importing. To prevent repeats, restrict console changes with IAM or SCPs, and consider stack policies on critical resources.
keyPoints: Stuck state: no updates are possible until the rollback completes
Read stack events to find the failing resource
Fix the cause, or use continue-update-rollback with resources to skip
Run drift detection afterwards and reconcile in code
Prevent manual changes with IAM, SCPs and stack policies

subjective.question: This conftest policy blocks PRs that delete old S3 buckets. It also fails buckets that get their owner tag from provider default_tags. Find both mistakes and fix them.

code.code:
package main

import rego.v1

deny contains msg if {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  not rc.change.after.tags.owner
  msg := sprintf("%s must have an owner tag", [rc.address])
}

subjective.answer: Mistake one: the rule ignores the planned action. For a delete, change.after is null, so 'not rc.change.after.tags.owner' is true and the deletion is blocked. The rule should only run on creates and updates. Add 'some action in rc.change.actions' and 'action in {"create", "update"}'. Mistake two: the AWS provider merges default_tags into the computed tags_all attribute, not into tags. A bucket tagged only through default_tags has no owner key in tags, so it fails wrongly. Check change.after.tags_all.owner instead, or accept either attribute. Note that if default tags depend on unknown values, tags_all can be unknown at plan time, so test that case. I would also add unit tests with conftest verify, covering create, update, delete and default-tag cases, so mistakes like these are caught before the policy reaches the pipeline.
keyPoints: Delete actions have a null 'after', which triggers false positives
Filter on change.actions for create and update
default_tags show up in tags_all, not tags
Watch for unknown values in plan JSON
Unit-test policies with conftest verify

subjective.question: Case study: You built an internal developer platform with golden-path templates. Six months later, most teams still click resources together in the console. What would you change?
subjective.answer: I would treat the platform as a product. That means talking to teams to find out why they avoid it. Common reasons are that the templates are slower than the console, too rigid, poorly documented, or missing the services teams need. Then I would make the golden path the easiest route. Offer one-click or one-PR scaffolding that produces a working repo, pipeline and environment in minutes. Allow escape hatches, such as extra modules or overridable variables, so teams are not trapped. Publish clear docs and examples. Next, reduce the console route. Give developers read-only console access in prod and allow write actions only through pipelines. In sandboxes, allow console use but auto-expire resources. Use policy and drift detection to surface unmanaged resources, not to punish people. Finally, measure adoption, lead time for new services and template satisfaction, and keep a public roadmap driven by requests.
keyPoints: Platform as a product: user research and a roadmap
Golden path must be the fastest, easiest option
Allow escape hatches and extensibility
Limit console writes in prod; sandboxes for experiments
Measure adoption and lead time

subjective.question: Case study: Your DR plan says 'we can rebuild the whole Region from Terraform'. In a test, the rebuild took eight hours and the application still did not work. What was probably missing, and how would you make IaC-based DR real?
subjective.answer: IaC rebuilds infrastructure, not everything a working system needs. Likely gaps: data, since databases and buckets were not replicated or backed up cross-Region; secrets and keys, since KMS keys and Secrets Manager or Key Vault entries are Region-scoped; container images in a single-Region registry; service quotas never raised in the DR Region; hard-coded Region names or AMI IDs in modules; DNS failover never configured; and manual console resources missing from code. Long plans on one giant state also slowed the rebuild. To fix it, parameterise Region in all modules, and replicate data, images and secrets continuously. Pre-provision the foundation layer, meaning network, IAM and logging, in the DR Region as pilot light, so only workloads deploy during an incident. Request quotas ahead of time and script DNS failover. Then run game days regularly, timed against the RTO, and fix every gap found in code.
keyPoints: IaC does not restore data; replicate or back up across Regions
Region-scoped secrets, keys, images and quotas must be prepared
Remove hard-coded Regions and IDs from modules
Pre-provision the foundation layer; split state for fast workload deploys
Regular timed game days against the RTO

steps.overview: This step teaches you to see, control and cut cloud spend on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. It covers tagging, budgets, right-sizing, commitment discounts, spot capacity and data transfer. Every architect exam (SAA-C03, SAP-C02, AZ-305, Professional Cloud Architect) has 'most cost-effective' questions, and interviewers expect you to price a design before it is built.
objectives: Design a tagging and cost allocation scheme that maps every resource to a team, environment and cost centre
Configure budgets and anomaly alerts on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and explain what they do and do not stop
Choose between right-sizing, autoscaling, scheduling, commitments and spot for a given workload
Identify hidden data transfer charges (NAT, cross-AZ, cross-region, internet egress) and redesign to reduce them
Estimate a design's monthly cost and write a savings plan with the saving from each change

concepts.explanation: Key-value metadata on resources, such as CostCentre=1234 and Env=prod, used to split the bill. On AWS, user-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags in the Billing console, and they only apply from activation onwards, not to past costs. Azure uses tags and Google Cloud uses labels. Enforce them with policy: AWS Organizations tag policies and SCPs, Azure Policy, or Google Cloud organisation policies and automation.

Showback reports each team's cost to them without moving money. Chargeback actually bills the cost back to the team's budget. Both need consistent tags or separate accounts, subscriptions or projects. Account, subscription or project separation is the most reliable allocation boundary, because some costs cannot be tagged.

Budgets alert when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold. Examples are AWS Budgets, Azure Cost Management budgets and Google Cloud Billing budgets. Budgets do not cap spend by themselves. To stop resources you must add automation, such as AWS Budgets actions, Azure action groups, or Pub/Sub plus Cloud Functions on Google Cloud. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection and Azure cost anomaly alerts use machine learning to flag unusual spend without you setting fixed thresholds.

Matching instance size and family to measured usage (CPU, memory, IOPS) over a representative period. Use AWS Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor or Google Cloud Recommender. Right-size first and commit second. Otherwise you lock a discount onto waste for one or three years.

Dev and test environments rarely need to run 24x7. Running only 12 hours on weekdays is 60 of 168 hours, about 36% of the time, which saves about 64% of compute. Tools include AWS Instance Scheduler, Azure Automation or VM auto-shutdown, and Google Cloud instance schedules. Note that attached disks and storage keep billing while instances are stopped.

AWS: Savings Plans (Compute, EC2 Instance, SageMaker) and Reserved Instances for EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, Redshift and OpenSearch. Azure: Reservations and Azure Savings Plan for compute, plus Azure Hybrid Benefit for existing Windows Server and SQL Server licences. Google Cloud: resource-based and spend-based committed use discounts (CUDs), plus automatic sustained use discounts on some machine series. All AWS and Azure commitments run for 1 or 3 years, and the 3-year all-upfront option gives the deepest discount.

Spare capacity sold at a large discount that the provider can reclaim. Examples are AWS EC2 Spot, Azure Spot VMs and Google Cloud Spot VMs. Use it only for fault-tolerant, stateless or checkpointed work such as batch, CI, rendering and big data. Diversify across instance types and AZs, and mix spot with on-demand in Auto Scaling groups or managed instance groups.

Inbound traffic from the internet is generally free. Egress to the internet, traffic between regions, and on AWS traffic between AZs are charged per GB. NAT gateways add a per-GB processing charge on top of their hourly charge. Fixes include gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, a CDN in front of origins, keeping chatty tiers in one AZ where resilience allows, and compressing or caching data.

Move data that is accessed less often to cheaper tiers using lifecycle rules. Examples are S3 Standard-IA, Glacier tiers and Intelligent-Tiering on AWS, Cool, Cold and Archive tiers on Azure Blob, and Nearline, Coldline and Archive on Google Cloud Storage. Watch minimum storage durations and retrieval fees, because tiering tiny or frequently read objects can cost more.

keyFacts: AWS Spot gives a 2-minute interruption notice. Azure Spot VMs and Google Cloud Spot VMs give about 30 seconds.
AWS states discounts of up to 90% for Spot, up to 72% for EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, and up to 66% for Compute Savings Plans.
Compute Savings Plans apply across instance family, size, region, OS and tenancy, and also cover Fargate and Lambda. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are locked to one family in one region.
AWS cost allocation tags must be activated in the payer (management) account, can take up to 24 hours to appear, and are not applied retroactively.
Budgets on all three clouds alert but do not stop spending unless you attach actions or automation.
Google Cloud sustained use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine series. CUDs require a 1- or 3-year commitment.
Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB have no charge and remove NAT gateway processing fees for that traffic. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) charge hourly and per GB.
On AWS, data between AZs in the same region is charged in each direction. Data between regions and egress to the internet cost more. Inbound from the internet is free.
Decision order for exam answers: eliminate waste, then right-size, then schedule or autoscale, then commit to the stable baseline, and run interruptible work on spot.
Use the AWS Pricing Calculator, Azure Pricing Calculator and Google Cloud Pricing Calculator to estimate a design's monthly cost before building it.

example.caption: Worked plan: cut a USD 20,000/month AWS bill by more than 30% (illustrative figures; verify with the Pricing Calculator for your region)
example.code:
BASELINE (monthly)                         USD
EC2 prod, on-demand                       8,000
EC2 dev/test, running 24x7                4,000
RDS (prod)                                3,000
NAT gateway data processing               1,500
S3 storage (all Standard)                 1,500
Data transfer out to internet             2,000
TOTAL                                    20,000

CHANGE                                         SAVING  HOW
1 Schedule dev/test 08-20 Mon-Fri               2,560  60/168h = 36% runtime -> save 64% of 4,000
2 Right-size prod (Compute Optimizer)           1,600  ~20% over-provisioned -> 8,000 to 6,400
3 1-yr Compute Savings Plan on 80% baseline     1,280  ~25% off 5,120 committed spend
4 S3 gateway endpoint (60% of NAT traffic)        900  removes NAT per-GB fee for S3 traffic
5 S3 lifecycle: logs >30d to IA, >90d Glacier     500  measured from access patterns
TOTAL SAVING                                    6,840  = 34.2% of 20,000

NEW MONTHLY BILL                               13,160
NOT DONE (risk/effort): RDS reservation after a 3-month usage review;
CloudFront in front of the origin to cut egress (needs a cache-hit analysis).
Order matters: steps 1-2 before 3, so we do not commit to waste.

pitfalls: Buying Savings Plans or reservations before right-sizing. You lock in the discount on over-sized capacity for 1-3 years.
Assuming a budget stops spending. It only alerts unless actions or automation are configured.
Putting stateful or long-running jobs with no checkpointing on spot. Interruptions will lose work. The exam answer for 'must not be interrupted' is never spot.
Forgetting that NAT gateway per-GB processing and cross-AZ traffic often exceed instance costs in chatty designs. Watch for 'unexpected data transfer charges' in questions.
Expecting newly activated cost allocation tags to report historical costs. They only apply from activation onwards.
Tiering small or frequently accessed objects to infrequent or archive classes, then paying minimum-duration and retrieval charges.

workflow.title: Price and optimise a design before and after it is built

steps.label: List every billable component
steps.detail: Write down compute, storage, databases, load balancers, NAT, endpoints and every data path between tiers, AZs, regions and the internet.

steps.label: Estimate with pricing calculator
steps.detail: Enter expected hours, sizes, GB stored and GB transferred into the provider's Pricing Calculator to get a monthly figure per component.

steps.label: Tag and separate accounts
steps.detail: Apply mandatory tags or labels through policy and isolate environments in separate accounts, subscriptions or projects so costs are attributable.

steps.label: Set budgets and anomaly alerts
steps.detail: Create forecast and actual budgets per account or team, and enable anomaly detection with alerts to an owner.

steps.label: Remove waste and right-size
steps.detail: Delete idle resources, schedule non-production, enable autoscaling and resize based on recommender data.

steps.label: Commit baseline, spot the rest
steps.detail: Cover the steady baseline with Savings Plans, reservations or CUDs, and run interruptible batch work on spot.

steps.label: Fix data transfer paths
steps.detail: Add gateway endpoints, a CDN and caching, and keep chatty traffic within one AZ or region where resilience requirements allow.

project.title: finops-bill-cutter
project.summary: A small FinOps project that reads a tagged sample AWS monthly bill of USD 9,000 and applies right-sizing, non-production scheduling, commitments, Spot, storage tiering, data-transfer fixes and orphan clean-up. It prints the saving from each change, a showback per cost centre, and passes only if the bill falls by at least 30%. The Python script and its config make the written plan, the bill CSV is the before picture, and the Terraform files add the guardrails and automation: tag activation, a budget, anomaly alerts, S3 lifecycle tiering and an after-hours stop schedule.

files.code:
# finops-bill-cutter

Week 12 hands-on task: cut a sample monthly bill by 30% with a written plan
and the saving from each change.

## Files
- `data/bill.csv` - sample monthly bill (USD 9,000). Every line carries `env` and `cost_center` tags.
- `config/assumptions.json` - discount rates and thresholds. These are ASSUMPTIONS. Check them against
  the current AWS pricing pages and Cost Explorer recommendations before you quote them.
