revision.examFocus: This step maps to the migration and modernisation domains: SAP-C02 'Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization', SAA-C03 design scenarios, the AZ-305 migration objectives, and the Google Professional Cloud Architect case studies that include migration planning. Exams give a business constraint such as a deadline, skills, licensing or downtime, and ask for the right R, tool or sequence. The trap answers are usually 'technically possible but slower, riskier or more expensive'.

compare.a: Rehost (AWS MGN, Azure Migrate server migration, Migrate to Virtual Machines)
compare.b: Replatform (e.g. move the self-managed database to RDS, Azure SQL Managed Instance or Cloud SQL)
compare.difference: Rehost changes only the hosting. Replatform swaps one component for a managed service to cut ops work, without touching the core application code.
compare.chooseA: Pick Rehost when the question stresses a hard deadline such as a data-centre exit, no code change, or no team bandwidth.
compare.chooseB: Pick Replatform when the question mentions patching, backup or HA burden on a database or runtime and accepts small configuration changes.

compare.a: Relocate (VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution, Google Cloud VMware Engine)
compare.b: Rehost to native VMs (EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine)
compare.difference: Relocate moves whole vSphere workloads at hypervisor level and keeps VMware tools and skills. Rehost converts each server into a native cloud VM.
compare.chooseA: Pick Relocate when the team must keep vCenter, existing VMware runbooks or licensing, or must move hundreds of VMs with no per-server conversion.
compare.chooseB: Pick Rehost when the goal is native cloud pricing, autoscaling and later modernisation, and VMware lock-in is not required.

compare.a: Refactor (re-architect to containers, serverless or microservices)
compare.b: Repurchase (move to SaaS, e.g. on-prem CRM or email replaced by a SaaS product)
compare.difference: Refactor keeps ownership of the code and spends engineering effort. Repurchase drops the code entirely and accepts the vendor's features and data model.
compare.chooseA: Pick Refactor when the app gives competitive advantage and needs scale or agility that the current design blocks.
compare.chooseB: Pick Repurchase when the app is a commodity function (HR, CRM, ticketing, email) and a mature SaaS product exists.

compare.a: Online transfer (AWS DataSync, Azure Storage Mover/AzCopy, Storage Transfer Service)
compare.b: Offline appliance (AWS Snow Family, Azure Data Box, Google Transfer Appliance)
compare.difference: The choice depends on transfer time. Divide the data volume by real usable bandwidth, then compare the result with the deadline. Also consider whether the link is shared with production.
compare.chooseA: Pick online transfer when the calculated time fits the window, or when data keeps changing and needs repeated syncs.
compare.chooseB: Pick an appliance when the calculation runs to weeks, the link is saturated or metered, or the site has poor connectivity.

compare.b: AWS DMS (database replication)
compare.difference: MGN copies whole disks block by block, including the OS. DMS copies database data logically, can change engines, and keeps the target in sync with CDC.
compare.chooseA: Pick MGN when the whole server, including any database on it, moves unchanged to EC2.
compare.chooseB: Pick DMS when the database moves to a managed service or a different engine, or when near-zero-downtime data sync is the requirement.

cues.cue: Data-centre lease ends in weeks; minimal effort
cues.pick: Rehost with automated replication (MGN, Azure Migrate, Migrate to Virtual Machines)
cues.why: The deadline rules out any option that needs code or design work.

cues.cue: Heavy investment in VMware skills and tooling; no re-training
cues.pick: Relocate to a VMware service in the cloud
cues.why: It keeps the hypervisor and operating model and avoids converting each VM.

cues.cue: Oracle to PostgreSQL / SQL Server to Aurora with minimal downtime
cues.pick: Schema conversion (SCT or DMS Schema Conversion) plus DMS full load and CDC
cues.why: A heterogeneous move needs schema conversion first, then continuous sync until a short cut-over.

cues.cue: Discovery shows servers at very low CPU for months with no owner
cues.pick: Retire after confirming with the business
cues.why: Moving idle servers only moves cost into the cloud.

cues.cue: Compliance or latency needs the system to stay on-premises for now
cues.pick: Retain, and revisit it in a later wave
cues.why: Retain is a deliberate, time-boxed decision, not a failure of the plan.

cues.cue: Modernise the monolith gradually without stopping releases
cues.pick: Strangler fig behind a routing facade (ALB/API Gateway, Application Gateway/API Management, Cloud Load Balancing URL maps)
cues.why: Routing moves one function at a time and keeps a rollback for each slice.

cues.cue: Need dependencies before planning waves
cues.pick: Agent-based discovery (AWS Application Discovery Service agents, Azure Migrate dependency analysis, Migration Center)
cues.why: Network-connection data shows which servers talk to each other, so they can be grouped into the same wave.

cues.cue: Multi-cloud 'for high availability' with a small team
cues.pick: Multi-Region or multi-zone on a single cloud
cues.why: It gives most of the resilience without double egress, tooling and skills cost.

scenario.situation: A retailer has 40 on-premises servers. They are 6 idle legacy reporting servers, a 12-server web/app/SQL Server stack for the online store, an on-prem Exchange cluster, 10 file and batch servers, and a VMware-hosted ERP that the vendor certifies only on vSphere. The data-centre contract ends in 5 months, the team is small, and the store can accept only 15 minutes of downtime. Which plan best meets the deadline with the lowest risk?
reasoning: Reject 'rehost all 40 in one wave'. It moves waste, creates a big-bang risk and ignores the vendor constraint on the ERP.
Reject 'refactor the store to microservices first'. Five months and a small team rule out a rewrite, and refactoring can follow later with strangler fig.

Assign an R to each group. Retire the 6 idle servers. Repurchase Exchange with SaaS email. Relocate the ERP to a VMware cloud service. Rehost the file and batch servers. Rehost the store's web/app tier and replatform SQL Server to a managed database using DMS with CDC.

Order the waves by risk. Wave 1 is the low-risk file and batch servers, to prove tooling and rollback. Wave 2 is the ERP as one dependency group. Wave 3 is the store stack together, with TTL lowered early and reverse replication or a written data-loss rule ready for rollback.
Keep the source servers running until each wave's stability period ends and its rollback window is formally closed.
scenario.answer: Use a mixed-R, three-wave plan: retire, repurchase, relocate, rehost, and replatform the database with DMS CDC. Move dependency groups together and give every wave a tested rollback. This meets the deadline, respects the vendor constraint and keeps the store's downtime within 15 minutes.

memoryAids: Cheapest to costliest effort: 'Really Relaxed Rabbits Run Rapidly Past Rivers' = Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Replatform, Purchase (Repurchase), Refactor. Start at the top; move down only when a business driver forces it.
Cut-over checklist 'TRaDe-OFF': TTL lowered, Replication in sync, Data rollback path agreed, Freeze writes, Switch DNS, Observe, keep source until window Formally closed.
Wave rule: 'Chatty servers travel together, easy servers travel first.'
cheatSheet: Every server needs one R and a business reason. 'Default rehost' is a wrong answer.
Retire and Retain come out of discovery. Do them first, because they shrink the migration scope.
Relocate is the VMware-to-VMware move: VMware Cloud on AWS, Azure VMware Solution, Google Cloud VMware Engine.
Replatform the database to a managed service is the most common 'less ops, small change' answer.
Heterogeneous database move = convert the schema first, then DMS full load plus CDC, then a short cut-over.
Transfer time ≈ data volume ÷ real usable bandwidth. If it exceeds the window, use an offline appliance.
Group servers into waves by dependency maps, not by department or OS. Wave 1 should be low-risk, to prove the process.
Test-launch replicated instances before cut-over. The source stays untouched, so rollback is mostly a DNS or routing switch.
A data rollback needs reverse replication or an agreed data-loss rule. A VM rollback alone is not enough.
Strangler fig: put a facade or router in front, carve out one capability, route traffic to it, retire that piece of the monolith, repeat.
Hybrid is justified by latency, data residency or a staged exit. Multi-cloud is justified by a specific best-of-breed or regulatory need, not by generic resilience.
Tool hubs: AWS Application Discovery Service/MGN/DMS; Azure Migrate plus Azure Database Migration Service; Google Migration Center plus Migrate to Virtual Machines and Database Migration Service.
selfCheck: I can assign one of the 7 Rs to any server in a scenario and defend it with a business constraint such as deadline, skills, licensing, ops burden or competitive value.
I can work out whether a dataset should move online or by appliance from its size, bandwidth and deadline.
I can build waves from a dependency map so that no chatty group is split across a VPN or Direct Connect link.
I can write a rollback for each wave that covers both compute (DNS or routing, with the source kept) and data (reverse replication or a data-loss rule).
I can explain how strangler fig modernises a monolith step by step, and name the routing service that acts as the facade on each cloud.
I can argue when hybrid or multi-cloud is worth its egress, tooling and skills cost, and when multi-Region on one cloud is the better answer.

objective.question: A company must move 25 Windows application servers to AWS within six weeks before its data-centre lease ends. The applications cannot be changed. Which migration strategy best fits?
options: Replatform
Repurchase
Rehost
Refactor
objective.explanation: The fastest route with no code change is Rehost (lift and shift), for example with AWS MGN. Refactor and Replatform both involve change and take longer. Repurchase replaces the application with a SaaS product, which the scenario does not ask for.

objective.question: An enterprise runs 300 VMs on vSphere. Its operations team wants to keep using vCenter and its existing VMware tooling, and wants to move to AWS quickly without converting VMs. Which R applies?
options: Relocate to VMware Cloud on AWS
Retain on premises
Replatform onto Amazon ECS
Rehost to Amazon EC2 using AWS MGN
objective.explanation: Relocate moves workloads to a cloud-hosted VMware environment, so VMware tooling and VM formats are kept. Rehost to EC2 converts the VMs, and the team loses vCenter-based operations. ECS involves changes to the workload, and Retain does not migrate anything.

objective.question: A company runs a self-hosted, heavily customised CRM. Upgrades are painful, and the business says a mainstream SaaS CRM now covers its needs. What is the most appropriate strategy?
options: Rehost
Relocate
Refactor
Repurchase
objective.explanation: Replacing an application with a SaaS product is Repurchase, sometimes called drop and shop. Refactor rewrites the existing application. Rehost and Relocate both keep the same software running in the cloud.

objective.question: A 4 TB on-premises Oracle database must move to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The allowed downtime is under 15 minutes. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Use AWS DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT for the schema, then run an AWS DMS full load with ongoing CDC replication, and cut over when lag is near zero
Use AWS MGN to replicate the Oracle server and launch it on EC2
Export to CSV, ship it on AWS Snowball Edge and import it into Aurora
Take an RMAN backup, copy it to Amazon S3 and restore it into Aurora
objective.explanation: This is a heterogeneous move, so the schema must be converted first with SCT or DMS Schema Conversion. DMS full load plus CDC then keeps the target in sync, so downtime is limited to the final switch. Aurora PostgreSQL cannot restore an RMAN backup. MGN keeps the database on Oracle. A Snowball import of a one-off export would mean long downtime.

objective.question: A company must move 500 TB of archive data to Amazon S3. Its only internet link is 100 Mbps and is already used by production traffic. What is the best option?
options: AWS Snow Family devices
AWS DMS with CDC
Upload with the AWS CLI using multipart upload
AWS DataSync over the existing link
objective.explanation: Even at full line rate, 500 TB over 100 Mbps takes more than a year, and the link is shared with production traffic. Offline transfer with Snow Family devices is the right choice. DataSync and the CLI both depend on the slow link. DMS is for databases, not file archives.

objective.question: A public web application's DNS record has a TTL of 86,400 seconds. Cut-over to AWS is on Saturday at 22:00. To make both the switch and any rollback take effect quickly, what should the team do?
options: Lower the TTL to 60 seconds at least 24 hours before the cut-over
Raise the TTL so resolvers cache the new record longer
Leave the TTL unchanged and use a weighted routing policy
Lower the TTL to 60 seconds at 21:55 on Saturday
objective.explanation: Resolvers keep the old 24-hour TTL until their cached copy expires. The TTL must therefore be lowered at least one old-TTL period (24 hours) before cut-over. Lowering it five minutes before has no effect on records already cached. Raising the TTL slows both the switch and a rollback. A weighted policy still suffers from the old cached TTL.

objective.question: A team is modernising a monolithic e-commerce application with the strangler-fig pattern. Which approach matches the pattern?
options: Put a routing layer, such as an API gateway or load balancer with path rules, in front of the monolith and move one capability at a time to new services
Rehost the monolith to EC2 and scale it vertically
Run two copies of the monolith in two clouds for redundancy
Freeze the monolith, rewrite everything as microservices and switch over in one release
objective.explanation: Strangler fig places a facade in front of the monolith. Traffic for each extracted capability is routed to the new service, and the monolith shrinks until it can be retired. A big-bang rewrite is the risk the pattern avoids. Rehosting and running duplicate copies are not modernisation patterns.

objective.question: Discovery data shows that an order-processing app server makes thousands of low-latency calls per minute to a SQL Server instance. The SQL Server instance is planned for wave 3, and the app server for wave 1. What should the architect do?
options: Move the database first, in its own wave, with no testing
Retire the database because it has dependencies
Move the app server and the database into the same wave, or confirm that the hybrid link's latency is acceptable before splitting them
Keep the plan and rely on a VPN between on premises and the cloud
objective.explanation: Dependency mapping exists to keep chatty, tightly coupled components together. Splitting them across a WAN link can break performance. A VPN alone does not fix the latency. Moving the database alone without testing creates the same split in reverse. Retiring a database that is in use is wrong.

objective.question: During a wave migrated with AWS MGN, the cut-over instances show data errors two days after go-live. The rollback window is still open. What makes rollback simplest, and when may the source servers be decommissioned?
options: Rebuild the source servers from backups; decommission after the first successful test launch
Rollback is not possible with MGN; decommission after replication finishes
Point DNS back to the untouched source servers; decommission only after the stability period passes and the rollback window is formally closed
Restore from EBS snapshots; decommission the sources immediately after cut-over
objective.explanation: MGN replicates at block level without changing the source, so rollback means redirecting traffic (low TTL helps) back to the source servers. Any data written in the cloud since cut-over must still be reconciled. Sources are decommissioned only after the stability period and formal closure of the rollback window. The other options either destroy the fallback too early or are wrong about MGN.

objective.question: A company runs 200 VMware VMs on-premises and plans to move them to Azure. Before it builds wave plans, it needs an inventory, agentless dependency data, right-sized Azure VM recommendations and monthly cost estimates. Which service should the architect use first?
options: Azure Migrate: Discovery and assessment, using the Azure Migrate appliance
Azure Database Migration Service in offline mode
Azure Advisor cost recommendations on the target subscription
Azure Site Recovery, configured with replication to a recovery vault
objective.explanation: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment tool uses an on-premises appliance. It collects inventory, performance data and agentless dependency data, then produces right-sized, costed assessments. Site Recovery replicates workloads but does not assess them. Advisor only analyses resources already in Azure, and DMS migrates databases rather than discovering servers.

objective.question: A team is strangling a monolith that runs behind an Application Load Balancer. The listener's default action forwards to the monolith target group. The team runs the command below. What is the effect, and what is the fastest rollback if the new service misbehaves?

code.code:
aws elbv2 create-rule \
  --listener-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:ap-south-1:111122223333:listener/app/shop-alb/abc/def \
  --priority 10 \
  --conditions Field=path-pattern,Values='/api/orders/*' \
  --actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:ap-south-1:111122223333:targetgroup/orders-svc/123

options: Requests matching /api/orders/* go to orders-svc and everything else still reaches the monolith. Roll back by deleting or modifying the rule.
The rule takes effect only after the monolith target group is deregistered. Roll back by re-registering it.
Requests for /api/orders/* are mirrored to both target groups. Roll back by disabling mirroring.
All traffic moves to orders-svc. Roll back by redeploying the monolith.
objective.explanation: A path-pattern rule sends only the matching requests to the new target group, while the default action keeps serving all other paths from the monolith. This is a classic strangler-fig facade. Removing the rule, or pointing it back at the monolith target group, reverses the change immediately. ALB listener rules forward traffic; they do not mirror it.

objective.question: A company adopted multi-cloud. Its transactional application and data run on AWS, but the analytics team runs BigQuery jobs that pull about 60 TB a month from Amazon S3. The cloud bill shows a large data-transfer-out charge. There is no regulatory reason for the split. What is the most cost-effective change?
options: Add a second VPN tunnel between AWS and Google Cloud to double the bandwidth
Compress data with gzip and keep the same cross-cloud architecture
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket
Co-locate analytics with the data, either by running it on AWS or by moving the data platform wholly to Google Cloud, so bulk data does not cross clouds
objective.explanation: Egress charges come from moving data out of one cloud into another. Removing the bulk cross-cloud flow is the only fix that addresses the root cause. Extra VPN tunnels add bandwidth and cost, not savings. Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads into S3 and is billed on top. Compression helps only at the margin.

objective.question: A company is using Google Cloud Migrate to Virtual Machines to move VMware VMs to Compute Engine. The application owners want to validate each migrated VM in an isolated VPC before the real cut-over, without stopping the source VM or the ongoing replication. Which step should the engineer use?
options: Export a disk image with gcloud compute images export and boot it manually
Create a test clone from the latest replicated data into a test VPC
Take a snapshot of the source VM in vCenter and copy it to Cloud Storage
Run a cut-over, then delete the target VM if testing fails
objective.explanation: Migrate to Virtual Machines supports test clones. A test clone builds a Compute Engine VM from replicated data while the source keeps running and replication continues. A cut-over shuts down the source and finalises the migration, so it is not a test step. The other two options are manual workarounds that bypass the replication workflow.

objective.question: An architect is choosing applications for the first wave of a 40-server migration. The organisation has never run production workloads in the cloud. Which set of applications is the best choice for wave 1?
options: A small number of low-criticality, loosely coupled apps with few dependencies and an owner who is willing to test
All database servers, so that later application waves find their data already in the cloud
Every server in one data-centre rack, so that the rack can be powered off early
The ERP system and its database, because they deliver the largest cost saving
objective.explanation: A pilot wave should be low-risk. Its purpose is to prove the landing zone, network, runbook, monitoring and rollback before critical systems move. Starting with the ERP adds business risk while the process is still unproven. Grouping by rack ignores application dependencies. Moving databases first splits chatty app-to-database traffic across the WAN.

objective.question: A team is preparing the cut-over of a rehosted web application. Which order of steps is correct?
options: Switch DNS → lower DNS TTL → freeze writes and run final sync → smoke-test → decommission the source → monitor
Launch cut-over instances → switch DNS → decommission the source → lower DNS TTL → freeze writes → final sync
Freeze writes → decommission the source → launch cut-over instances → switch DNS → lower DNS TTL → monitor
Lower DNS TTL days ahead → freeze writes and run final sync → launch cut-over instances and smoke-test → switch DNS → monitor during the rollback window → decommission the source
objective.explanation: The TTL must drop well before cut-over so that resolver caches expire, and the final sync happens only after writes are frozen. The source is decommissioned last, after the rollback window closes. The other sequences either switch traffic before the data is consistent or destroy the rollback path early.

objective.question: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) shows a newly installed source server stuck in 'Initiating replication'. The agent registered with the service successfully. The on-premises firewall allows only outbound TCP 443. What is the most likely cause?
options: The IAM role for the launch template is missing EC2 permissions
The target subnet in the launch settings has no internet gateway
The source server's DNS TTL is too high
The source server cannot reach the replication servers in the staging subnet on TCP 1500
objective.explanation: The MGN agent uses TCP 443 to talk to the service endpoint, which is why registration worked. It sends replicated data to the replication servers on TCP 1500, so blocking that port stalls replication. Launch-template and target-subnet settings only matter when instances are launched, and DNS TTL has no role in replication.

objective.question: A 2 TB MySQL database must move to Amazon RDS for MySQL with under 10 minutes of downtime. An engineer creates the AWS DMS task below. What is wrong?

code.code:
aws dms create-replication-task \
  --replication-task-identifier orders-migration \
  --source-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:ap-south-1:111122223333:endpoint:SRC \
  --target-endpoint-arn arn:aws:dms:ap-south-1:111122223333:endpoint:TGT \
  --replication-instance-arn arn:aws:dms:ap-south-1:111122223333:rep:RI1 \
  --migration-type full-load \
  --table-mappings file://mappings.json

options: The task must use the cdc migration type only, because a full load is not supported for MySQL
The task is missing a --schema-conversion flag
Nothing is wrong. A full load of 2 TB always finishes in under 10 minutes
The migration type should be full-load-and-cdc, so ongoing changes replicate until the cut-over
objective.explanation: A full-load-only task copies a snapshot, so the source must stay frozen for the whole copy, which far exceeds 10 minutes. With full-load-and-cdc, DMS keeps the target in sync through change data capture until the final short cut-over. DMS has no schema-conversion flag; schema conversion is done with DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT.

objective.question: A company must copy 20 TB of NFS file data to Amazon EFS. It has a 1 Gbps link with spare capacity. Files keep changing during the two-week migration, and the team needs scheduled incremental syncs with integrity checks before cut-over. Which service fits best?
options: AWS Snowball Edge
AWS Application Migration Service
AWS Transfer Family
AWS DataSync with an agent on-premises
objective.explanation: DataSync copies data over the network, runs scheduled incremental transfers, verifies integrity and supports NFS sources and EFS targets. Snowball suits cases where bandwidth is insufficient, which is not true here. Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTPS endpoints for partners, and MGN replicates whole servers, not file shares.

objective.question: A new Billing service is being strangled out of a monolith. It must read customer records from the monolith, whose data model is old and inconsistent. The team does not want that model to leak into the new service's design. Which pattern should it add?
options: A shared database schema used by both the monolith and the new service
A big-bang rewrite of the customer module first
Two-phase commit across the monolith and the new service
An anti-corruption layer that translates between the monolith's model and the new service's model
objective.explanation: An anti-corruption layer isolates the new service from the legacy model by translating requests and data at the boundary. A shared schema couples both systems tightly. A big-bang rewrite defeats incremental strangling, and two-phase commit adds coupling without solving the model problem.

objective.question: A manufacturer wants to run an AWS-based control application in its factory. It needs single-digit-millisecond latency to on-site machines, and production data must stay on the premises. Developers want the same AWS APIs and tooling they use in the Region. What should the architect recommend?
options: A Site-to-Site VPN to the nearest Region
Rehosting the application to EC2 in the nearest Region
Multi-Region deployment across two AWS Regions
AWS Outposts racks installed in the factory
objective.explanation: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure and APIs on-premises, which meets both the local-latency and the data-residency requirements. Multi-Region, VPN and in-Region EC2 all place processing and data off-site and add network latency.

objective.question: A bank runs a core application on a mainframe that it upgraded last year. A regulator must approve any change to the platform, and the approval process takes over a year. Which R should the migration plan assign to it for now?
options: Retire
Repurchase
Rehost
Retain
objective.explanation: Retain fits workloads that cannot move yet because of recent investment, compliance or business constraints; they are revisited later. The application is still needed, so Retire is wrong. Rehost and Repurchase both need the regulatory change that is not yet possible.

objective.question: After an AWS MGN cut-over, a rehosted engineering application fails to start with the error 'License invalid for this machine'. The binaries and data replicated correctly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The security group blocks inbound TCP 1500
The instance was launched in the wrong Availability Zone
The EBS volumes were replicated with the wrong volume type
The licence is bound to a hardware identifier such as the MAC address, which changed on the new EC2 instance
objective.explanation: Rehosting changes hardware identifiers such as MAC addresses, so node-locked licences often fail. Discovery should flag these licences so the team can rehost the licence or move to a licence server or BYOL terms. The volume type and Availability Zone do not invalidate licences, and port 1500 is only used for replication.

objective.question: A team uses Google Cloud Database Migration Service to run a continuous migration of MySQL to Cloud SQL. Replication lag is near zero, and writes to the source are now stopped. Which action makes the Cloud SQL instance the standalone, writable primary?
options: Restart the Cloud SQL instance
Create a read replica of the source
Delete the connection profile
Promote the migration job
objective.explanation: Promoting a continuous migration job ends replication from the source and turns the destination Cloud SQL instance into a standalone primary. Deleting the connection profile or restarting the instance does not stop replication, and adding a read replica of the source does nothing for the target.

objective.question: An application runs on Tomcat with a self-managed MySQL server. The team wants to cut patching and backup work during migration but can make only configuration-level changes, not code changes. Which option is the better fit?
options: Rehost both servers to EC2 with AWS MGN
Refactor the application into Lambda functions with DynamoDB
Repurchase a SaaS product
Replatform to AWS Elastic Beanstalk (Tomcat platform) and Amazon RDS for MySQL
objective.explanation: Replatforming to managed runtimes removes OS and database operations while needing only configuration changes such as connection strings. A rehost keeps all the patching and backup work. Refactoring needs code changes, and there is no SaaS product that matches a custom application.

subjective.question: List the 7 Rs of migration and give the one-line decision signal for each.
subjective.answer: In AWS terms, the 7 Rs are as follows. Retire: the application is unused or duplicated, so switch it off. Retain: keep it where it is for now, because of compliance, a recent hardware refresh or an unresolved dependency. Rehost (lift and shift): move as is, with no code change; use it when speed matters most. Relocate: move a VMware estate to a cloud VMware service, such as VMware Cloud on AWS, and keep the tooling. Replatform (lift, tinker and shift): make a small change to reduce operations work, for example moving a self-managed database to Amazon RDS. Repurchase: replace the application with SaaS. Refactor: re-architect, often as cloud-native or serverless, when you need scale or agility and code change is accepted. In exams, match the keywords. 'Fastest, no change' means Rehost. 'Keep VMware' means Relocate. 'Less ops, minor change' means Replatform. 'SaaS' means Repurchase. 'Agility, code change' means Refactor.
keyPoints: Names all seven: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Replatform, Repurchase, Refactor
Links each R to a clear trigger or keyword
Gives concrete examples (MGN, VMware Cloud on AWS, RDS, SaaS)
Notes the effort and benefit trade-off from Rehost to Refactor

subjective.question: How do Retire and Retain differ, and how does discovery help you find candidates for each?
subjective.answer: Retire means switching an application off because it no longer delivers value. Retain means keeping it on premises for now, with a planned review date. Discovery provides the evidence for both. Utilisation and connection data from tools such as AWS Application Discovery Service, Azure Migrate or Google Cloud Migration Center show servers with near-zero CPU, no inbound connections or no recent logins. These are retire candidates, once the business owner confirms. Retain candidates include systems under data-residency rules, mainframes or appliances that cannot move yet, servers with recently bought hardware, and applications waiting on a vendor licence change. Retiring even 10–20% of an estate cuts migration effort and run cost. Retain is not 'forget about it': record the reason and set a date to revisit, because a retained system often becomes a hybrid dependency.
keyPoints: Retire means decommission; Retain means keep for now, with a stated reason
Low utilisation and zero connections point to retire candidates
Owner sign-off is needed before retiring
Common retain reasons: compliance, hardware not yet depreciated, unresolved dependency
Retained systems may create hybrid connectivity needs

subjective.question: Give a practical Replatform example and explain why you might choose it over Refactor.
subjective.answer: A typical example is a Java application on Tomcat with a self-managed MySQL server. Rehost the app tier to EC2 or containers with no code change. Move the database to Amazon RDS for MySQL or Aurora MySQL, changing only the connection string. Patching, backups, Multi-AZ failover and minor version upgrades then become managed tasks. The equivalent on Azure is Azure Database for MySQL, and on Google Cloud it is Cloud SQL. I would choose Replatform when the main pain is operations work rather than the application design. It needs little code change and little testing, and it delivers savings quickly. Refactor makes sense when the business needs elastic scale, faster releases or new features that the current architecture blocks. It costs months of engineering. A common path is to replatform now and refactor selected parts later with the strangler-fig pattern.
keyPoints: Concrete example: self-managed database to a managed database service
Only minor change, such as configuration or a connection string
Benefit: lower ops work (patching, backups, HA)
Refactor is justified only by scale or agility needs
Replatform first, then refactor later, is a valid sequence

subjective.question: Describe how you would run discovery and dependency mapping, and name the native tools on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
subjective.answer: First, I build an inventory from the CMDB and virtualisation platform, then verify it with automated discovery. Agentless collectors give configuration and utilisation data. Agents add process and network-connection data, which is what reveals real dependencies. I collect data over a representative period, including month-end, so batch jobs and peak loads appear. I then map which servers talk to each other, on which ports, and how often. I group tightly coupled servers into move groups and tag each one with an owner, business criticality and a proposed R. Tools: on AWS, AWS Application Discovery Service feeding AWS Migration Hub, within the Assess phase. On Azure, Azure Migrate is the central hub for discovery, assessment and migration, including dependency analysis. On Google Cloud, Migration Center handles discovery and assessment, including cost estimates. The output drives right-sizing, the business case and wave planning.
keyPoints: Verify the CMDB with automated discovery; agents capture network dependencies
Collect over a representative period, including peaks and batch jobs
Group tightly coupled servers into move groups
Tools: Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub, Azure Migrate, Migration Center
Output feeds right-sizing, the business case and waves

subjective.question: You must migrate 40 on-premises servers in three waves, with a rollback for each wave. Outline your plan.
subjective.answer: After discovery, every server gets an R and a reason. For example, retire 5 idle servers, retain 3 for compliance, repurchase the CRM, replatform the databases, and rehost most of the rest. Wave 1 (pilot): 8–10 low-risk, loosely coupled servers, such as internal tools and dev and test. Rehost them with MGN or Azure Migrate. Rollback: sources stay untouched, so repoint DNS back. Wave 2: mid-criticality application groups moved together with their dependencies, plus replatformed databases using DMS with CDC. Rollback: the source database stays live. Plan reverse replication, or reconcile data written after cut-over, then switch DNS back. Wave 3: business-critical systems, in a change window. Rollback: a tested runbook, clear go/no-go criteria and a decision deadline. For every wave: lower DNS TTLs in advance, run test launches, set an owner sign-off and a stability period. Decommission sources only after the rollback window formally closes. Lessons from each wave feed into the next.
keyPoints: Each server has an R and a reason, including retire and retain
Pilot wave of low-risk servers first; critical systems last
Dependent servers move in the same wave
Wave-specific rollback: untouched source, DNS switch-back, data reconciliation or reverse replication
Go/no-go criteria, stability period, and delayed decommissioning

subjective.question: Walk through a cut-over runbook for a rehosted web application.
subjective.answer: Days before: replication is healthy and lag is low. Test instances have been launched and validated by the application owner. DNS TTL is lowered to around 60 seconds, at least one old-TTL period earlier. A change window is approved, and the go/no-go criteria and rollback trigger are written down. Cut-over: announce the freeze, then stop writes or stop the application on the source. Wait for final replication sync and launch the cut-over instances with MGN or the equivalent tool. Run smoke tests for login, key transactions, integrations and monitoring. Switch DNS or the load balancer to the new target. Watch error rates and latency. Go/no-go: if the criteria fail before the deadline, roll back. Point DNS back to the untouched source and restart it. After cut-over: hypercare, backups configured, cost tags applied. Close the rollback window formally, then decommission the source.
keyPoints: Validated test launch and healthy replication before the window
TTL lowered well in advance
Freeze writes, final sync, then smoke tests
Explicit go/no-go criteria with a time-boxed rollback decision
Hypercare and formal closure before decommissioning

subjective.question: Explain the strangler-fig pattern and the main pitfalls when applying it to a monolith.
subjective.answer: Strangler fig modernises a monolith gradually. First, put a facade in front of it, such as an API gateway, reverse proxy or load balancer with path-based rules. All traffic goes through the facade. Then pick one bounded capability, for example product search, build it as a new service, and route only its paths to that service. Repeat this until the monolith handles nothing and can be retired. Each step is small, testable and reversible by changing a route. Pitfalls: first, the shared database. If the new service still writes to the monolith's tables, you have not decoupled anything. Give the service its own data and sync it with events or CDC during transition. Second, choosing a first slice that is too tangled; start with something well bounded. Third, the facade becoming a single point of failure or a bottleneck. Fourth, never finishing, which leaves you paying for both systems. Track progress and retire code as you go.
keyPoints: The facade or routing layer intercepts all traffic
Extract one bounded capability at a time; rollback is a route change
Shared database coupling is the main pitfall
The facade must be highly available
Finish the job to avoid paying for two systems

subjective.question: When do hybrid and multi-cloud architectures genuinely help, and when do they only add cost?
subjective.answer: Hybrid helps when some systems must stay on premises for data residency, latency to factory equipment or mainframes, or during a multi-year migration. It also helps when you need steady connectivity through Direct Connect, ExpressRoute or Cloud Interconnect. Multi-cloud helps when there is a specific reason. Examples are a best-of-breed service on one provider, a regulatory demand for exit capability, an acquisition that arrives on another cloud, or customer requirements. It mostly adds cost when chosen as a vague 'avoid lock-in' or 'resilience' strategy. You pay for duplicated skills, tooling, security controls, egress charges, interconnect links, and lowest-common-denominator designs that avoid managed services. For resilience, multi-Region within one provider is usually simpler and cheaper. Good practice: pick a primary cloud, use others for clear reasons, and standardise identity, policy, observability and IaC across them.
keyPoints: Valid hybrid drivers: residency, latency, long migrations
Valid multi-cloud drivers: specific services, regulation, mergers and acquisitions
Hidden costs: skills, egress, duplicated tooling, lowest-common-denominator design
Multi-Region on one provider is usually better for resilience
Standardise identity, policy and IaC if multi-cloud is used

subjective.question: How would you migrate a large production database with minimal downtime, and how would you keep a rollback option?
subjective.answer: First, I decide whether the move is homogeneous, such as MySQL to RDS MySQL, or heterogeneous, such as Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL. For heterogeneous moves, I convert the schema and code objects with AWS SCT or DMS Schema Conversion and fix any items it flags. Next, I run an AWS DMS full load followed by ongoing replication with change data capture, so the target stays in sync while the source stays live. I validate row counts and data, and test the application against the target. At cut-over, I stop writes on the source, wait for CDC lag to reach zero, switch connection strings or DNS, and reopen. For rollback, the source remains intact. To avoid losing writes made after cut-over, I can set up replication from the new target back to the old source, or plan a reconciliation step. If the data set is huge and the link slow, I seed it with Snow Family and catch up with CDC.
keyPoints: Distinguishes homogeneous from heterogeneous; SCT or DMS Schema Conversion for the latter
DMS full load plus CDC keeps downtime small
Validate data and test the application before cut-over
Rollback via an intact source plus reverse replication or reconciliation
Offline seeding with Snow Family when bandwidth is insufficient

subjective.question: After wave 1 is rehosted to AWS, users report that an invoicing application takes 8 seconds per page, compared with 1 second on-premises. CPU and memory on the new EC2 instances are low. How would you troubleshoot this, and how would you prevent it in later waves?
subjective.answer: Low CPU combined with high latency points to network waits, not compute. I would check VPC Flow Logs and the application's connection strings for traffic that still flows back on-premises over the VPN or Direct Connect link. Common causes are a hard-coded IP for a file share, an LDAP server, a licence server or a database that was left behind. Each call now pays WAN round-trip time, and chatty protocols multiply that delay. The quick fix is to move the dependency into the same wave, add a caching tier, or put a replica in the cloud. For later waves, I would run agent-based dependency mapping for long enough to capture month-end jobs. I would group tightly coupled servers into the same wave, and audit configuration for hard-coded IPs and hostnames. I would also make a performance baseline comparison a go/no-go criterion in the cut-over runbook, so that a problem like this triggers rollback rather than surfacing as a user complaint.
keyPoints: Low CPU plus high latency suggests network or dependency waits
Find cross-WAN calls using flow logs and configuration review
Move dependencies together or add caching or replicas
Longer dependency mapping and hard-coded IP audits for future waves
Make performance baselines a go/no-go criterion

subjective.question: Review this extract from a wave plan. Identify the problems and explain how you would fix them before approval.

code.code:
wave: 2
window: 2026-03-14T22:00+05:30
servers:
  - name: web-01
    strategy: rehost
    depends_on: [app-02]
  - name: app-02
    strategy: replatform   # to managed runtime
    wave_override: 3
  - name: sql-01
    strategy: refactor
    reason: ""
  - name: fax-gw
    strategy: rehost
    note: "last used 2023"
rollback: "restore from backup if needed"
dns_ttl: 86400

subjective.answer: First, web-01 depends on app-02, but app-02 is overridden into wave 3. That would split a dependency across the WAN, so the two servers should move together or the dependency should be removed. Second, sql-01 has no reason recorded. That fails the checkpoint, and refactoring a database server is rarely the right R; replatforming to a managed database is more usual. Third, fax-gw has not been used since 2023, so it is a Retire candidate after the owner signs off, not a Rehost. Fourth, the rollback line is vague. It should name the trigger criteria, the decision owner, a time limit, and the exact steps, such as repointing DNS to the still-running source servers. It should also say how data written after cut-over will be reconciled. Finally, a TTL of 86,400 seconds makes any switch slow, so the TTL should be lowered to about 60 seconds at least a day before the window.
keyPoints: Dependency split across waves 2 and 3
Missing reason for sql-01, and Refactor is doubtful for a database server
Unused server fax-gw should be Retired
Rollback needs triggers, an owner, a time limit, steps and data reconciliation
Lower the DNS TTL well before cut-over

subjective.question: A company wants to move 30 on-premises SQL Server instances to Azure. Some use SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries and linked servers. A few depend on OS-level components. How would you choose between Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs, and which R does each represent?
subjective.answer: I would start with an Azure Migrate assessment for Azure SQL. It reports compatibility blockers and right-sizing for each target. SQL Server on an Azure VM is a Rehost. It gives full OS and instance control, so it suits databases that depend on OS-level components or unsupported features, but we keep patching work. Azure SQL Managed Instance is a Replatform. It offers near-complete instance compatibility, including SQL Agent, cross-database queries and linked servers, while Azure handles patching, backups and high availability. That makes it the natural home for most of these instances. Azure SQL Database is also a managed Replatform target, but it is database-scoped. Cross-database queries and SQL Agent need changes there, so it fits new or simple, self-contained databases. For cost, I would apply Azure Hybrid Benefit where Software Assurance licences exist. For the move itself, I would use online migration through the Azure SQL migration extension to keep downtime low.
keyPoints: Use an Azure Migrate assessment to find blockers and sizing
SQL on a VM is Rehost: full control, more operational work
Managed Instance is Replatform: instance-level compatibility, managed operations
SQL Database is database-scoped and may need code changes
Azure Hybrid Benefit and online migration reduce cost and downtime

subjective.question: Three months after a lift-and-shift, the CFO says the cloud bill is higher than the on-premises business case predicted. What are the likely causes, and what FinOps actions would you take?
subjective.answer: The usual cause is that servers were sized to match on-premises hardware, not their real use, so many instances are oversized and run 24x7. Other causes include dev and test machines that never stop, unattached disks and old snapshots, premium storage tiers used everywhere, and data transfer or NAT gateway charges that the business case missed. Licences can also be charged twice when BYOL was not applied. My actions would be as follows. First, enforce tagging so that every cost has an owner. Second, right-size using utilisation data from tools such as AWS Compute Optimizer or Azure Advisor. Third, schedule non-production machines to shut down outside office hours. Fourth, clean up orphaned storage. Fifth, buy Savings Plans, reservations or committed-use discounts only after right-sizing, to cover the steady baseline. Sixth, apply licence benefits such as Azure Hybrid Benefit. Finally, I would set budgets and anomaly alerts, and put the next set of rehosted apps on a Replatform backlog so they can move to managed or autoscaled services.
keyPoints: On-premises sizing copied 1:1 and machines running 24x7
Hidden costs: storage, snapshots, egress, NAT, licences
Tagging and cost ownership come first
Right-size before buying commitments
Budgets, anomaly alerts and a Replatform backlog

subjective.question: You are extracting an Orders service from a monolith with the strangler-fig pattern. The monolith and many of its modules read and write the same ORDERS tables in one shared database. How do you handle the data, and what can go wrong?
subjective.answer: The new service must eventually own its data, but cutting the tables over in one step is risky. I would first route all order writes through one path. That means changing the monolith to call the new Orders API, or wrapping the old module behind an interface. Next, I would give the service its own schema or database and keep the two copies in step during the transition. Change data capture, such as AWS DMS or Debezium streaming from the old tables, works well for this, with one clear direction of sync at any time. Other monolith modules that read orders should move to the API or to a read model, so they stop querying the tables directly. An anti-corruption layer translates between the old and new models. Pitfalls include dual writes without a single source of truth, which cause data divergence. Others are reporting jobs that silently read the old tables, distributed transactions that the monolith used to get for free, and the slower performance of API calls compared with in-process joins. Reconciliation checks and feature flags make rollback possible.
keyPoints: Have a single write path and a single source of truth at any time
Use a separate service database kept in step with CDC during transition
Move readers to the API or a read model, with an anti-corruption layer
Dual-write divergence, hidden readers and lost transactions are key risks
Reconciliation checks and feature flags make rollback possible

subjective.question: Case study: A retailer has 60 on-premises servers: a PCI-scoped payment gateway, a 10-year-old reporting server used by two people, a vendor ERP whose vendor now offers SaaS, Tomcat web servers, and an Oracle data warehouse. A trading freeze runs from October to December, and the data-centre contract ends in March. How would you assign Rs and sequence the waves?
subjective.answer: I would run discovery first so the choices rest on utilisation and dependency data, not opinion. The reporting server is a Retire candidate, after I confirm with its two users and archive its data. The ERP goes to Repurchase as SaaS, timed with the vendor's contract. The Tomcat servers are Replatform candidates on a managed runtime with a managed database. The data warehouse needs assessment; it could be replatformed to a managed warehouse later. To meet the March deadline, I might rehost it first and modernise afterwards. The PCI gateway needs care. I would rehost it into a dedicated, segmented PCI account and schedule a QSA review, or Retain it until after the assessment. For sequencing, I would run a low-risk pilot wave in July to September. Then I would honour the freeze with no production cut-overs from October to December. The remaining waves would run in January and February, which leaves March as buffer and keeps rollback windows open before the exit.
keyPoints: Discovery data drives each R
Retire idle servers and repurchase where SaaS fits
Change freeze respected in wave timing
PCI scope isolated and reviewed
Buffer before the data-centre exit date

subjective.question: After moving a wave of Windows servers to Azure, users see logons that take minutes, Group Policy failures and intermittent 'domain not available' errors. The domain controllers are still on-premises and connected over a site-to-site VPN. What is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: Identity is a dependency that was left behind. Every Kerberos ticket request, LDAP query and Group Policy download now crosses the VPN. When the tunnel has latency, packet loss or MTU problems, authentication slows or fails. A second cause is often DNS. If the VNet uses Azure-provided DNS instead of the domain DNS servers, the VMs cannot find domain controllers through SRV records. To fix it, I would first point the VNet's DNS settings at the domain DNS servers and check that the AD ports are open in the NSGs. Then I would deploy domain controllers in Azure as a new AD site, with subnets mapped in Sites and Services. That way the VMs authenticate locally and replication crosses the link instead of logons. I would also consider ExpressRoute for a stable link. To prevent it next time, identity and DNS belong in the landing-zone foundation before wave 1.
keyPoints: Authentication traffic crossing the VPN
VNet DNS must point to domain DNS
Azure-based domain controllers in their own AD site
Check NSG ports and VPN MTU
Identity and DNS built before the first wave

subjective.question: For a database server, compare rehosting the whole VM with AWS MGN against migrating only the data with AWS DMS to a managed service. When is each one better?
subjective.answer: MGN rehosts the whole VM by block-level replication. It is better when the database depends on OS-level customisation, uses an engine version or feature that the managed service does not support, or when the deadline leaves no time for testing. It is quick and low-risk, but you keep the patching, backups, HA setup and licences. DMS moves only the data, using a full load plus CDC, into a target such as RDS or Aurora. It is better when you want to drop operational toil, use managed Multi-AZ, or change engines. For engine changes you add schema conversion. It needs more testing of compatibility, performance and application connection strings. DMS also gives a cleaner data rollback, because a reverse CDC task can keep the old source current. My rule is to rehost when there is time pressure or a blocking dependency, and to replatform with DMS when the engine is supported and the team can test.
keyPoints: MGN replicates the whole VM and keeps the ops burden
DMS full load plus CDC into a managed target
Compatibility and testing effort
Reverse replication as a data rollback
Choice driven by deadline and dependencies

subjective.question: Put these strangler-fig steps in the correct order and justify the order: route a small percentage of traffic to the new service; identify a seam with clear boundaries; delete the old code path from the monolith; place a routing facade in front of the monolith; build the new service and shadow-test it; increase traffic to 100%.
subjective.answer: The correct order is as follows. First, place a routing facade, such as a load balancer, API gateway or reverse proxy, in front of the monolith. Initially it sends 100% of traffic to the monolith, which changes nothing but creates a control point. Second, identify a seam: a capability with clear inputs, outputs and minimal shared data, such as notifications or catalogue search. Third, build the new service and shadow-test it. Mirror real requests and compare the responses with the monolith, without affecting users. Fourth, route a small percentage of traffic, or one user segment, through the facade, and watch error rates and latency. Fifth, increase traffic in steps to 100%; rollback at any stage is just a routing change. Sixth, and only after a stable period, delete the old code path. The facade comes first because every later step depends on reversible routing. Deletion comes last because it removes the rollback.
keyPoints: Facade first as a control point
Seam chosen by clear boundaries
Shadow testing before live traffic
Gradual percentage shift with routing rollback
Old code deleted only after a stable period

subjective.question: This NGINX facade config is meant to send only the Orders API to a new service and everything else to the monolith. Find the mistakes.
subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, the default location / sends all traffic to orders_svc instead of the monolith, which in effect is a big-bang cut-over. It should be proxy_pass http://monolith. Second, the prefix /api/order is too loose. It also matches paths such as /api/orders-admin or /api/ordertracking, which may still belong to the monolith. I would use a precise prefix such as /api/orders/ with a trailing slash, or an exact or regex match, and list the routes from real access logs. Third, the config has no way to stage or roll back gradually. There is no weighted split, such as split_clients or a canary upstream, and no health checks or timeouts. A slow new service would then hang users. I would also check the data side: if both systems write orders, there must be a single owner or a sync mechanism. Finally, I would keep this config in version control so that rollback is a quick revert and reload.
keyPoints: Default route must point to the monolith
Prefix match too broad
No weighted canary or health checks
Timeouts needed
Data ownership during strangling

subjective.question: During a migration, a team must choose between a site-to-site VPN and a dedicated connection (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute or Google Cloud Interconnect). Which is better, and why?
subjective.answer: It depends on data volume, the duration of the hybrid period and latency sensitivity. A VPN can be set up in hours, costs little and is fine for a pilot wave or modest replication. But it runs over the internet, so latency and throughput vary, and each tunnel has bandwidth limits. A dedicated connection gives predictable latency and higher bandwidth, and it often lowers the per-GB egress price. Provisioning can take weeks, so it must be ordered early. During migration you usually have a hybrid phase of months, with continuous block replication, CDC streams, AD and DNS traffic, and some cross-site calls from applications in different waves. That pattern favours a dedicated link, with a VPN as backup for resilience. For a small estate, a short project or a tight budget, a VPN may be enough. Even with a dedicated link, chatty dependency groups still move together, because no link removes the round-trip latency.
keyPoints: VPN is fast to set up but has variable performance
Dedicated link gives predictable latency and bandwidth but has lead time
Replication and hybrid-period traffic size the choice
VPN as backup to the dedicated link
Dependency groups still move together

subjective.question: An AWS DMS full-load-and-cdc task finished the full load, but CDC latency keeps growing for hours, and the cut-over cannot be scheduled. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: I would split the latency into source latency and target latency using the CloudWatch metrics CDCLatencySource and CDCLatencyTarget. If source latency is high, DMS cannot read the logs fast enough. I would check source log retention, such as binlog or archive logs, network bandwidth and the load on the source. If target latency is high, applying the changes is the bottleneck. Common causes are secondary indexes, triggers or foreign keys left enabled on the target, tables without primary keys that force slow updates, large LOB columns in full LOB mode, and target instance limits. I would also check the replication instance's CPU, memory and swap; if it is undersized, I would scale it up. Fixes include adding primary keys, using limited LOB mode, enabling batch apply where suitable, disabling triggers until cut-over, and splitting large tables across tasks. The cut-over is scheduled only when latency stays near zero.
keyPoints: Separate source and target latency metrics
Log retention and network on the source side
Indexes, triggers, LOBs and missing primary keys on the target side
Size of the replication instance
Cut over only at near-zero lag

subjective.question: You are migrating Windows Server and SQL Server workloads to Azure. Compare pay-as-you-go licence-included VMs with Azure Hybrid Benefit, and explain when each makes sense.
subjective.answer: With licence-included pricing, the Windows and SQL Server licence is part of the hourly VM price. It is simple and needs no licence tracking. It suits short-lived or bursty workloads and organisations that do not own eligible licences. Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you apply existing Windows Server and SQL Server licences that have Software Assurance, or eligible subscriptions, to Azure resources. You then pay closer to the base compute rate, which can cut costs significantly on steady workloads. It also helps during migration, because licences can be used on-premises and in Azure for a limited dual-use period while waves move. The risks are compliance and tracking: you must prove eligibility and not over-assign cores. I would combine it with right-sizing and reservations or savings plans for steady machines. In the business case, I would model both options per server. Applying the benefit wrongly, or forgetting it, often explains a bill that is higher than planned.
keyPoints: Licence-included is simple and good for short-lived use
Hybrid Benefit needs Software Assurance or eligible subscriptions
Dual-use period during migration
Compliance tracking of cores
Combine with right-sizing and reservations

subjective.question: Your company, which runs on AWS, acquires a firm that runs entirely on Google Cloud. Leadership asks whether the group should now be multi-cloud or consolidate. How do you decide?
subjective.answer: This is multi-cloud by circumstance, so I would decide with data, not ideology. First, I would inventory the acquired estate and how deep it is tied to the platform. Workloads built on BigQuery, GKE and Cloud Run cost more to move than VMs do. Next, I would map the integration points between the two companies. Heavy data flows across clouds create recurring egress charges and latency. Then I would count the hidden costs of staying on both: two sets of skills, security tooling, landing zones, identity federation and compliance audits. If the products stay largely separate and the Google Cloud estate is well run, keeping it in the short term is reasonable. I would unify identity, governance, security monitoring and FinOps reporting across both clouds. If the products will merge, I would plan a consolidation using the 7 Rs, prioritising workloads with high cross-cloud traffic. In both cases, I would make a costed recommendation with a timeline, not an indefinite 'both'.
keyPoints: Inventory and depth of platform tie-in
Cross-cloud integration and egress costs
Duplicated skills, tooling and governance
Unify identity, security and FinOps if keeping both
Consolidate with the 7 Rs if products merge

subjective.question: How do you define go/no-go criteria, rollback triggers and the point of no return for a migration wave?
subjective.answer: Before the wave, I agree measurable go/no-go criteria with application owners. These include replication lag near zero, successful test cut-overs, passed smoke and user-acceptance tests, a confirmed backup, a lowered DNS TTL, and the people for the rollback on call. During and after cut-over, rollback triggers must be objective. Examples are error rate or p95 latency above an agreed threshold for a set time, failed critical transactions, data-integrity check failures, or a security issue. One named decision owner calls it, so the team does not debate at 2 a.m. The point of no return is the moment rollback becomes costly. Usually it comes when users start writing to the cloud database without reverse replication, or when the source is decommissioned. I would push it later by running reverse CDC and keeping the source powered off but intact. I would document it in the runbook so the business knowingly accepts that data written after this point is either replicated back or lost if we roll back.
keyPoints: Measurable go/no-go checklist
Objective rollback triggers with thresholds
Single decision owner
Point of no return tied to data writes and decommissioning
Reverse replication delays the point of no return

steps.overview: This final step turns everything you have learned into exam-ready judgement. You will work through the Google Professional Cloud Architect case studies, SAP-C02 multi-account, hybrid and migration scenarios, and the four AZ-305 design areas. You will then defend one full architecture to a peer. Scenario reasoning is what these exams test: choosing the option that best meets the stated business and technical requirements, not just one that works.
objectives: Analyse an official Google PCA case study and map its business and technical requirements to specific Google Cloud services.
Solve SAP-C02 scenarios on multi-account governance, hybrid connectivity and large-scale migration by eliminating options that break a stated constraint.
Design Azure solutions across the four AZ-305 areas: identity and governance, data storage, business continuity and infrastructure.
Write Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), a cost estimate and a DR plan with explicit RTO and RPO targets.
Present and defend an architecture to stakeholders in 20 minutes, then book your first exam after scoring above 80% on practice tests.

concepts.explanation: Google publishes several fictional company case studies, and part of the exam asks questions about them. Always download the current set from the official exam guide page, because Google refreshes them. Recent sets have included companies such as EHR Healthcare, Cymbal Retail, Altostrat Media and KnightMotives Automotive. Before exam day, read each one and list its business requirements, technical requirements and existing environment.

Turn every requirement sentence into a design decision. For example, 'reduce latency for global users' points to a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN. 'Minimise operational overhead' points to managed or serverless services such as Cloud Run, GKE Autopilot or Cloud SQL. 'Comply with data residency' points to Organization Policy resource location constraints. Exam answers usually hinge on one keyword like cheapest, least operational effort, fastest or most secure.

The exam has four domains. Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity is 26%, Design for New Solutions is 29%, Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions is 25%, and Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization is 20%. Questions are long and have several plausible answers. The winning answer meets every constraint with the least custom work.

AWS Organizations groups accounts into organizational units (OUs). Service control policies (SCPs) set the maximum permissions an account can have, but they never grant permissions. AWS Control Tower builds a landing zone with log archive and audit accounts and applies controls, also called guardrails. IAM Identity Center gives workforce single sign-on across accounts. AWS RAM shares resources such as Transit Gateway or subnets across accounts.

Site-to-Site VPN is quick to set up and runs over the internet using two tunnels per connection. Direct Connect gives private, consistent bandwidth but takes time to provision. A common answer is Direct Connect as primary with VPN as backup. Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-premises networks in a hub-and-spoke design. A Direct Connect gateway lets one connection reach VPCs in multiple Regions. Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints handle hybrid DNS.

The seven strategies are Retire, Retain, Rehost (lift and shift), Relocate, Replatform, Repurchase and Refactor. AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is the main rehost tool. AWS DMS migrates databases, and the Schema Conversion Tool handles heterogeneous engines. For offline bulk data, use the Snow Family or DataSync. Match the strategy to the stated deadline and skills: a tight deadline points to rehost, and 'cloud-native agility' points to refactor.

The four areas and their weights are: Design identity, governance, and monitoring solutions (25–30%), Design data storage solutions (20–25%), Design business continuity solutions (15–20%) and Design infrastructure solutions (30–35%). Typical choices include Microsoft Entra ID with Conditional Access and PIM, management groups with Azure Policy, Azure SQL versus Cosmos DB, Azure Site Recovery versus Azure Backup, and hub-spoke or Virtual WAN networking.

RTO is how long the business can be down. RPO is how much data loss it can accept. From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest, the four strategies are backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active-active. In every scenario, pick the cheapest strategy that still meets the stated RTO and RPO.

An ADR is a short document that records one significant decision. It has a title, status, context, the decision itself, options considered and consequences. ADRs show stakeholders why you chose something, not just what you chose. Interviewers often ask you to justify trade-offs in exactly this format.

Start with the business problem and the success metrics, then show the diagram at a level your audience understands. Cover security, resilience, cost and risks, and end with the decisions you need from them. Executives care about cost, risk and timelines. Engineers care about failure modes and operations.

keyFacts: SAA-C03: 65 questions, 130 minutes, USD 150, passing score 720/1000.
SAP-C02: 75 questions, 180 minutes, USD 300, passing score 750/1000. That gives you about 2.4 minutes per question, so flag long questions and come back to them.
Google Professional Cloud Architect: 50–60 questions, 2 hours, USD 200, with questions based on the case studies. Always use the case studies linked from the current official exam guide.
AZ-305: about 40–60 questions in 120 minutes. You must also hold AZ-104 (Azure Administrator Associate) to earn the Azure Solutions Architect Expert certification.
SAP-C02 weights: Organizational Complexity 26%, New Solutions 29%, Continuous Improvement 25%, Migration and Modernization 20%.
AZ-305 weights: Identity, governance and monitoring 25–30%; Data storage 20–25%; Business continuity 15–20%; Infrastructure 30–35%.
SCPs restrict permissions and never grant them. Effective permission requires both the SCP and the IAM policy to allow the action.
DR cost order, lowest to highest: backup and restore, then pilot light, then warm standby, then multi-site active-active.
Decision rule: when a question says 'least operational overhead', prefer managed or serverless services over self-managed VMs.
Readiness rule: take timed practice exams from a reputable source and book the exam only when you score consistently above 80%.

example.caption: A one-page ADR with cost and DR summary for the 20-minute presentation (an AWS retail workload)
example.code:
ADR-004: Primary database and disaster recovery for the Orders service
Status: Accepted   Date: 2026-03-10   Owner: Platform team

Context:
- Orders must survive a Region outage. Business set RTO <= 1 hour and RPO <= 5 minutes.
- The team is 4 engineers, so we want the least operational overhead.
- Traffic is mostly from India, with occasional global users.

Options considered:
1. RDS Multi-AZ plus cross-Region snapshots. Cheapest, but RPO is hours, so it fails the RPO target.
2. Aurora Global Database (primary ap-south-1, secondary ap-southeast-1). Replication lag is typically about 1 second and failover is managed.
3. Self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2 with streaming replication. High operational overhead.

Decision: Option 2, using a warm standby pattern.
- Secondary Region runs a scaled-down ECS service plus the Aurora secondary cluster.
- Route 53 failover routing with health checks points to the secondary ALB.

Consequences:
+ Meets RTO and RPO. Failover runbook is tested every quarter.
- Higher cost than backup and restore. Some Aurora engine features are limited in Global Database.

Cost view (estimate it with AWS Pricing Calculator, then track it in Cost Explorer):
- Primary Region: about 70% of monthly spend.
- DR Region (warm standby): about 20%.
- Cross-Region data transfer and backups: about 10%.

DR test: Run a game day each quarter. Measure the actual RTO and RPO and record them in the ADR log.

pitfalls: Picking an answer that works but ignores one stated constraint, such as 'without changing application code' or 'within two weeks'. Re-read the last line of each scenario.
Over-engineering DR. If the RTO is 24 hours, multi-site active-active is wrong because it is too expensive.
Thinking SCPs grant access, or that they apply to the management account. They do neither.
Studying an old set of Google case studies. Always download the current set from the official exam guide.
Confusing Azure Backup (point-in-time restore of data) with Azure Site Recovery (replication and failover of whole workloads) in business continuity questions.
Presenting only a diagram. Without ADRs, cost and a DR plan with tested RTO and RPO, stakeholders and interviewers cannot judge the trade-offs.
